questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true about renal tubular transport?
options: H+ is absorbed in proximal tubule
Amino acid is reabsorbed in proximal tubule
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Amino acid is reabsorbed in proximal tubule

Glucose and amino acids(proteins) are completely reabsorbed in the proximal tubule.

Option A: Maximum reabsorption occurs in the proximal tubule

Option B: Urea is reabsorbed and secreted. It is reabsorbed in PCT and in the collecting duct. It is secreted in the thin ascending loop of Henle.

Option C: H+ is secreted in PCT as well as in collecting ducts.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: DNA is present in which one of the organelle?
questions.explanation: In animal cells, while the vast majority of genetic material is located within the nucleus, mitochondria are unique organelles that possess their own independent DNA. This mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is typically circular and is inherited maternally. It encodes for essential proteins required for the electron transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation, which are the primary processes used to generate ATP for cellular energy. Lysosomes (Option B) are involved in intracellular digestion and waste removal but do not contain DNA. The endoplasmic reticulum (Option C) is responsible for protein and lipid synthesis but lacks its own genome. The cytoplasm (Option D) is the fluid environment of the cell where translation and glycolysis occur; while viral DNA might temporarily be present there during infection, it is not a normal site for cellular DNA storage. Mitochondrial DNA is essential for the organelle's function, and mutations in it can lead to various mitochondrial diseases affecting energy-hungry tissues like muscle and brain
questions.learning: In animal cells, while the vast majority of genetic material is located within the nucleus, mitochondria are unique organelles that possess their own independent DNA.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: During wound healing, which cells are the first to migrate to the site of injury in response to chemotaxis?
questions.explanation: The inflammatory phase of wound healing is initiated immediately following injury. Neutrophils are the first leukocytes to be recruited to the site of a wound via chemotaxis, typically arriving within the first 6 to 24 hours. Their primary roles are to phagocytize bacteria and debris and to release proteases that clear the area for future tissue repair. Monocytes (Option B) and their tissue-mature form, macrophages (Option C), arrive later, usually predominating by 48 to 72 hours; they are considered the "orchestrators" of the later stages of healing. Lymphocytes (Option D) participate in the chronic inflammatory phase or in specific immune responses but are not the early responders. Because neutrophils are the quintessential "acute" inflammatory cells designed for rapid response to tissue damage and potential infection, they are definitively the first cells to appear
questions.learning: The inflammatory phase of wound healing is initiated immediately following injury. Neutrophils are the first leukocytes to be recruited to the site of a wound via chemotaxis, typically arriving within the first 6 to 24 hours.

questions.text: A person has been consuming contaminated bajra (pearl millet) for a prolonged period. Which of the following toxins is responsible for the resulting food adulteration–related disease?

Correct answer: C. Ergot toxin

Consumption of bajra (pearl millet) contaminated with Claviceps species leads to ergotism, caused by ergot alkaloids. Ergotism has historically been called “St. Anthony’s fire.”

Sources-

Ergot toxins produce vasoconstriction and neurotoxic effects, resulting in manifestations such as gangrene, convulsions, and paresthesia.

Other toxins like BOAA (lathyrism), sanguinarine (epidemic dropsy), and Fusarium toxins are linked to different staple foods and clinical syndromes.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following hormones is responsible for gallbladder contraction and release of bile into duodenum?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cholecystokinin

Cholecystokinin (CCK) is a hormone secreted by the I cells of the duodenum and jejunum in response to fatty acids and amino acids in the intestinal lumen. It is the principal hormone responsible for gallbladder contraction and relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi, facilitating the release of bile into the duodenum for fat digestion.

• Secretin: Stimulates bicarbonate-rich secretion from the pancreas and bile ducts; does not cause gallbladder contraction.
• Gastrin: Stimulates gastric acid secretion and gastric mucosal growth.
• Cholecystokinin (CCK): Contracts the gallbladder, relaxes the sphincter of Oddi, stimulates enzyme-rich pancreatic secretion, and slows gastric emptying.
• Vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP): Relaxes gastrointestinal smooth muscle and increases intestinal water and electrolyte secretion.
questions.learning: Cholecystokinin Cholecystokinin (CCK) is a hormone secreted by the I cells of the duodenum and jejunum in response to fatty acids and amino acids in the intestinal lumen.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A primi presented to the hospital in active labor and was found to be HIV positive. She is not on any antiretroviral therapy. According to the NACO guidelines, what is the minimum prophylactic antiretroviral therapy to be started in the neonate after birth?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Nevirapine + zidovudine 6 weeks

A baby born to an HIV-positive mother who is not on ART is classified as a high-risk infant. The recommended minimum ARV prophylaxis is syrup nevirapine + syrup zidovudine from birth to 6 weeks. For exclusively breastfed infants, this is extended till 12 weeks.

According to the National AIDS Control Organization (NACO), antiretroviral therapy (ART) should be given to all pregnant women, including during labor hours and breastfeeding. They are started on a triple-drug ART. ART should be given irrespective of the CD4 count, and clinical stage and should be continued lifelong.

Exclusive breastfeeding (EBF) is recommended for all HIV-exposed infants. At 6 months of age, these infants should be offered complementary foods along with breast milk.

Infants should receive ARV prophylaxis. A single drug or dual drug regimen is followed depending on the risk of transmission which can be low or high risk.

* Low-risk infants are those born to mothers with a low viral load which is detected after 32 weeks of pregnancy till delivery.

* High-risk infants are those born to HIV-positive mothers, not on ART, with viral load not estimated beyond 32 weeks, maternal viral load not suppressed after 32 weeks, or mothers newly diagnosed with HIV within 6 weeks of delivery.

HIV Risk
ARV prophylaxis
Duration

Low-risk infants
Syrup nevirapine or zidovudine

Birth to 6 weeks of age irrespective of feeding

High-risk infants
Syrup nevirapine + syrup zidovudine

• Exclusive replacement feeding: Birth to 6 weeks
• Exclusive breastfeeding: Birth till 12 weeks
questions.learning: Nevirapine + zidovudine 6 weeks — A baby born to an HIV-positive mother who is not on ART is classified as a high-risk infant. The recommended minimum ARV prophylaxis is syrup nevirapine + syrup zidovudine from birth to 6 weeks.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A middle-aged man complains of very early ejaculation during intercourse. What is the non-pharmacological management that can be advised to the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Squeeze technique

The clinical scenario of ejaculation very early on vaginal penetration is suggestive of premature ejaculation (PE), and the squeeze technique is a non-pharmacological management (behavioral method) used to prevent it.

PE is a disorder of the orgasm phase of the normal sexual cycle.

In premature ejaculation, there is a persistent or recurrent achievement of orgasm and ejaculation before the patient actually wishes to. According to DSM-5, it is classified as follows:

• Mild if ejaculation occurs within approximately 30 seconds to 1 minute of vaginal penetration
• Moderate if ejaculation occurs within approximately 15 to 30 seconds of vaginal penetration
• Severe if ejaculation occurs at the start of sexual activity or within approximately 15 seconds of vaginal penetration.

Pharmacologic therapy when combined with behavioral treatment appears to be more effective in treating premature ejaculation.

The squeeze technique is a behavioral method used on the penis to prevent premature ejaculation. Here, the penis is stimulated until just before orgasm after which it is gently squeezed.

Other options:

Option A: Although Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) can be beneficial for some patients with sexual dysfunction. It is not a specific technique for managing PE. Instead, CBT is more useful in addressing underlying psychological issues or relationship problems that may contribute to the condition. CBT is used in the treatment of depression, phobia, anxiety and panic disorders, OCD, personality disorders, and somatoform disorders.

Option B: Exposure and response prevention therapy is a strategy within CBT that is effective in the management of OCD. It is also useful in other conditions like tics but is not a suitable method for managing premature ejaculation.

Option D: Sensate focus therapy is a couple-oriented sex therapy that involves the exchange of sensual touch between partners to alleviate anxiety and negativity associated with sex and to build better sexual intimacy and communication. It does not specifically address the issue of premature ejaculation like the squeeze technique does and is hence not useful.
questions.learning: Squeeze technique — The clinical scenario of ejaculation very early on vaginal penetration is suggestive of premature ejaculation (PE), and the squeeze technique is a non-pharmacological management (behavioral method) used to prevent it.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman receives neo-adjuvant chemotherapy for invasive ductal carcinoma. Clinical assessment shows that the tumor has shrunk to 3 cm on mammography with no nodal involvement or metastasis. Which of the following accurately represents the current staging?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. уT2N0M0

Breast cancer staging uses TNM categories, and the stage can be modified with prefixes that indicate when and how the staging assessment was performed. This becomes especially important after neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NACT), because treatment alters tumor size and nodal status.

Prefix “y” is used when the TNM stage is assessed after neoadjuvant therapy (chemotherapy, endocrine therapy, targeted therapy, etc.

So, in this patient:

• Tumor has shrunk to 3 cm → T2 (>2 cm and ≤5 cm)
• No nodal involvement → N0
• No metastasis → M0
• Assessed after NACT → prefix y

Therefore, the correct staging is yT2N0M0 (Option B)

Key prefixes (high yield):

• cTNM = clinical stage (before any definitive treatment; based on exam/imaging/biopsy)
• pTNM = pathologic stage (after surgery)
• yTNM = stage assessed after neoadjuvant therapy
• rTNM = stage at recurrence/restaging after a disease-free interval
• aTNM = stage determined at autopsy
questions.learning: уT2N0M0 Breast cancer staging uses TNM categories, and the stage can be modified with prefixes that indicate when and how the staging assessment was performed.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the subsequent conditions is Bone Anchored Hearing Aid (BAHA) implemented?
questions.explanation: A Bone Anchored Hearing Aid (BAHA) is a specialized device that bypasses the external and middle ear by transmitting sound vibrations directly through the skull bone to the functioning inner ear (cochlea). It is primarily indicated for patients with significant conductive or mixed hearing loss where conventional hearing aids cannot be worn. Congenital external auditory atresia (Option C), where the ear canal is absent or closed, is a classic indication for BAHA because a traditional aid cannot be inserted. Standard sensorineural hearing loss (Option A) is typically managed with conventional aids or cochlear implants. Acoustic neuroma (Option B) usually requires surgery or radiosurgery. Otitis media (Option D) is generally managed medically or with ventilation tubes. While chronic otitis media with persistent discharge might eventually necessitate a BAHA, the structural anatomical absence of the canal makes it the most definitive implemented condition
questions.learning: A Bone Anchored Hearing Aid (BAHA) is a specialized device that bypasses the external and middle ear by transmitting sound vibrations directly through the skull bone to the functioning inner ear (cochlea).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the marked structure in the endoscopic image of nasopharynx.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fossa of Rossenmuller

The structure marked in the image is the Fossa of Rossenmuller.

Fossa of Rossenmuller is the most common site for carcinoma in the nasopharynx.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma:

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma usually originates from the nasopharynx in the fossa of Rossenmuller. It presents with the following symptoms:

* Nasal- Nasal obstruction due to blockage of the choana or the nasal cavity, denasal speech, nasal discharge, epistaxis.

* Otologic- Obstruction of the eustachian tube leads to unilateral conductive hearing loss, serous or suppurative otitis media.

* Ophthalmologic- These symptoms occur due to the involvement of cranial nerves.

* Squint and diplopia- involvement of cranial nerve VI.

* Facial pain and reduced corneal reflex- cranial nerve V.

* Exophthalmos and blindness- cranial nerve II.

* Cervical node metastasis- Usually between the angle of the jaw and the mastoid.

* Distant metastasis- to bone, liver, lung, etc.

The treatment of choice for nasopharyngeal carcinoma:

* Radiotherapy for stages I and II.

* Radiotherapy + chemotherapy for stages III and IV.

* Radical neck dissection can be done in case of recurrent or residual disease.
questions.learning: Fossa of Rossenmuller — The structure marked in the image is the Fossa of Rossenmuller. Fossa of Rossenmuller is the most common site for carcinoma in the nasopharynx.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · Integrated Gi Hpb
questions.text: The serologic marker detectable during the ‘window’ period of hepatitis B infection is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anti-HBc IgM

The window period of hepatitis B infection is the interval when HBsAg has disappeared but anti-HBs has not yet appeared. During this period, the only reliable serological marker is anti-HBc IgM.

Why not the other options?

• A. Anti-HBsAb: Appears after the window period, indicating recovery or vaccination.
• B. Anti-HBc IgG: Appears later and persists lifelong; not the marker of the window period.
• D. HBeAg: Marker of active viral replication and high infectivity, not specific for the window period.
questions.learning: Anti-HBc IgM — The window period of hepatitis B infection is the interval when HBsAg has disappeared but anti-HBs has not yet appeared. During this period, the only reliable serological marker is anti-HBc IgM.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What type of material is the mesh used in Lichtenstein hernioplasty?
questions.explanation: The Lichtenstein hernioplasty is a "tension-free" open surgical technique for inguinal hernia repair. The standard material used for the mesh in this procedure is Polypropylene. Polypropylene is a synthetic, non-absorbable, monofilament material that is favored because it triggers a strong fibroblastic response, leading to robust tissue integration and a permanent strengthening of the posterior inguinal wall. Polyglactin (Option D, Vicryl) and Polydioxanone (Option B, PDS) are absorbable suture materials that would lose their strength over time, leading to high recurrence rates if used as a primary hernia mesh. Polyacrylamide (Option C) is not a standard surgical mesh material. The use of polypropylene mesh has dramatically reduced the recurrence rate of inguinal hernias compared to older suture-only techniques (like Bassini's). While generally safe, potential complications include chronic pain due to nerve entrapment or rare mesh infection. The monofilament nature of the mesh helps reduce the risk of harboring bacteria within the weave
questions.learning: The Lichtenstein hernioplasty is a "tension-free" open surgical technique for inguinal hernia repair. The standard material used for the mesh in this procedure is Polypropylene.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Given the RNA sequence CAAGGU, what would be the corresponding template DNA strand?
questions.explanation: To determine the template DNA strand from a given RNA sequence, remember that RNA is synthesized complementary to the DNA template strand during transcription. Given RNA sequence: 5′–CAAGGU–3′ Base pairing rules: 1. C ↔ G 2. A ↔ T (in DNA) 3. G ↔ C 4. U ↔ A Now, find the complementary DNA template strand: RNA: C A A G G U DNA: G T T C C A So, the template DNA sequence is: 3′–GT TCCA–5′, which is written as GTTCCA However, if written in the 5′→3′ direction, it becomes: TGGAAC Why other options are wrong: (A) CAAGGT → Coding strand (similar to RNA, U→T) (B) GTTCCA → Correct sequence but in 3′→5′ direction (C) ACCTTG → Reverse complement, incorrect
questions.learning: To determine the template DNA strand from a given RNA sequence, remember that RNA is synthesized complementary to the DNA template strand during transcription.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is not seen in the floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tail of caudate nucleus

The tail of the caudate nucleus is not seen on the floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle. It is present on the roof of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle.

The inferior horn is the largest compartment of the lateral ventricle and extends up to 2.5 cm from the temporal pole. The relations are:

Roof - Tapetum of corpus callosum laterally and tail of caudate nucleus medially.

Floor (lateral to medial) - Collateral eminence produced by collateral fissure, hippocampus.

The floor of the temporal horn consists of the hippocampus medially and the collateral eminence, formed by the infolding of the collateral sulcus, laterally. The inferior part of the choroidal fissure, located between the fimbria of the fornix and the inferolateral aspect of the thalamus, lies in the medial wall.

The lateral ventricle is divided into the body and 3 horns. The locations of the parts are:

• Body - parietal lobe
• Anterior horn - frontal lobe
• Posterior horn - occipital lobe
• Inferior horn - temporal lobe.

The anterior horn extends from the genu of the corpus callosum up to the interventricular foramen. The relations of the anterior horn are:

• Anteriorly - Genu and rostrum of the corpus callosum
• Roof - Anterior part of the body of the corpus callosum
• Floor and lateral wall - Caudate nucleus
• Medial wall - Septum pellucidum and anterior column of fornix

The body or central part extends from the interventricular foramen to the splenium of the corpus callosum. The relations of the body are:

• Roof - Body of the corpus callosum
• Medial wall - Septum pellucidum
• Floor (from lateral to medial) - Caudate nucleus, stria terminalis, thalamostriate vein, thalamus, choroid plexus, and body of the fornix

The posterior horn extends from the splenium to the occipital pole. The relations are:

• Roof and lateral wall - Tapetum of corpus callosum
• Medial wall - Forceps major and calcar avis (calcarine sulcus

Note: There is no lateral wall for the lateral ventricle.
questions.learning: Tail of caudate nucleus — The tail of the caudate nucleus is not seen on the floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle. It is present on the roof of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient with schizophrenia, currently on antipsychotic medication, develops acute dystonia. What is the appropriate management for this patient?
questions.explanation: Acute dystonia is a common extrapyramidal side effect (EPS) of antipsychotic therapy. The appropriate management involves using an anticholinergic medication. Benzhexol (Trihexyphenidyl) is a standard anticholinergic drug used to treat and prevent dystonia and parkinsonian symptoms induced by antipsychotics. Fluphenazine (Option B) would likely worsen the EPS. Increasing the dose of haloperidol (Option C) is incorrect as it would increase the dopamine blockade responsible for the dystonia. Clozapine (Option D) is an atypical antipsychotic used for treatment-resistant schizophrenia but is not the acute management for a dystonic crisis. Patients often receive these anticholinergics alongside their antipsychotic to maintain neurological stability. Clinicians must balance the benefits of symptom control with the anticholinergic side effects like dry mouth and blurred vision. Benzhexol remains a foundational tool in the management of antipsychotic side effects. **************
questions.learning: Acute dystonia is a common extrapyramidal side effect (EPS) of antipsychotic therapy. The appropriate management involves using an anticholinergic medication.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following features will not be manifested in an infection of the post-styloid compartment of the parapharyngeal space?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Trismus

Trismus is not a feature of infection of the post-styloid compartment of the parapharyngeal space. Trismus is seen in pre-styloid abscess due to the involvement of medial pterygoid muscle.

Parapharyngeal space is divided into two compartments by the styloid process and its attachments. Clinical features depend on the compartment involved.

In a post-styloid abscess, there is a bulge of the pharynx behind the posterior pillar, accompanied by paralysis of cranial nerves IX, X (resulting in vocal cord paralysis), XI, XII, and the sympathetic chain, which can manifest as Horner's syndrome. Swelling in the parotid region may also be present. Notably, trismus, the inability to fully open the mouth, is usually absent in this type of abscess.

A pre-styloid abscess exhibits distinct features including the prolapse of the tonsil and tonsillar fossa, along with trismus caused by the spasm of the medial pterygoid muscle. Marked odynophagia is common. Additionally, an external swelling can be observed behind the angle of the jaw.

Fever, sore throat, torticollis (caused by spasm of the prevertebral muscles), and signs of systemic toxicity are common features.

Diagnosis can be established using a contrast-enhanced CT scan (CECT). If there is suspicion of thrombosis of the internal jugular vein or an aneurysm of the internal carotid artery, magnetic resonance arteriography (MRA) can be useful.

Patients require intravenous antibiotic therapy with amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, carbapenem antibiotics plus drugs that target anaerobic organisms, such as clindamycin or metronidazole. A parapharyngeal abscess is drained by an external horizontal incision made on the skin a few centimeters below the angle of the mandible.

questions.learning: Trismus Trismus is not a feature of infection of the post-styloid compartment of the parapharyngeal space. Trismus is seen in pre-styloid abscess due to the involvement of medial pterygoid muscle.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: On performing a histamine test on an individual with brachial plexus trunk injury, you can expect ________.
options: Central capillary dilatation → wheal → Surrounding flare
Central capillary dilatation → wheal without surrounding flare
Central capillary dilatation → wheal with exaggerated surrounding flare
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Central capillary dilatation → wheal without surrounding flare

Brachial plexus trunk injury leads to anesthetized skin over the region. On performing a histamine test on such an individual, one can expect central capillary dilatation → wheal without surrounding flare. The incomplete triple response over the anesthetic skin is characteristic of postganglionic lesions.

Intradermal injection of histamine usually causes a triple response in the surrounding skin i.e, red reaction→ flare → wheal

• Red reaction is independent of innervation and is due to histamine-mediated relaxation of the precapillary sphincters
• Flare reaction (Flush, Axon reflex) is due to Substance P mediated arteriolar dilatation (antidromic conduction of afferent impulses via collaterals of the sensory nerve fiber that lead to the release of vasoactive mediators)
• Wheal (skin edema) is due to histamine-mediated increased capillary permeability
• The triple response persists after total sympathectomy
• Flare is absent in locally anesthetized skin

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: On fundoscopic examination, the findings shown in the image below are observed. What is the most likely diagnosis based on these findings?
questions.explanation: The fundus image shows a pale, edematous retina with a prominent cherry-red spot at the macula. This is the classic appearance of Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO). In CRAO, there is sudden blockage of the central retinal artery, leading to ischemia of the inner retinal layers, which appear pale. The macula remains relatively red (cherry-red spot) because it is supplied by the choroidal circulation, which is unaffected. The retinal vessels may also appear attenuated (narrowed). Why Other Options Are Wrong (B) CRVO: Shows “blood and thunder” appearance with hemorrhages and dilated tortuous veins (C) Diabetic retinopathy: Shows microaneurysms, hemorrhages, exudates, neovascularization (D) Cystoid macular edema: Shows retinal thickening and cystic spaces, not cherry-red spot
questions.learning: The fundus image shows a pale, edematous retina with a prominent cherry-red spot at the macula. This is the classic appearance of Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 21-year-old female patient underwent surgery on her middle ear and a nerve was injured intraoperatively. She came a week later to OPD with difficulty in closing her eyes on the same side. Ocular examination reveals decreased corneal sensation and dryness of the cornea. Which of the following cranial nerves was most likely injured during the surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. VII

This patient with a past history of intra-op nerve injury during middle ear surgery presented with dry eye, decreased corneal sensation, and incomplete eyelid closure (lagophthalmos) due to injury to cranial nerve (CN)VII.

Lagophthalmos can be caused by conditions such as facial nerve injury, parkinsonism (reduced muscle tone), lid scarring, and proptosis. The facial nerve runs horizontally in the medial wall and vertically in the posterior wall of the middle ear. Hence, they can be injured due to surgery of the middle ear.  Clinical features include dry eyes, decreased corneal sensation which can eventually lead to  mild punctate epithelial changes and epithelial breakdown.

CN VII lies in proximity to the middle ear. Hence there are chances of nerve injury during middle ear surgery.
The given image shows the course of the facial nerve within the middle ear cavity.

Treatment depends on whether the exposure is reversible or permanent. Reversible exposure can be treated with artificial tears and eye ointments. The eyelid can be taped closed at night or external barriers like bandage silicone hydrogel or scleral contact lenses can be used. Permanent exposure requires permanent tarsorrhaphy.

Other options:

Option B - CN IV palsy leads to paralysis of superior oblique muscles.

Option C - CN VI palsy leads to lateral rectus palsy and lateral gaze palsy.

Option D - CN III injury leads to injury of levator palpebrae superioris and ptosis.

None of these nerves pass through the middle ear.
questions.learning: VII — This patient with a past history of intra-op nerve injury during middle ear surgery presented with dry eye, decreased corneal sensation, and incomplete eyelid closure (lagophthalmos) due to injury to cranial nerve (CN)VII.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A mental health practitioner is evaluating aripiprazole for a patient with psychotic symptoms. Compared to other antipsychotics, how do its pharmacological properties and side effect profile differ?
options: No intrinsic activity, high affinity for D2 receptor, less extrapyramidal symptoms, and more weight gain
High intrinsic activity, no affinity for D2 receptor, more extrapyramidal symptoms, and less weight gain
Low intrinsic activity, high affinity for D2 re- ceptor, less extrapyramidal symptoms, and less weight gain
High intrinsic activity, high affinity for D2 re- ceptor, less extrapyramidal symptoms, and less weight gain
questions.explanation: Low intrinsic activity, high affinity for D2 receptor, less extrapyramidal symptoms, and less weight gain Aripiprazole is a unique "third-generation" atypical antipsychotic. Its pharmacological hallmark is being a D2 receptor partial agonist. This means it has a high affinity for the D2 receptor but only low intrinsic activity (Option C) . This allow it to act as an antagonist in areas of dopamine excess (improving positive symptoms) and as an agonist in areas of dopamine deficiency. Because of its partial agonist mechanism, it is associated with significantly less extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) and minimal elevation of prolactin levels. Furthermore, compared to other atypicals like olanzapine, it has a very low risk of metabolic side effects, resulting in less weight gain. Options A, B, and D are incorrect descriptions of its receptor profile or clinical tolerability. Therefore, the combination of high affinity, low intrinsic activity, and a favorable metabolic profile makes Option C the definitive pharmacological description of aripiprazole.
questions.learning: Low intrinsic activity, high affinity for D2 receptor, less extrapyramidal symptoms, and less weight gain Aripiprazole is a unique "third-generation" atypical antipsychotic.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Two compartments each contain 1 L of water and are separated by a semipermeable membrane permeable to water and glucose but impermeable to fructose. Which statement is true at equilibrium?
options: Fructose concentration becomes equal in both compartments
Water level becomes equal in both compartments
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Water is more in compartment 1

• Glucose is permeable and diffuses until its concentration becomes equal on both sides.

• Fructose cannot cross the membrane.
• Therefore, fructose acts as the effective osmole.

• Initially, compartment 1 contains more fructose.

• Water moves toward compartment 1 by osmosis.
• Hence, compartment 1 gains water and its volume increases.

• Water levels do not become equal.

• Glucose concentration becomes equal because it diffuses freely.
• Fructose concentration remains unequal because it cannot diffuse.

• The direction of water movement is determined by the impermeant solute.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 54-year-old patient receiving chemotherapy with cisplatin develops notable adverse effects. Which side effect is most commonly associated with cisplatin therapy?
questions.explanation: Cisplatin is a potent platinum-based alkylating agent used for various solid tumors, but it has a very high "emetic potential". The most common and immediate side effects of cisplatin are severe GI symptoms, specifically nausea and intractable vomiting. These symptoms are so prevalent that almost all patients require aggressive pre-treatment with anti-emetics like 5-HT3 antagonists (e.g., ondansetron) and dexamethasone. While Neuropathy (Option B, specifically sensory peripheral neuropathy) and Nephrotoxicity (damage to renal tubules) are significant dose-limiting toxicities, they are typically cumulative rather than immediate. Cardiotoxicity (Option C) and Myopathy (Option D) are rare side effects compared to the near-universal GI distress. Clinicians must also vigilantly monitor renal function and hearing (ototoxicity), as cisplatin can cause permanent damage to the hair cells in the cochlea. Aggressive hydration is a standard preventive measure used during administration to minimize the risk of acute kidney injury
questions.learning: Cisplatin is a potent platinum-based alkylating agent used for various solid tumors, but it has a very high "emetic potential". The most common and immediate side effects of cisplatin are severe GI symptoms, specifically nausea and intractable vomiting.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 23-year-old farm worker from a remote village presents 8 hours after a snake bite that occurred early in the morning. He complains of headache, blurred vision, perioral tingling, dizziness, vertigo, and has had repeated vomiting since the bite. On examination, he shows respiratory depression and bradycardia (heart rate < 50/ min). The bite site has mild swelling and blistering without bleeding. He has already received 10 vials of antivenom. What should be the next step in management for this patient?
questions.explanation: The patient is displaying classic signs of neurotoxic snake envenomation, likely from a cobra or krait bite. Symptoms such as blurred vision (ptis), respiratory depression, and tingling are hallmark neurological effects. While Polyvalent Anti-Snake Venom (ASV) has been started, the presence of respiratory distress requires adjunct therapy. Neostigmine, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, can transiently improve neuromuscular transmission in neurotoxic envenomation (particularly cobra bites). It must always be given with Atropine to block the muscarinic side effects, such as bradycardia and increased secretions. Checking the coagulation profile (Option A) is more relevant for vasculotoxic (Viper) bites where bleeding is prominent. Epinephrine (Option C) and hydrocortisone (Option D) are used to manage ASV-induced anaphylaxis, but not for the primary neurotoxic symptoms. Therefore, the neostigmine-atropine challenge is the critical next step to potentially reverse muscle paralysis and stabilize the patient
questions.learning: The patient is displaying classic signs of neurotoxic snake envenomation, likely from a cobra or krait bite. Symptoms such as blurred vision (ptis), respiratory depression, and tingling are hallmark neurological effects.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text:
A patient who was watching a movie suddenly developed acute pain in the eye and diminution in vision. He was brought to the emergency department and on examination, a shallow anterior chamber was noted. What would be the appropriate management for this condition?

IV-Intravenous

e/d- Eyedrops
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. IV Mannitol + pilocarpine e/d

The given clinical scenario, supported by the image of the mid-dilated pupil, with a shallow anterior chamber (AC), is suggestive of acute angle-closure glaucoma and the appropriate management for this patient includes intravenous mannitol and topical medications like pilocarpine, which is given to reduce the IOP, and constrict the pupil and help relieve the acute angle closure attack.

The primary goal in managing Primary Angle-Closure Glaucoma (PACG) is to prevent optic nerve damage by reducing IOP. In acute attacks, treatment involves aggressively lowering IOP using intravenous mannitol and oral acetazolamide to quickly control symptoms. Topical medications such as pilocarpine, beta-blockers, cholinergic agents, and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors are also used to address the acute episode.

Once the immediate crisis is managed, YAG laser iridotomy (YAG PI) is performed to create an alternate drainage pathway for the aqueous humor, both in the affected eye and the fellow eye. For ongoing management, patients with PACG may require glaucoma medications to maintain target IOP. In cases where maximal medical therapy fails, surgical options such as trabeculectomy or glaucoma drainage devices may be necessary, particularly if there is progressive visual field loss or non-compliance with treatment. Cyclodestructive procedures may be considered for patients with a painful, blind eye or those with recurrent surgical failures.

Acute primary angle-closure glaucoma refers to the occlusion of the trabecular meshwork by the peripheral iris (iridotrabecular contact [ITC]), obstructing aqueous outflow.

Angle closure can be primary when it occurs in an anatomically predisposed eye or secondary to another ocular or systemic factor.

Classification:

Primary angle-closure suspect (PACS)

• Gonioscopy shows posterior meshwork ITC in three or more quadrants but no peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS).
• Intraocular pressure (IOP), optic disc, and visual field are normal.
• No PAS are seen
• The risk of PACG at 5 years may be around 30%.

Primary angle closure (PAC)

• Gonioscopy shows three or more quadrants of ITC with raised IOP and/or PAS or excessive pigment smudging on the TM.
• Normal optic disc and field.

Primary angle-closure glaucoma (PACG)

• ITC in three or more quadrants, with glaucomatous optic neuropathy.
• Optic nerve damage from an episode of severe IOP elevation, such as acute angle closure, may not appear as typical glaucomatous cupping.

Symptoms: Pain, redness, photophobia, impaired vision, watering

Signs:

• Corneal edema- coloured halos
• Conjunctiva- congestion, chemosis
• IOP- elevated 40–70 mm Hg
• AC very shallow
• Pupil- vertically oval, mid-dilated
• Angle- completely closed, Grade 0

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the most common complication associated with the following abnormality?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Exposure keratopathy

The given image shows a coloboma of the upper eyelid. The most common complication associated with this condition is exposure keratopathy since the defect leaves the cornea exposed. If left untreated, it can lead to corneal ulceration.

Coloboma of the eyelid is a partial or full-thickness eyelid defect. It usually occurs near the nasal side. It more frequently involves the upper lid than the lower lid. It occurs when eyelid development is incomplete, due to failure of migration of lid ectoderm to fuse with the lid folds.

Small defects can be managed by primary closure, while large defects require skin grafts and rotation flaps.

Upper lid colobomas occur at the junction of the middle and inner thirds. It has a relatively strong association with cryptophthalmos, facial abnormalities, and Goldenhar syndrome. Cryptophthalmos is a congenital anomaly in which the eyelids are absent, replaced by a continuous layer of skin.

Lower lid colobomas occur at the junction of the middle and outer thirds and are frequently associated with systemic conditions.

Treacher Collins syndrome (mandibulofacial dysostosis) is a genetically heterogeneous condition. It is characterized by mandibular and ear anomalies. lower eyelid coloboma, slanted palpebral apertures, cataract, microphthalmos, and lacrimal atresia.
questions.learning: Exposure keratopathy — The given image shows a coloboma of the upper eyelid. The most common complication associated with this condition is exposure keratopathy since the defect leaves the cornea exposed.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the WHO definition of blindness?
questions.explanation: The World Health Organization (WHO) provides specific clinical criteria to define blindness for standardized global health monitoring. Blindness is defined as a visual acuity (VA) of less than (on the Snellen chart) in the better eye with the best possible correction. This corresponds to the inability of a person to count fingers at a distance of 3 meters. Visual acuity of (Option A) is the threshold for "visual impairment" but does not reach the definition of blindness. Visual acuity of (Option C) is considered the upper limit of normal vision in many screening contexts; anyone with better vision is not categorized as impaired. Visual acuity of (Option D) is technically within the category of blindness, but it is not the standard "threshold" level used for definition. The definition also includes a visual field restricted to less than 10 degrees from the point of fixation. Consistent use of this definition is vital for tracking progress in initiatives like "VISION 2020."

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 25-year-old male with Marfanoid features presented with sudden onset breathlessness. The chest X-ray is given below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pneumothorax

The chest X-ray demonstrating tracheal deviation and displacement of the heart away from the affected side along with the partial collapse of the left lung in the above condition points to a diagnosis of left-sided pneumothorax.

Marfan's syndrome is one of the causes for seconday spontaneous pneumothorax in adults.

Pneumothorax refers to the collection of air in the pleural space.

Chest radiograph in spontaneous pneumothorax demonstrates:

• Thin, sharp white line, demarcating the visceral pleural edge
• Absence of lung markings seen peripheral to this line
• Peripheral space radiolucent compared to adjacent lung
• Complete lung collapse, as well as subcutaneous emphysema and pneumomediastinum, may be seen
• Deep sulcus sign (on supine chest radiograph)

Deep sulcus sign: On a supine position(common in the ICU), air collects anteriorly and basally, within the non-dependent portions of the pleural space, abnormally deepening the costophrenic angle. This sign is indicative of pneumothorax in such patients and may be the only visible clue, especially when patient can not be imaged upright.

The image below is plain chest x-ray showing pneumothorax with deep sulcus sign (shown by arrow):

When there is a progressive accumulation of air intrapleurally in the thoracic cavity (caused by a valve effect during inspiration and expiration), it is called Tension pneumothorax. It can result in compression of mediastinal structures and compromise cardiopulmonary function. It is life-threatening and requires emergency intervention.
questions.learning: Pneumothorax — The chest X-ray demonstrating tracheal deviation and displacement of the heart away from the affected side along with the partial collapse of the left lung in the above condition points to a diagnosis of left-sided pneumothorax.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: All of the following oncogenic viruses can integrate with the human genome to initiate carcinogenesis except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. HTLV

HTLV - Human T cell lymphotropic virus causes microbial carcinogenesis by indirect mechanisms. Even, Hepatitis C virus, a flavivirus, does not generate a provirus and appears to induce cancer indirectly.

Oncogenic viruses:

Integration of viral genome into the host cell thereby leading to the formation of a pro-virus is commonly a mechanism of viral microbial carcinogenesis. DNA tumor viruses encode viral oncoproteins that are important for viral replication. Some portion of this may become integrated into the host cell chromosome. For RNA tumor viruses that mostly belong to the retrovirus family are known to cause microbial carcinogenesis by indirect mechanisms.

Note:

HPV causes carcinogenesis by both integrations and by the E6, E7 protein systems.
questions.learning: HTLV HTLV - Human T cell lymphotropic virus causes microbial carcinogenesis by indirect mechanisms. Even, Hepatitis C virus, a flavivirus, does not generate a provirus and appears to induce cancer indirectly.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Vitamin B12 is found maximum in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Animal products

Vitamin B12 is found maximum in animal products.

Vitamin B12 or cobalamin is synthesized only by microorganisms. Thus, the only source of cobalamin for humans is animal products. It is not found in plant sources. Therefore, individuals who are strict vegetarians are usually at the risk of developing vitamin B12 deficiency.
questions.learning: Animal products Vitamin B12 is found maximum in animal products. Vitamin B12 or cobalamin is synthesized only by microorganisms.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 10-year-old presents with muscle cramps, especially following high-intensity exercise. What is the type of glycogen storage disorder?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. McArdle's disease

A clinical scenario of a patient with muscle cramps with exertion is suggestive of McArdle's disease, which is due to the deficiency of muscle glycogen phosphorylase.

A unique feature associated with McArdle is the improvement in symptoms after rest for a few minutes. This is termed the second wind phenomenon. This occurs due to the increased blood flow to the muscles, liver glycogen release and increased utilisation of free fatty acids (FFAs) for energy production after resting for a few minutes. This compensates for the impaired ATP generation from glycogenolysis. Patients with McArdle disease can benefit from engaging in regular aerobic exercises, such as walking or cycling, which can help increase their exercise tolerance and cardiovascular fitness. However, they should avoid high-intensity exercises or activities that can trigger muscle cramps and rhabdomyolysis. Glucose administration before exercise can improve tolerance. Vitamin B6 is also recommended.

McArdle disease, also known as type V glycogen storage disorder, is an autosomal recessive condition. It typically presents during late childhood or in the second decade of life. The muscle glycogen phosphorylase enzyme deficiency interferes with ATP generation by glycogenolysis in the muscles. This causes muscle glycogen accumulation.

Symptoms are exercise intolerance associated with muscle cramps. Due to high-intensity exercise, sudden persistent muscle contraction occurs. This leads to severe muscle damage resulting in a massive release of muscle proteins and myoglobin in the blood. Myoglobinuria secondary to rhabdomyolysis leads to the passage of burgundy-coloured urine in some patients.

Rarely, it can present during infancy as hypotonia, muscle weakness, and respiratory complications. It is generally fatal. Muscle biopsy to measure glycogen content is the standard diagnosis.

Other options:

Option B: Cori's disease (type III glycogen storage disorder) – It is caused by a deficiency of glycogen debranching enzyme. Patients with Cori's disease present with hepatomegaly, growth retardation, and hypoglycemia. Muscle weakness may be present, but not muscle cramps or myoglobinuria.

Option C: Pompe's disease results from a deficiency in the enzyme lysosomal alpha-glucosidase.

Option D: Andersen disease (type IV glycogen storage disorder) – It is caused by the deficiency of the glycogen branching enzyme. This disease presents with hepatomegaly, cirrhosis, and liver failure. It does not cause muscle cramps or myoglobinuria.
questions.learning: McArdle's disease — A clinical scenario of a patient with muscle cramps with exertion is suggestive of McArdle's disease, which is due to the deficiency of muscle glycogen phosphorylase.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient presents with swelling and tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox after sustaining a fall on their outstretched hand. The image given below shows the cast used to manage the patient's injury. Identify the fracture.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Scaphoid fracture

The cast applied to a patient in the glass holding position is known as the scaphoid cast. It is used to treat scaphoid fractures.

To apply a scaphoid cast, the wrist is held in slight dorsiflexion and the thumb is in abduction and slight flexion as if the glass is being held between the index finger and thumb. It extends from just below the elbow to just proximal to the metacarpal necks of the digits. On the thumb, the cast extends to just proximal to the interphalangeal joint.

Scaphoid fracture presents with pain and swelling over the radial aspect of the wrist. A fall on an outstretched hand could result in such a fracture. The fracture can be confirmed (when an x-ray doesn't show a fracture) if there is pain elicited in the anatomical snuff box on the radial border of the wrist.

An oblique x-ray of the wrist should be able to show a scaphoid fracture.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The recommended temperature of water bath for a patient with frost bite is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 37 degree C

The temperature of the water bath for a patient with frostbite should be maintained between 37- 40°C (Option A). Circulating water is preferred for treatment.

In frostbite, tissue damage results from severe environmental cold exposure or from direct contact with a very cold object. Tissue injury results from both freezing and vasoconstriction. It usually affects the distal aspects of the extremities or exposed parts of the face, such as the ears, nose, chin, and cheeks.

The treatment includes - extraction from cold environment, rapid rewarming, analgesics for pain during thawing, antithrombotics or thrombolytics, cleaning of the injured area with soap or antiseptics, tetanus prophylaxis, monitoring for compartment syndrome and finally, elective late amputation after imaging in severe cases.
questions.learning: 37 degree C The temperature of the water bath for a patient with frostbite should be maintained between 37- 40°C (Option A). Circulating water is preferred for treatment.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text:
G6PD can manifest with which of the following drugs?

G6PD - Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Primaquine

G6PD deficiency will manifest with primaquine.

G6PD deficiency is an X-linked recessive (XLR) disorder that causes congenital hemolytic anemia due to enzyme deficiency. Hemolysis occurs in conditions of high oxidative stress that are triggered by infections, fava beans, and certain drugs.

G6PD is an enzyme in the hexose monophosphate pathway (HMP) that maintains the cellular levels of NADPH. NADPH then provides reducing equivalents needed for the conversion of oxidized glutathione to reduced glutathione. Reduced glutathione helps neutralize free radicles, protecting against oxidant injury.

Clinically, most patients are asymptomatic. Some patient develops episodic hemolysis, causing hemolytic anemia, hemoglobinemia, and hemoglobinuria.

Both primaquine and chloroquine cause hemolysis in G6PD-deficient individuals, but hemolysis is rare with chloroquine and it can be used in patients with G6PD deficiency, whereas primaquine is contraindicated in these individuals.

Hematological findings in G6PD deficiency are shown below:

Drugs that carry a risk of clinical hemolysis in persons with G6PD deficiency:

CLASS

Primaquine > Chloroquine

Dapsone/chlorproguanil

Sulphonamides/sulphones

Cotrimoxazole, Ciprofloxacin, Chloramphenicol, Nalidixic acid, Norfloxacin, Nitrofurantoin

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 17-year-old boy presents with a painless lump on the lateral aspect of his left knee. A radiograph is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Osteochondroma, also known as exostosis, is the most common benign bone tumor in children and adolescents. It typically presents as a painless, slow-growing lump near the growth plate of long bones, especially around the knee (distal femur or proximal tibia). The radiograph classically shows a bony outgrowth with a cortex and medulla continuous with those of the host bone, often described as "pedunculated" or "sessile." Enchondroma (Option A) is a benign cartilage tumor that grows within the medullary cavity, usually in the small bones of the hands. Osteosarcoma (Option B) is a highly malignant tumor presenting with deep-seated pain, night pain, and characteristic "sunburst" or "Codman's triangle" radiological features. Osteomyelitis (Option C) is an infection of the bone presenting with acute pain, fever, and local inflammatory signs. Given the adolescent age, painless clinical presentation, and pathognomonic radiological appearance of a bony outgrowth, osteochondroma is the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: Osteochondroma, also known as exostosis, is the most common benign bone tumor in children and adolescents. It typically presents as a painless, slow-growing lump near the growth plate of long bones, especially around the knee (distal femur or proximal tibia).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the correct dose of administration of antenatal steroids for lung maturity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dexamethasone 6 mg 12 hours apart 4 doses

The correct dose of administration of antenatal steroids for lung maturity is dexamethasone 6 mg 12 hours apart 4 doses.

Maternal administration of corticosteroids is advocated where the pregnancy is less than 34 weeks. This helps in fetal lung maturation. This is beneficial when the delivery is delayed beyond 48 hours of the first dose. The benefit persists as long as 18 days. Either betamethasone 12 mg IM 24 hours apart for two doses or dexamethasone 6 mg IM every 12 hours for 4 doses is given. Betamethasone is the steroid of choice (RCOG–2004).

Antenatal steroids also reduce the incidence of respiratory distress syndrome, necrotizing enterocolitis, intraventricular hemorrhage and patent ductus arteriosus.

Risks of antenatal corticosteroid use:

• Premature rupture of the membranes especially with evidence of infection, as the infection may flare-up
• Insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus where patients need insulin dose readjustment
• Transient reduction of fetal breathing and body movements.
questions.learning: Dexamethasone 6 mg 12 hours apart 4 doses — The correct dose of administration of antenatal steroids for lung maturity is dexamethasone 6 mg 12 hours apart 4 doses.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A child presents with developmental delays, learning disabilities, and signs of organ damage. His mother reports a habit of eating wall paint. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lead poisoning

Children sometimes develop pica, a condition where they eat non-food substances such as:

• Soil
• Chalk
• Paint chips

Old wall paints often contain lead, leading to Lead poisoning, also called plumbism.

The history of eating wall paint (pica) strongly suggests lead exposure, especially from lead-based paints.

| System | Manifestations

| ------ | --------------

| Neurological | Developmental delay, learning disabilities

| Gastrointestinal | Abdominal pain, vomiting

| Hematological | Anemia

| Renal | Kidney damage

Chronic lead poisoning in children leads to developmental delay, learning disabilities, and multi-organ involvement, particularly affecting the nervous system.

Iron deficiency may cause pica but does not explain organ damage, while sideroblastic anemia and lithium toxicity have different clinical contexts.
questions.learning: Lead poisoning Children sometimes develop pica, a condition where they eat non-food substances such as: • Soil • Chalk • Paint chips Old wall paints often contain lead, leading to Lead poisoning, also called plumbism.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: When a doctor is summoned to court to give evidence, the nature of the testimony depends on the doctor’s professional knowledge and the circumstances of the case. Which statement correctly describes the role or type of witness in this situation?
questions.explanation: In legal proceedings, a doctor typically testifies as an "expert witness." Unlike a common witness (Option B), who can only testify to facts they personally perceived through their senses (what they saw or heard), an expert witness is permitted to provide opinions based on their specialized training, skill, and experience. For example, a doctor can testify not just that a wound existed, but also offer an expert opinion on the type of weapon used or the cause of death. Oral evidence (Option A) refers to the medium of delivery rather than the status of the witness. A hostile witness (Option D) is someone who shows bias against the party that called them, leading the court to allow cross-examination by that same party. While a doctor's testimony is a form of oral evidence, their primary legal classification in a professional capacity is that of an expert, whose role is to assist the court in understanding complex medical facts

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which type of thyroid carcinoma has the least likelihood of lymph node metastasis? (NEET PG 2017)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Follicular carcinoma of the thyroid

Follicular carcinoma of the thyroid has the least likelihood of lymph node metastasis among the given options. Follicular carcinoma typically presents as a solitary thyroid nodule with a strong tendency for hematogenous spread rather than lymphatic spread. While it commonly metastasizes to bones (particularly thoracic vertebrae and skull) via blood vessels, lymph node involvement is rare, except in the Hurthle cell variant which may show lymph node metastases.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common association with Tetralogy of Fallot?
questions.explanation: Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease. Among the provided genetic disorders, Downs syndrome (Trisomy 21) is the most frequently associated condition . While the most common heart defect specifically in Down syndrome is an endocardial cushion defect (AVSD), TOF occurs at a significantly higher rate in this population than in the general public. Klinefelter's (Option A, 47,XXY) and Turner's (Option D, 45,X) syndromes have different cardiac associations, such as coarctation of the aorta in Turner's. Edwards syndrome (Option B, Trisomy 18) features severe multi-organ defects and VSDs but is less commonly associated with surviving TOF cases than Down syndrome. TOF involves four specific defects: VSD, pulmonary stenosis, right ventricular hypertrophy, and an overriding aorta. Therefore, in clinical genetics and pediatrics, Trisomy 21 is recognized as the most frequent chromosomal association for children born with TOF
questions.learning: Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease. Among the provided genetic disorders, Downs syndrome (Trisomy 21) is the most frequently associated condition .

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 38-year-old man presents with bleeding gums for 20 days. He has gingival hyperplasia, hepatosplenomegaly, and lymphadenopathy. On investigation, Hb - 11 g/dL, platelet count - 95,000 platelets/mm3, and WBC count - 45000 cells/mm3. Bone marrow biopsy shows 100% cellularity with many blast cells that are peroxidase negative and non-specific esterase positive. The most likely diagnosis is _____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Acute myeloid leukemia M5 (AML M5)

The most likely diagnosis from the clinical presentation and cytochemistry is acute myeloid leukemia (AML) M5 or acute monocytic leukemia.

Diagnostic features of AML M5:  20% or more blasts in the bone marrow. Markedly elevated white blood cell count with organomegaly, lymphadenopathy, gingival hyperplasia, CNS involvement and other tissue infiltration. Monoblasts have folded or lobulated nuclei, lack Auer rods, and are nonspecific esterase positive. Classified as AML with recurrent genetic abnormalities such as inv(16)(p13;1q22), t(16;16)(p13.1q22) or t(9;11)(p22;q23)

Note:

Myeloperoxidase is present in the azurophilic granules of neutrophils and its precursors. It is positive in AML M1, M2, M3, M4 and negative in AML M0. Monoblasts and monocytes may be negative or positive. When positive, the granules are smaller than in neutrophils and diffusely scattered throughout the cytoplasm.

Image: Bone marrow aspirate in AML M5
questions.learning: Acute myeloid leukemia M5 (AML M5) — The most likely diagnosis from the clinical presentation and cytochemistry is acute myeloid leukemia (AML) M5 or acute monocytic leukemia.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text:
Which of the following is true regarding CORADS?

CORADS- COVID-19 Reporting and Data System
options: Pleural thickening is typical of COVID-19
Lobar consolidation is typical of COVID-19
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. CORADS-5 is typical of COVID-19

Among the given options, CORADS-5 is typical of COVID-19 is the true statement.

Normal or non-infectious

CO-RADS 2
Typical features of other infections but not of COVID-19

CO-RADS 3
Features compatible with COVID-19 but also with other diseases

CO-RADS 4
Suspicious for COVID-19

CO-RADS 5
Typical for COVID-19

CO-RADS 6
Proven COVID-19 by positive RT-PCR test

CO-RADS categories:

• CO-RADS 0: Not interpretable - Technically insufficient to assign a score: Scans are incomplete or of inferior quality.
• CO-RADS 1: Very low level of suspicion for pulmonary involvement by COVID-19. Mild or severe emphysema, perifissural nodules, lung tumors, or fibrosis.
• CO-RADS 2: Low level of suspicion for pulmonary involvement by COVID-19. Includes infectious etiology that is not compatible with COVID-19 such as bronchitis, bronchiolitis, bronchopneumonia, lobar pneumonia, abscess.
• CO-RADS 3: Equivocal findings for pulmonary involvement by COVID-19. Findings overlap with other viral or infectious etiologies. Could include perihilar ground-glass, homogenous extensive ground-glass with or without sparing of secondary pulmonary lobules.
• CO-RADS 4: High level of suspicion for pulmonary involvement by COVID-19. Findings are similar to CO-RADS 5 but are not present in the typical locations. Findings may also be superimposed on severe pre-existing pulmonary abnormalities.
• CO-RADS 5 based on typical CT findings. It requires the presence of at least one confirmatory pattern (mentioned below).
• CO-RADS 6: Proven COVID-19 by positive RT-PCR test.

CT features typical of pulmonary involvement in COVID-19 include:

• Obligatory features

• Ground glass opacities, with or without consolidation in areas close to the visceral pleural surface, including the fissures.

• Confirmatory features

• Ground glass regions
• Crazy paving pattern
• Organizing pneumonia compatible patterns
• Thickened vessels with parenchymal abnormalities
questions.learning: CORADS-5 is typical of COVID-19 Among the given options, CORADS-5 is typical of COVID-19 is the true statement. COVID-19 Reporting and Data System (CO-RADS) is a categorical assessment for pulmonary involvement of COVID-19 on chest CT.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Choose the correct sequence with respect to the stages of changes that the breast undergoes in a female?
questions.explanation: The physiological development and functioning of the breast follow a strictly programmed sequence. 1. Mamogenesis: Growth and development of the mammary glands (primarily during puberty and pregnancy). 2. Lactogenesis: The initiation of milk secretion (typically occurring in the late stages of pregnancy and immediately postpartum). 3. Galactokinesis: The ejection of milk from the breast (the "let-down reflex," primarily mediated by oxytocin in response to suckling). 4. Galactopoiesis: The ongoing maintenance of established milk production (primarily mediated by prolactin and the regular removal of milk). Options A, B, and D provide incorrect chronological orders of these biological events. Understanding this sequence is vital for diagnosing and managing lactation-related disorders. For example, a failure in lactogenesis prevents the initial milk "coming in," while a failure in galactokinesis prevents the child from receiving the milk despite its production. Proper knowledge of these terms and their hormonal drivers (Estrogen/Progesterone for mamogenesis, Prolactin for lactogenesis/galactopoiesis, and Oxytocin for galactokinesis) is essential for obstetric and pediatric care
questions.learning: The physiological development and functioning of the breast follow a strictly programmed sequence. Mamogenesis: Growth and development of the mammary glands (primarily during puberty and pregnancy).

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: The following condition develops due to which vessel?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Medial circumflex femoral artery

The MRI demonstrates avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head, characterized by:

• Hip pain aggravated by weight-bearing
• Subchondral collapse (crescent sign in later stages)
• Patchy/serpiginous marrow signal abnormalities on MRI
• MRI is the most sensitive investigation for early AVN

The principal blood supply to the adult femoral head is from the: ✅ Medial circumflex femoral artery (MCFA)

Its retinacular (ascending cervical) branches run along the femoral neck beneath the capsule and supply most of the femoral head. Interruption of these vessels leads to osteonecrosis.

High-yield Blood Supply of the Femoral Head

| Vessel | Contribution

| ------ | ------------

| Medial circumflex femoral artery | Major blood supply to the adult femoral head ✅

| Lateral circumflex femoral artery | Minor contribution

| Artery of ligamentum teres (from obturator artery) | Important in children; minimal in adults

Common Causes of Avascular Necrosis

• Trauma (femoral neck fracture, hip dislocation)
• Corticosteroid therapy
• Alcohol abuse
• Sickle cell disease
• Systemic lupus erythematosus
• Decompression sickness
• Gaucher disease

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 21-year-old patient with a history of chronic alcohol abuse presents with confusion, tremors, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia. What is the underlying cause responsible for this clinical presentation?
questions.explanation: The classic triad of confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia in a patient with chronic alcoholism is diagnostic of Wernicke’s Encephalopathy. This condition is caused by a severe deficiency of Vitamin B1, also known as thiamine. Thiamine is a vital cofactor for several enzymes in glucose metabolism; its deficiency leads to neuronal damage, particularly in the mamillary bodies and periaqueductal gray matter. Vitamin B12 deficiency (Option A) typically causes subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord. Vitamin B9 or folic acid deficiency (Option B) results in megaloblastic anemia. Vitamin B3 or niacin deficiency (Option D) leads to pellagra, characterized by the "3 Ds": dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia. Immediate treatment with high-dose intravenous thiamine is mandatory to prevent progression to the irreversible Korsakoff syndrome
questions.learning: The classic triad of confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia in a patient with chronic alcoholism is diagnostic of Wernicke’s Encephalopathy. This condition is caused by a severe deficiency of Vitamin B1, also known as thiamine.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 1-year-old child presents to a village clinic with a two-day history of fever and cough and is now refusing feeds. Examination shows the child is calm, with a respiratory rate of 51/min and stridor. According to the IMNCI guidelines, how should this child be classified?
questions.explanation: According to IMNCI guidelines, the classification of respiratory illness depends on "danger signs" and breathing rate. In a 1-year-old child, a respiratory rate of 51 bpm indicates "fast breathing" (threshold is ). However, the presence of stridor in a calm child and the fact that the child is refusing feeds (an IMNCI general danger sign) automatically upgrades the classification to Severe Pneumonia or Very Severe Disease (Option C) . Pneumonia (Option A) is classified by fast breathing without danger signs. Cough and cold (Option B) is used when there is no fast breathing and no danger signs. ARDS (Option D) is a severe ICU-level clinical syndrome not typically part of the basic IMNCI classification colors. Because the child has both an audible airway obstruction (stridor) and is unable to feed, they require urgent referral to a hospital for oxygen and parenteral antibiotics. Thus, Severe Pneumonia is the definitive IMNCI category
questions.learning: According to IMNCI guidelines, the classification of respiratory illness depends on "danger signs" and breathing rate. In a 1-year-old child, a respiratory rate of 51 bpm indicates "fast breathing" (threshold is ).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Phase zero in the adjoining image is due to which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Calcium influx

This question refers to the pacemaker action potential seen in:

• SA node
• AV node

These cells have slow response action potentials.

Important difference: Pacemaker cells do NOT use fast sodium channels for depolarization. Instead, calcium channels mediate depolarization.

The diagram represents a slow-response action potential seen in SA/AV nodal tissue.

In these cells, phase 0 depolarization is mediated by L-type calcium channel–mediated calcium influx, not sodium.

Fast sodium channels are absent or inactivated in nodal tissue.

Potassium currents are involved in repolarization phases, not phase 0.

| Feature | Ventricular Cells | Pacemaker Cells

| ------- | ----------------- | ---------------

| Phase 0 | Na⁺ influx | Ca²⁺ influx

| Phase 4 | Stable | Gradual depolarization

| Automaticity | No | Yes

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child diagnosed with Kawasaki disease developed multiple large coronary artery aneurysms. The child has now recovered from the acute phase. What is the most appropriate next step in long-term management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Aspirin lifelong

Children with Kawasaki disease who develop large or giant coronary artery aneurysms (CAAs) are at high risk of thrombosis and long-term complications. Therefore, the child should continue lifelong aspirin for secondary prevention.

Kawasaki's disease is also known as mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome. It is a vasculitis condition of unknown etiology.  Clinical features include a high spiking fever that is unresponsive to antipyretics. The fever can last between 5 days to 3-4 weeks.

Diagnosis of typical Kawasaki disease is made by fever for 5 or more days along with four of the symptoms listed below:

* Bilateral conjunctival congestion (not purulent conjunctivitis)

* Oral changes: erythematous, cracked lips, and strawberry tongue

* Non-suppurative cervical lymphadenopathy, usually unilateral

* Polymorphous rash

* Changes in extremities: erythema and edema, desquamation of palms and soles

Laboratory findings:

Important laboratory findings of Kawasaki disease are anaemia, elevated ESR and CRP.Thrombocytosis is a characteristic finding in Kawasaki disease and commonly occurs in the second week.

Treatment:

Acute KD:
• IVIG 2 g/kg over 10-12 hr
• High dose aspirin (80-100 mg/kg/day, q6h) until patient is afebrile for at least 48 hr
Convalescent phase:
• Aspirin 3-5 mg/kg once daily for 6-8 wk after illness onset, if  coronary findings are normal throughout the course.

Long term therapy for patients with coronary abnormalities

* Small aneurysms: Aspirin 3-5 mg/kg/d

* Medium aneurysms:

* Aspirin 3-5 mg/kg once daily plus

* Clopidogrel 1 mg/kg/day (maximum: 75 mg/day)

* Giant aneurysms: Aspirin + anticoagulation with warfarin, low molecular weight heparin, or direct oral anticoagulants

Acute coronary thrombosis
•Fibrinolytic therapy to be started with tissue plasminogen activator
or other thrombolytic agents.

Major complications of Kawasaki disease are arteritis and aneurysms of coronary vessels, myocarditis, myocardial infarction and pericarditis.
questions.learning: Aspirin lifelong Children with Kawasaki disease who develop large or giant coronary artery aneurysms (CAAs) are at high risk of thrombosis and long-term complications.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: In which of the following pathologies is the cobra-head appearance seen on an IVU, as shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ureterocele

The cobra-head (adder-head) sign on Intravenous Urography (IVU) is the classic radiological appearance of a ureterocele.

A ureterocele is a cystic dilatation of the distal intravesical ureter caused by congenital stenosis of the ureteric orifice. On IVU, contrast fills the dilated distal ureter, producing a round contrast-filled sac surrounded by a thin radiolucent halo, giving the characteristic cobra-head appearance.

Why not the other options?

• A. Vesicoureteric reflux (VUR): Diagnosed by MCU/VCUG, showing retrograde reflux of contrast into the ureter.
• B. Posterior urethral valves (PUV): MCU shows a dilated posterior urethra (“keyhole sign”).
• C. Duplication of ureter: May be associated with ureterocele but does not itself produce the cobra-head sign.
questions.learning: Ureterocele — The cobra-head (adder-head) sign on Intravenous Urography (IVU) is the classic radiological appearance of a ureterocele. A ureterocele is a cystic dilatation of the distal intravesical ureter caused by congenital stenosis of the ureteric orifice.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient diagnosed with tuberculosis and HIV was started on both anti-tubercular therapy (ATT) and antiretroviral therapy (ART). After 2 months, the patient experienced a deterioration in his health. What is the most likely cause?
options: Drug-drug interaction between TB and HIV medications
Development of drug resistance to anti-tubercular drugs
Development of drug resistance to ART
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Immunological changes in the body

In a patient diagnosed with TB and HIV who was started on ATT and ART, the deterioration in health after treatment initiation point to a diagnosis of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) due to immunological changes in the body.

Following the initiation of effective anti-retroviral therapy, a paradoxical worsening of preexisting or untreated opportunistic infections may be seen in people living with HIV (PLHIV). This is known as immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS). IRIS is seen in up to 30% of the patients who are started on ART, and is particularly common in patients with untreated mycobacterial or fungal infections, or with CD4+ T-cell counts <50 cells/μL. Other risk factors for the development of IRIS include:

* Rapid initial fall in HIV viral load due to ART

* Severity of TB disease

* Male sex and younger age

The underlying pathogenesis appears to be similar to a type IV hypersensitivity reaction and reflects the immediate improvements in immune function as there is a drop in the levels of HIV RNA. IRIS related to a known pre-existing infection is called paradoxical IRIS; IRIS associated with a previously undiagnosed condition is referred to as unmasking IRIS. Signs and symptoms can appear within two weeks to two years of starting ART and can include lymphadenitis, prolonged fever, pulmonary infiltrates, hepatitis and increased intracranial pressure.

IRIS is generally self-limiting and interruption of ART is rarely indicated. In most cases, recognition and management of ongoing infection with antimicrobial therapy is sufficient. Short-term therapy with corticosteroids or NSAIDs can be given to reduce the inflammation. Temporary cessation of ART is to be considered for potentially life-threatening forms of IRIS. For the prevention of IRIS in a patient with HIV and TB co-infection, anti-tubercular treatment is started first and then ART is added two weeks later.

Pearl PF2098: Opportunistic Infections/HIV related conditions and ART initiation

Clinical scenario
Action

Any undiagnosed active infection with fever
Diagnose and treat first; start Anti-Retroviral Therapy (ART) when stable

Tuberculosis (TB)
Start TB treatment first; start ART as soon as possible after 2 weeks and before 2 months. For those with CD4 less than 50/cmm, start ART within 2 weeks Caution is needed for PLHIV with TB meningitis, since immediate ART is associated with more severe adverse events than initiating ART 2 months after the start of TB treatment

Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP)

Treat PCP first; start ART when PCP treatment is completed

Invasive fungal diseases: Oesophageal candidiasis, penicilliosis, histoplasmosis
Start treatment for oesophageal candidiasis first; start ART as soon as the patient can swallow comfortably. Treat penicilliosis, and histoplasmosis first; start ART when the patient is stabilized or opportunistic infection treatment is completed.

Cryptococcal meningitis
Treat cryptococcal meningitis. ART initiation should be deferred until there is evidence of sustained clinical response to anti-fungal therapy and after 4 weeks of induction and consolidation treatment with amphotericin B containing regimen.

Bacterial pneumonia
Treat pneumonia first; start ART when treatment is completed

Malaria
Treat malaria first; start ART when treatment is completed

Acute diarrhoea which may reduce absorption of ART
Diagnose the cause and treat diarrhoea first; start ART when diarrhoea is stabilized or controlled

Non-severe anaemia (Hb< 9 g/dl)
Start ART if no other causes for anaemia are found (HIV is often the cause of anaemia)

Skin conditions such as PPE and seborrhoeic dermatitis, psoriasis, HIV-related exfoliative dermatitis
Start ART (ART may resolve these problems)

Suspected Mycobacterium Avium Complex (MAC), Cryptosporidiosis and Microsporidiosis
Start ART (ART may resolve these problems)

Cytomegalovirus retinitis
Start treatment for CMV urgently and start ART after 2 weeks of CMV treatment

Toxoplasmosis
Treat toxoplasmosis; start ART after 6 weeks of treatment and when the patient is stabilized
