questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is the constituent of the marked area in the electron microscopic picture of muscle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Alpha actinin

Alpha actinin is the constituent of the marked area.

The image depicts sarcomere and the arrow points towards Z-line. Alpha actinin binds actin to Z-lines.

The orderly arrangement of actin, myosin, and related proteins that produces this pattern. The area between two Z-lines is called sarcomere.

The thick filaments, which are about twice the diameter of the thin filaments, are made up of myosin, which are lined to form A bands; the thin filaments are made up of actin, tropomyosin, and troponin. The array of thin filaments extends out of the A band and into the less dense staining I bands.

The lighter H bands in the center of the A bands are the regions where, when the muscle is relaxed, the thin filaments do not overlap the thick filaments.  The Z lines allow for anchoring of the thin filaments.

Actinin, titin and desmin are additional structural proteins.Titin connects Z-lines to the M line and provides the scaffolding to the sarcomere.  Desmin adds structure to Z-lines by connecting Z-line to plasma membrane.

Note: Some sources say that even titin is a component of Z-disc so if alpha actinin is not given in the options titin is the second best answer.
questions.learning: Alpha actinin Alpha actinin is the constituent of the marked area. The image depicts sarcomere and the arrow points towards Z-line.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are major criteria under the Jones Criteria for Acute Rheumatic Fever? 1. Chorea 2. Erythema marginatum 3. Subcutaneous nodules 4. Polyarthralgia Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

The five major Jones criteria are:

1. Carditis
2. Polyarthritis
3. Chorea (Sydenham's chorea)
4. Erythema marginatum
5. Subcutaneous nodules

So Chorea, Erythema marginatum, and Subcutaneous nodules are all major criteria.

Why option with Polyarthralgia is wrong: This is the key trap in the question — polyarthralgia is a minor criterion, not major. The major criterion is polyarthritis (objective joint inflammation), while polyarthralgia (joint pain without objective inflammation) only counts as minor — and importantly, if polyarthritis is already used as a major criterion, polyarthralgia cannot also be counted as a minor criterion in the same patient (to avoid double-counting the same joint symptom).

Minor criteria (for reference, high-yield alongside majors):

• Fever
• Polyarthralgia (only if polyarthritis isn't used as major)
• Elevated ESR/CRP
• Prolonged PR interval on ECG (only if carditis isn't used as major)
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 3 The five major Jones criteria are: 1. Subcutaneous nodules So Chorea, Erythema marginatum, and Subcutaneous nodules are all major criteria.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for __________________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 6 months

Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for 6 months.

Breastfeeding should be started as soon as possible after birth. For an infant to be called exclusively breastfed, pre-lacteal feeds and even water are not to be given. However, giving vitamin drops, if indicated, is included under the definition of exclusive breastfeeding.

Complementary foods rich in iron and other micronutrients should be introduced at about 6 months of age. Breastfeeding should be continued for at least the first year and beyond, as long as the mother and child mutually agree.
questions.learning: 6 months Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for 6 months. Breastfeeding should be started as soon as possible after birth.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presented with a cold and cough. He tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 virus. What test is done to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. RT-PCR

In the clinical scenario of a patient diagnosed with SARS-CoV-2, the confirmation test performed is RT-PCR.

Reverse Transcription Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR) is the gold standard test for diagnosing COVID-19, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus. This technique detects viral RNA in respiratory samples, such as nasopharyngeal or throat swabs, with high sensitivity and specificity. PCR (RT-PCR) is used as the gold standard test for the detection of SARS-CoV-2 due to its benefits as a specific and simple qualitative assay. Moreover, real-time RT-PCR has adequate sensitivity to help us much for diagnosing early infection.

In RT-PCR, the viral RNA is first converted into complementary DNA (cDNA) using reverse transcriptase, followed by amplification of specific viral gene sequences (e.g., N, E, S, or RdRp genes) using PCR. If viral RNA is present, the test produces a positive result, confirming infection. RT-PCR can detect the virus even in asymptomatic or early-stage infections, making it crucial for early diagnosis, contact tracing, and outbreak control.

RT-PCR involves the reverse transcription of the virus's genetic material (RNA) to complementary DNA (cDNA), followed by amplification of some regions of the cDNA. Four regions of the SARS CoV2 genome are used as targets:

* RdRp gene (RNA-dependent RNA polymerase)

* Genes from structural proteins

* E (virus envelope)

* N (virus nucleocapsid),

* ORF1ab gene (open reading frame 1a and 1b)

The results can be quantified as well. When RT PCR and qPCR are combined, they can be used to determine the relative concentrations of a particular mRNA molecule in a cell.

CBNAAT (cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification test) uses small, chip-based, portable, battery-operated devices that detect target genetic material of SARS CoV2. Examples include TrueNat and Cepheid Xpert Xpress SARS CoV-2

Other options:

Options A and B: Antibody testing- Antibodies of IgA, IgM, and IgG isotypes specific to different virus proteins are detected by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) or chemiluminescence immunoassays (CLIA). CLIA is more sensitive compared to ELISA.

Option C: Rapid antigen test (RAT)- Antigen-based assays are used as point-of-care tests for early detection of SARS-CoV-2. They are used at the field level for early detection of infection and quick containment. Most of such tests have relatively moderate sensitivity but high specificity. They are used for diagnosis along with RT-PCR.

ICMR has recently approved CoviSelf (nasal swab) for home testing of COVID-19 by RAT. It is advised only in symptomatic individuals and immediate contacts of laboratory confirmed positive cases. All individuals who test positive may be considered as true positives and no repeat testing is required.
questions.learning: RT-PCR — In the clinical scenario of a patient diagnosed with SARS-CoV-2, the confirmation test performed is RT-PCR. Reverse Transcription Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR) is the gold standard test for diagnosing COVID-19, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the underlying cause of the symptoms— fever, fatigue, and abnormal vital signs—in this 55-year-old man, and which causative organism is identified on microscopic examination of his peripheral blood smear?
questions.explanation: The peripheral blood smear provides two diagnostic hallmarks of Plasmodium falciparum: 1) multiple delicate ring-form trophozoites within a single red blood cell, and 2) the presence of crescent or banana-shaped gametocytes. These features are unique to P. falciparum and are not seen in the other species. P. vivax (Option A) and P. ovale (Option C) typically show enlarged RBCs with Schüffner's dots and round gametocytes. P. malariae (Option D) shows "band-form" trophozoites. P. falciparum is the most dangerous species because it can infect RBCs of all ages, leading to high parasitemia and complications like cerebral malaria or blackwater fever. The abnormal vital signs in this 55-year-old male suggest potentially severe malaria. Immediate treatment with Artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) is essential. Given the pathognomonic crescentic gametocytes, the identification of Plasmodium falciparum is definitive
questions.learning: The peripheral blood smear provides two diagnostic hallmarks of Plasmodium falciparum: 1) multiple delicate ring-form trophozoites within a single red blood cell, and 2) the presence of crescent or banana-shaped gametocytes.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following acts as a major intracellular antioxidant and helps in detoxifying reactive oxygen species?
questions.explanation: Glutathione is the primary intracellular antioxidant responsible for neutralizing reactive oxygen species (ROS). It is a tripeptide composed of glutamate, cysteine, and glycine. Glutathione detoxifies ROS by donating electrons, converting harmful radicals into less reactive compounds, and is also essential for regenerating other antioxidants like vitamins C and E. While other enzymes are involved in the antioxidant defense, they have more specific roles: Superoxide dismutase (Option C) specifically converts superoxide radicals into hydrogen peroxide. Catalase (Option B) then converts that hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. Peroxidase (Option D) breaks down peroxides using reducing agents, often utilizing glutathione as a donor. Because glutathione acts as the central hub for electron donation and cellular redox balance, it is classified as the major intracellular antioxidant
questions.learning: Glutathione is the primary intracellular antioxidant responsible for neutralizing reactive oxygen species (ROS). It is a tripeptide composed of glutamate, cysteine, and glycine.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A young man presented with hearing loss and tinnitus. Histology image is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Schwannoma

The history of hearing loss and tinnitus and the histology showing Verocay bodies are suggestive of Schwannoma.

Vestibular Schwannoma (acoustic neuroma), is a benign tumor that predominantly originates from the Schwann cells in the vestibular division of the eighth cranial nerve, but it rarely arises from the cochlear division. It commonly affects individuals aged 40-60, with no gender preference. Bilateral schwannomas occur in neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2).

The most common presenting manifestations are progressive, unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, often accompanied by tinnitus.

It can involve all cranial nerves except the first and second. Apart from the 8th cranial nerve, the earliest cranial nerve to be involved is the 5th cranial nerve leading to reduced corneal sensitivity and paraesthesia of the face. This indicates that the tumor is roughly 2.5 cm in diameter and occupies the cerebellopontine angle.

Facial nerve involvement causes hypoaesthesia of the posterior meatal wall (Hitzelberger sign), taste loss, and delayed blink reflex. The earliest sign is a delayed blink reflex.

Glossopharyngeal (IX) and vagus (X) nerve involvement result in dysphagia and hoarseness. Brainstem involvement manifests as ataxia, limb weakness, numbness, and increased tendon reflexes. Cerebellar involvement leads to an unsteady gait and dysdiadochokinesia.

Histopathologically, the tumor comprises dense Antoni A areas with spindle cells in a palisading pattern and Antoni B areas with loosely arranged spindle cells in a myxoid matrix. Verocay bodies are formed in the Antoni A region, characterized by nuclear-free zones surrounded by palisaded nuclei.

Pure tone audiometry reveals sensorineural hearing loss, particularly in high frequencies. Speech audiometry shows the roll-over phenomenon. The absence of the recruitment phenomenon is noted. Short Increment Sensitivity Index (SISI) ranges from 0-20%.

Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry (BERA) demonstrates a significant delay of >0.2 ms in wave V between the two ears. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) with gadolinium contrast is considered the gold standard for diagnosis.

The primary management is the surgical removal of the tumor via the middle cranial fossa approach, the trans-labyrinthine approach, the suboccipital (retro sigmoid) approach, or a combined trans-labyrinthine-suboccipital approach.

Conventional radiotherapy using external beam radiation is not effective. In cases where surgery is contraindicated, refused by the patient, or when a residual tumor remains, alternative treatments such as the x-knife or gamma knife can be considered.

Other options:

Option A: Neurofibromas are also benign nerve sheath tumours and the histological picture shows the presence of bland Schwann cells admixed with stromal cells such as mast cells, perineural cells, and fibroblasts. The stroma of the tumour contains loose collagen arranged in wavy bundles resembling carrot shavings.

Option C: Leiomyomas are benign smooth muscle neoplasms that may occur single or multiple. Microscopically, leiomyomas are comprised of well-differentiated, regular, spindle-shaped smooth muscle cells associated with hyalinization. Very less mitotic figures are seen.

Option D: Rhabdomyomas are the most frequent primary tumours of the heart in children. Microscopically, they are composed of bizarre, markedly enlarged myocytes with abundant glycogen. But due to routine histological processing, the glycogen content is reduced and looks like thin strands that stretch from the nuclei to the surface membrane, which appears like spider cells.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following are causes of acquired systemic amyloidosis? 1. Tuberculosis 2. Multiple myeloma 3. Untreated rheumatoid arthritis 4. Chronic osteomyelitis Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, 3 and 4

Systemic amyloidosis is characterized by extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils in various organs, leading to progressive organ dysfunction. The two major forms of acquired systemic amyloidosis are AL (light-chain) amyloidosis, associated with plasma cell disorders, and AA (secondary) amyloidosis, associated with chronic inflammatory or infectious diseases.

Why is D correct?

• 1. Tuberculosis: Chronic inflammation leads to increased Serum Amyloid A (SAA) protein, resulting in AA amyloidosis.
• 2. Multiple myeloma: Causes AL amyloidosis due to deposition of monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains.
• 3. Untreated rheumatoid arthritis: A classic cause of secondary (AA) amyloidosis due to persistent inflammation.
• 4. Chronic osteomyelitis: Long-standing infection increases SAA production, leading to AA amyloid deposition.
questions.learning: 1, 2, 3 and 4 Systemic amyloidosis is characterized by extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils in various organs, leading to progressive organ dysfunction.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient's eye was hit by a tennis ball and developed Hyphema. What is the likely source of bleeding ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Circulus arteriosus major

Circulus arteriosus major is responsible for Hyphaema (blood in the anterior chamber).

Hyphaema:

Causes of Hyphaema:

* Ocular injuries

* Postoperative

* Herpes zoster iritis

* Gonococcal iritis

* Intraocular tumor

* Spontaneous (from rubeosis iridis)

Two-way irrigation and aspiration cannula can be used for aspirating hyphaema.

Blood Supply of Eye:

Cornea: Avascular

Uvea: 3 arteries are important.

* Short post ciliary artery- Choroid

* Long post ciliary artery-2 in number join each other near ciliary muscle with anterior ciliary arteries to form circulus arteriolar major (C A major).

* Short anterior ciliary arteries join long posterior ciliary arteries to form C A major.

* Branches from circulus arteriolar major go to the pupillary border to form circulus arteriosus minor(C A minor).

Retina:

* Outer four layers-choriocapillaries (RPE, rods and cones, ELM, outer nuclear layer)

* Inner layers- Central retinal artery

* Macula- Branches of central retinal artery + Choriocapillaries.

* Foveola- Avascular

Optic Nerve Head:

* Surface nerve fibre layer- From retinal arteriole.

* Lamina cribrosa- From ciliary vessels derived from posterior ciliary artery and arterial circle of Zinn and Haller.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · Ascites Chronic Diarrhoea
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding Ménétrier’s disease: 1. There is excessive production of Transforming Growth Factor-alpha (TGF-α). 2. Majority of the patients present with features of protein-losing enteropathy. 3. Mucus secreting cells are replaced by parietal and chief cells. 4. The mucosal folds of the body and fundus of the stomach are greatly enlarged. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

• 1. Excessive production of TGF-α: Correct

• Ménétrier disease is associated with overexpression of transforming growth factor-α (TGF-α), which activates EGFR signaling and causes gastric foveolar hyperplasia.

• 2. Protein-losing enteropathy: Correct

• The enlarged gastric mucosa causes excessive protein loss into the gastric lumen, resulting in hypoalbuminemia and edema.
• Protein-losing gastropathy is a characteristic clinical feature.

• 3. Mucus-secreting cells are replaced by parietal and chief cells: Incorrect

• The opposite occurs: parietal and chief cells are reduced/replaced by proliferating mucus-secreting foveolar cells.

• 4. Enlarged mucosal folds of body and fundus: Correct

• There is marked giant gastric rugal/fold enlargement, predominantly involving the body and fundus, with relative sparing of the antrum.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Sabin-Feldman dye test is used for diagnosis of which of the following condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Toxoplasmosis

Sabin-Feldman dye test is used for the diagnosis of toxoplasmosis.

It is based on the principle that the presence of anti-toxoplasma antibodies in the patient's serum inhibits the staining of trophozoites by alkaline methylene blue dye. Toxoplasma trophozoites and complement are added to the patient's serum which is then incubated for an hour at 37°C. After incubation, methylene blue dye is added.

• If anti-toxoplasma antibodies are present in the serum, these are activated by complement and the parasite membrane is lysed. Thus, the trophozoites are not stained (positive result).
• If there are no antibodies, trophozoites will take up the stain and appear blue under the microscope (negative result).

The dilution of the test serum at which 50% of the tachyzoites are not stained is reported as the antibody titer of the test serum. The test is highly sensitive and specific. However, it cannot differentiate between recent or past infections as it detects only IgG antibodies.
questions.learning: Toxoplasmosis Sabin-Feldman dye test is used for the diagnosis of toxoplasmosis. It is based on the principle that the presence of anti-toxoplasma antibodies in the patient's serum inhibits the staining of trophozoites by alkaline methylene blue dye.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.topic: General Pharmacology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 35-year-old man underwent an allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant for aplastic anemia. Eight months later, he develops progressive cutaneous sclerosis, oral lichenoid lesions, and restrictive lung disease. He has an inadequate response to systemic corticosteroids and calcineurin inhibitors. A newer oral agent approved specifically for steroid-refractory chronic graft-versus-host disease is initiated. Which of the following drugs is most appropriate in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Belumosudil

• Belumosudil is a ROCK2 inhibitor
• Approved for chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGVHD)
• Used in patients after failure of ≥2 prior lines of systemic therapy

Acts by:

• ↓ Pro-fibrotic signaling
• Modulating Th17 / Treg balance

Given orally

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Ruxolitinib: A JAK1/2 inhibitor mainly approved for steroid-refractory acute GVHD.

B. Ibrutinib: A BTK inhibitor approved for cGVHD but less specific for fibrotic manifestations.

D. Sirolimus: An mTOR inhibitor used as immunosuppression, not a newer targeted therapy for steroid-refractory cGVHD.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is the most dependent part of a female?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rectouterine pouch

The rectouterine pouch, which is also called the pouch of Douglas is the most dependent part of a female.

Peritoneum of the female pelvis:

In females, the peritoneum covers the anterior and anterolateral surfaces of the rectum, uterus, and urinary bladder. Spaces found in the female pelvis are:

Pararectal fossae: Present on either side of the rectum. They are limited laterally by the peritoneum that covers the uterosacral ligaments.

Paravesical fossae: Present on either side of the bladder. It is limited laterally by the peritoneum which covers the round ligament of the uterus.

Rectouterine pouch: The peritoneum which covers the anterior surface of the rectum is reflected anteriorly to cover the posterior surface of the posterior fornix of the vagina and the uterus, forming a rectouterine pouch.  This is also known as the pouch of Douglas or posterior pelvic cul-de-sac. It forms the most dependent part when a woman is sitting or standing.

Vesicouterine pouch: The peritoneum covering the fundus and body of the uterus, is reflected anteriorly to cover the posterosuperior surface of the bladder forming a vesicouterine pouch.

Ovarian fossa: It is a shallow depression in the peritoneal lining of the lateral pelvic wall between the peritoneal ridges. It is formed by the obliterated umbilical arteries anteriorly, the ureter posteriorly, and the external iliac vessels above. It lies behind the lateral attachment of the broad ligament and contains the ovary in nulliparous females.

questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All are features of venous thrombus, except:
options: Composed mainly of red cells (red thrombi)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Caused by turbulent blood flow

Venous thrombi (red thrombi) typically form due to blood stasis and hypercoagulability, which are key components of Virchow’s triad.

Features of venous thrombi:

• Commonly occur in deep veins of the legs (DVT).
• Propagate in the direction of blood flow (antegrade) toward the heart.
• Rich in red blood cells and fibrin, giving them a red appearance.

Important distinction:

• Turbulent blood flow is mainly associated with arterial thrombus formation, not venous thrombi.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with a fish bone impacted in the pyriform sinus. During its removal, an accidental nerve injury occurs. Which nerve is most likely to be damaged in this situation?
options: Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
questions.explanation: The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (IBSLN) provides sensory innervation to the laryngeal mucosa above the vocal cords, the pharynx, and the pyriform sinus. It pierces the thyrohyoid membrane along with the superior laryngeal artery. During procedures in the pyriform sinus, this purely sensory nerve is at high risk of accidental injury due to its close proximity. Damage to this nerve results in the loss of the protective cough reflex in the supraglottic region, significantly predisposing the patient to aspiration. The recurrent laryngeal nerve (Option A) supplies motor innervation to most intrinsic laryngeal muscles but is not typically exposed during pyriform sinus surgery. The glossopharyngeal nerve (Option B) provides sensation to the oropharynx and posterior tongue rather than the pyriform sinus. The external branch (Option D) is located more superficially and provides motor supply to the cricothyroid muscle
questions.learning: The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (IBSLN) provides sensory innervation to the laryngeal mucosa above the vocal cords, the pharynx, and the pyriform sinus.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient is brought to the OPD with complaints of speaking nonsensical and made-up words. However, his speech is easy and fluent. His family claims his speech was fine until a few hours back. Which type of aphasia does the patient most likely have?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fluent aphasia

The patient is most likely suffering from fluent aphasia/ Wernicke's aphasia. The speech is easy and fluent but there are difficulties related to the output of language like paraphasia (substitution of similar-sounding, non-words, or incorrect words) and neologisms (non-existent words).

It is a type of aphasia that is seen in the lesions of the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus due to the involvement of the Wernicke's area. The speech is full of jargon and neologisms that make little sense.

Other options:

Option B- Broca's or motor/non-fluent aphasia is seen in lesions of the inferior frontal gyrus which contains the motor speech area. Speech is non-fluent and interrupted, with a paucity of functional words.

Option C- Comprehension of written language and the ability to name objects are compromised in anomic aphasia. This aphasia is caused by damage to the angular gyrus that disrupts visual information processing and transmission to the Wernicke area.

Option D- Conduction aphasia is seen in lesions of the arcuate fasciculus, the bundle of nerve fibers connecting the Wernicke and Broca's areas. Repetition of words is impaired and paraphasias are observed, though not as much as in Wernicke aphasia.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What are the effects of posterior lesions in a Brodmann's area 22 in a stroke patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Receptive Speech Function

A posterior lesion in Brodmann's area 22, which is located in the superior temporal gyrus, typically affects receptive speech function. It is the sensory speech area.

The patient will most likely have Wernicke’s aphasia due to the damage to Wernicke’s area - area 22.

In Wernicke's aphasia, there is difficulty in finding words leading to poorly understood content for the listener. These patients also find it difficult to repeat sentences and name things properly. It is a type of fluent aphasia in which the speech is easy and fluent but there are difficulties related to the output of language like paraphasia (substitution of similar-sounding, non-words, or incorrect words). The speech is full of jargon and neologisms (non-existent words) that make little sense.

Other options:

Option A: Auditory Function is primarily mediated by Brodmann area 41, which is located in the primary auditory cortex within the superior temporal gyrus.

Option C: Expressive Speech Function is associated with Brodmann areas 44 and 45 (Broca's area), which are involved in language production and speech articulation. Lesions here can cause difficulty in producing coherent speech (Broca's aphasia).
Option D: Visual function primarily associated with Brodmann areas 17, 18, and 19 (the primary and secondary visual cortices).
questions.learning: Receptive Speech Function — A posterior lesion in Brodmann's area 22, which is located in the superior temporal gyrus, typically affects receptive speech function.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Rukmini is participating in the Village Health, Nutrition, and Sanitation Day. How often is this program organized?
questions.explanation: The Village Health, Nutrition and Sanitation Day (VHNSD) is a critical platform for the delivery of essential health services at the community level in India. According to the National Health Mission guidelines, VHNSD is conducted every month in every village across the country. Usually organized at the Anganwadi center, the day brings together health workers (ASHAs and ANMs) and Anganwadi workers to provide services such as immunization, antenatal care, growth monitoring of children, and counseling on nutrition and sanitation. Options B, C, and D are incorrect frequencies for this specific program. The monthly VHNSD ensures regular contact between the community and the primary health system, facilitating early detection of health issues and improving the coverage of life-saving interventions. It also provides an opportunity for health education on topics like handwashing, toilet use, and diversified diets. This community-based approach is fundamental for reducing maternal and child mortality in rural areas
questions.learning: The Village Health, Nutrition and Sanitation Day (VHNSD) is a critical platform for the delivery of essential health services at the community level in India.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following pathological features is incorrectly matched with the disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Suppurative and purulent lesions: Syphilis

Syphilis is not known to cause suppurative and purulent lesions. It causes macular, papular or mixed maculopapular lesions.

Syphilis presents with the following lesions as it progresses through different stages :

• Primary syphilis - Hard chancre, which is painless papule that becomes eroded and indurated.
• Secondary Syphilis - Skin rashes on palms and soles which may be macular, papular, papulosquamous and nodular, but never vesicular or bullous.

• Condylomata lata- mucocutaneous papules that coalesce to form large pink to grey lesions in warm moist intertriginous areas)
• Generalized lymphadenopathy is seen

• Tertiary Syphilis - Gummas, which are locally destructive granulomatous lesions. They are most commonly seen in bone and skin.

Other options :

Option A - Immunodeficient individuals lack the normal response to antigens. This is the reason for the false negative Mantoux test seen in such individuals.

Option B - Chickenpox belongs to the alpha subfamily of herpes group of viruses which has a cytopathic effect of formation of multinucleated giant cells, with rounding and ballooning of infected cells

Option C - Berryliosis is an occupational lung disease, causing a chronic granulomatous inflammatory disease similar to sarcoidosis. Biopsy reveals non-caseating granulomas with monocytic infiltration.
questions.learning: Suppurative and purulent lesions: Syphilis Syphilis is not known to cause suppurative and purulent lesions. It causes macular, papular or mixed maculopapular lesions.

A study is conducted to identify the association between vaccination and the development of a disease in a community. Based on the data, 6 vaccinated individuals and 12 unvaccinated individuals developed severe disease. Calculate the relative risk for this community.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 0.5

The relative risk in this case will be 0.5.

Relative risk is the ratio of the incidence of disease (or death) among exposed and the incidence among non-exposed. It is a direct measure of the strength of the association between suspected cause and effect in a cohort study.

Here,

Incidence of disease among exposed (Vaccinated) = 6

Incidence of disease among non-exposed (Unvaccinated) = 12

Relative risk (RR) = Incidence exposed/incidence unexposed = 6/12 = 0.5

Relative Risk

* The ratio of incidence of disease or death among exposed to that among the non-exposed is called relative risk (RR).

* It is also called the risk ratio.

* It is the direct measure of the strength of association between suspected cause and effect in cohort studies.

* RR = 1 indicates no association.

* RR of 2 or higher indicates a 100% increase in risk.

questions.text: A 65-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to a 3-day history of headaches localized to the right temporal region. The headaches are accompanied by intermittent blurring of vision in both eyes. The patient has also felt fatigued for the past week, with stiffness in the shoulders and hips. Laboratory studies show an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 115 mm/hr. Which of the following is the most important mediator of this patient's current condition?

Correct answer: D. IL-6

This patient has giant cell (temporal) arteritis, suggested by:

• Age >50 years
• Temporal headache with visual symptoms
• Polymyalgia rheumatica symptoms (shoulder/hip stiffness)

Interleukin-6 (IL-6) is the key inflammatory mediator driving:

• Systemic inflammation and constitutional symptoms
• Elevated ESR and CRP
• Vascular inflammation and intimal proliferation
• IL-6 inhibitors (eg, tocilizumab) are effective treatments in giant cell arteritis.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Magistrate's inquest is done in _________
options: When the family wants to reconduct the inquest
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Death due to police firing

Magistrate's inquest is done in the case of death due to police firing.

BNSS 196 or section 176 Cr. P.C. deals with magistrate inquest in which the cause of death is not under natural circumstances. A magistrate’s inquest is an inquest conducted by a District Magistrate, Subdivisional Magistrate, and magistrate of the first class rank or any other magistrate as empowered by the State Government, such as Collector, Deputy Collector, or Tehsildar (Executive Magistrates).

Special Magistrate’s inquests are held in cases of:

* Lock-up deaths

* Deaths while under police interrogation

* Deaths in prison

* Deaths in police custody

* Deaths due to police firing

* Exhumation

* Alleged dowry death

* In all cases where the police normally conduct inquests, magistrate can hold an additional inquest, or in place of the police inquest.

Note: It is practised throughout India. However, it is not held routinely but held only on special indications mentioned above. In any case of unnatural death, the magistrate may hold an inquest instead of/ in addition to the police inquest.

Police Inquest: The inquest is held by a police officer (called Investigating Officer) not below the rank of Senior Head Constable. It is practised throughout India.
questions.learning: Death due to police firing Magistrate's inquest is done in the case of death due to police firing. P.C. deals with magistrate inquest in which the cause of death is not under natural circumstances.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: According to National Programme for Control of Blindness and Visual Impairment which of the following is incorrect about the reach in approach?
options: People with cataract are treated in a makeshift operation centre
IOL placement by small incision cataract surgery is preferred
Reach in approach has lesser post operative complications
People with cataract are identified and sent to higher centre
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. People with cataract are treated in a makeshift operation centre

Patients with cataract are not operated in makeshift operation centres but are rather shifted to base hospitals (reach-in approach) as the visual acuity results indicate that the Base Hospital had significantly higher final corrected visual acuity compared to the Peripheral Eye Camps.

The Base Hospital approach, also known as the reach-in approach, and the Peripheral Eye Camp approach, also known as the reach-out approach, are two community-oriented strategies implemented within the framework of the National Programme for the Control of Blindness. These techniques aim to address the existing backlog of cataract-related blindness. Both methods have demonstrated efficacy and possess distinct advantages and disadvantages. Both community participation and intersectoral coordination, together with the utilization of suitable technology at an affordable price, are essential components for both endeavours.

Based on recent developments, there is a shift in emphasis from the 'Reach-out' approach to the 'Reach-in' approach. The Reach-in Approach involves the organization of screening camps in rural and remote locations that lack access to eye-care institutions. Comprehensive eye care treatments, including refraction, are offered to patients. Subsequently, those requiring cataract surgery are conveyed to the nearest hospitals that possess adequate resources and facilities, following the base hospital strategy. To conduct ocular surgery, it is imperative to comply with the guidelines established by the Government of India.

• It is imperative to have at least one anesthesiologist who is well prepared to address typical crises to ensure patient safety and optimal care.
• It is recommended that a minimum of one, ideally two, operating surgeons be present, with each surgeon limiting their daily caseload to no more than 30 procedures.
• Currently, the preferred approach for cataract extraction is extracapsular surgery, with a preference for manual small incision cataract surgery (SICS) or phacoemulsification, together with the implantation of a posterior chamber intraocular lens.
• It is ideal to limit the number of surgical procedures conducted in a day to no more than 50.
• Simultaneous surgery on both eyes should be avoided.
• Patients who have a high surgical risk due to conditions such as severe diabetes, severe hypertension, and cardiac issues should not undergo surgery in camp settings. Cases related to such issues should be appropriately referred to the base hospitals.

National Programme for the Control of Blindness and Visual Impairment (NPCBVI). The levels of eye care, according to NPCBVI are:

Primary level: Sub-district level hospitals, community health centres, mobile ophthalmic units, upgraded PHCs, link workers, and Panchayats.
Secondary level: District hospitals, NGO eye hospitals
Tertiary levels: Regional institutes of Ophthalmology, medical colleges.
The goal is to reduce the prevalence of blindness to 0.3% by 2020.

questions.text: A 36-year-old woman has severe dyschezia and cyclical rectal pain. MRI suggests deep rectosigmoid endometriosis. The MRI sign as shown in the image is classically associated with deep rectosigmoid endometriosis. What is this sign called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mushroom cap sign

Deep infiltrating endometriosis (DIE) of the rectosigmoid typically involves the serosa and muscularis propria, producing a characteristic T2-hypointense plaque or mass with retraction and thickening of the bowel wall.

• Mushroom cap sign on MRI is classically associated with rectosigmoid deep infiltrating endometriosis.
• It reflects T2-dark fibromuscular infiltration with intact mucosa/submucosa forming the “cap,” implying extrinsic or mural involvement rather than primary mucosal disease.

Other options

A. Double decidual sac sign

Incorrect. This is an early intrauterine pregnancy sign on ultrasound, not related to endometriosis or bowel DIE.

C. Cogwheel sign

Incorrect. “Cogwheel” is classically used for thickened endosalpingeal folds seen in hydrosalpinx (often on ultrasound) and is not the signature MRI sign for rectosigmoid DIE.

D. Beads-on-string sign

Incorrect. This term is classically used in other systems (for example, gallbladder adenomyomatosis) and is not the hallmark MRI descriptor for rectosigmoid DIE.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with a severe headache and neck stiffness. There is no history of fever. The CT brain taken is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Subarachnoid haemorrhage

The given clinical scenario of an afebrile patient with a severe headache, neck stiffness with CT head showing hyperdense areas in the basal cisterns and sulci, is highly suggestive of Subarachnoid haemorrhage.

Subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) is the bleeding into the subarachnoid space, which is the area between the arachnoid membrane and the pia mater surrounding the brain. It usually occurs due to bleeding from a ruptured aneurysm or arteriovenous malformation. Most of the ruptured aneurysms are located at the circle of Willis.

Patients present with a sudden and severe headache referred to as thunderclap headache, which may be associated with vomiting, decreased consciousness, and seizures. Neck stiffness and photophobia may develop after a few hours.

Non-contrast CT scan is the imaging modality of choice if done within 12 hours. It shows an increased density of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) spaces. A lumbar puncture should be done if there is a strong suspicion of SAH but negative CT findings. It is ideally done 12 hours later. This allows for red blood cell lysis to occur and bilirubin to be detected in the CSF.

Other options:

Option A: Bacterial meningitis is characterised by high fever, neck stiffness, and positive Brudzinski's sign.

Option B: Subdural haemorrhage is often due to the rupture of bridging veins that crosses the subdural space. In subdural hemorrhage, the CT shows crescentic opacity.

Option D: Extradural haemorrhage is mostly due to the rupture of the middle meningeal artery. Since the dura matter tends to adhere to the skull, the hemorrhage is seen in CT as a biconvex dense area. They usually do not cross cranial sutures.

Pearl PF2181: Types of Intracranial Hemorrhage

1. Extradural hemorrhage/epidural hematoma (EDH)

* Source: Arterial - middle meningeal artery (m/c)

* Cause: Trauma - fracture of the squamous part of the temporal bone

* Lens or lentiform shaped opacity

* Presence of a characteristic lucid interval

* Treatment: Surgical evacuation of large/rapidly evolving EDH

2. Acute subdural hemorrhage (SDH)

* Source: Venous - bridging veins

* Cause: Trauma

* Common in old age, alcoholics, patients on anticoagulants, shaken baby syndrome (a form of child abuse seen in infants and toddlers)

* Clinical features: Acute SDH may be associated with a lucid interval; chronic SDH is associated with drowsiness, headache

* CT findings: Crescent opacity

* Treatment: May resolve spontaneously or require surgical drainage

3. Acute on chronic SDH

* Source: Venous - bridging veins

* Cause: Usually, trivial trauma in old age or patients on anticoagulants

* Crescent clots

* Presence of a history of headache, confusion, and being prone to falls

4. Subarachnoid hemorrhage

* Source: Arterial

* Causes: Trauma (most common), berry aneurysm (2nd most common)

* M/c sites: Terminal ICA, MCA bifurcation, top of basilar artery

* Clinical features: Characteristic thunderclap headache

* CSF: Xanthochromia

* Hyperdensity in the subarachnoid space

* Treatment: Early repair by clipping/coiling of berry aneurysm. Nimodipine and IV fluids with monitoring to prevent vasospasm.

5. Intra-parenchymal hemorrhage

* Most common type of intracranial hemorrhage

* Cause: Hypertension (most common cause)

* Hyperdensity within the brain parenchyma

* Site: Putamen of the basal ganglia (most common)

* Treatment: Correction of any identified coagulopathy by infusing prothrombin complex concentrates, FFP, or fresh platelets as required; surgical evacuation for cerebellar hematoma >3 cm in size

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A middle-aged female patient with RA for 5 years also has a family history of RA. She's on treatment with methotrexate with worsening symptoms. She was enrolled in a trial of a new epigenome-modifying drug. After 8 weeks, her symptoms improved. All of the following regarding this drug is true except:
options: It directly binds to cytokine receptors to block inflammatory signalling
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. It directly binds to cytokine receptors to block inflammatory signalling

The stem gives:

• RA patient (chronic autoimmune arthritis)
• Methotrexate failure → escalation therapy
• “Epigenome-modifying drug” → think upstream gene regulation

Epigenetic drugs regulate gene expression upstream; they do NOT directly block cytokine receptors (that’s biologics like tocilizumab). Epigenetics = changing gene expression WITHOUT altering DNA sequence

Mechanisms include:

• Histone modification (acetylation/deacetylation)
• DNA methylation
• microRNA regulation

These affect inflammatory gene transcription.

| Feature | Epigenetic Drugs | Biologics

| ------- | ---------------- | ---------

| Level of action | Gene expression | Protein/cytokine

| Target | DNA/chromatin | Cytokines/receptors

| Example | HDAC inhibitors | Tocilizumab, Etanercept

| IL-6/TNF effect | ↓ production | Block action

| Specificity | Broad | Targeted

D) It directly binds to cytokine receptors to block inflammatory signalling

• This is the mechanism of biologics, not epigenetic drugs

| Drug | Target

| ---- | ------

| Tocilizumab | IL-6 receptor

| Etanercept | TNF-α

| Infliximab | TNF-α

These are receptor-level blockers, not gene modulators.

• RA synovium shows abnormal DNA methylation patterns
• Epigenetic therapy aims to “reset” this inflammatory memory

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Identify the instrument:
questions.explanation: The instrument shown is the Bohler Braun Splint, a heavy metallic frame equipped with four pulleys for applying traction to the lower limb. It is used for fractures of the femoral shaft, supracondylar area, and occasionally tibial fractures. Its design helps prevent foot drop and ensures traction is maintained in the appropriate anatomical line. A Thomas splint (Option B) is another common traction device but features a distinct proximal ring to support the thigh. The Volkmann splint (Option C) is primarily used for the forearm to prevent contractures after injury. Cramer wire (Option D) is a simple, malleable metal ladder-like splint used for temporary immobilization and kontouring to limb shapes. While effective, the Bohler Braun splint is cumbersome and poses risks associated with long-term recumbency, such as bedsores or pneumonia

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient comes to you with a history of unprotected sex 96 hours ago. Which of the following emergency contraceptives can be used in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Intra uterine contraceptive device (IUCD)

Since the patient had unprotected sex 96 hours ago, an intrauterine contraceptive device(IUCD) can be used for emergency contraception in this case. It can be inserted within 5 days of coitus as a method of emergency contraception. All other methods of emergency contraception mentioned above need to be administered within 72 hours.

The administration of postcoital contraceptive agents that interfere with postovulatory events that can lead to pregnancy is known as the emergency contraception method. They are used to prevent pregnancy after unprotected intercourse.

IUCD (Intrauterine contraceptive device) prevents the implantation of a fertilized ovum. It does so by acting as a foreign body within the uterine cavity. This leads to increased contractility, tubal peristalsis, and promotes leukocytic infiltration in the endometrium so that the fertilized egg is unable to implant.

* The hyoid bone is a 'U-shaped' bone suspended from the tips of the styloid processes by the stylohyoid ligaments.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient came to medical OPD with complaints of polyuria. He has a history of undergoing total hypophysectomy. His Na+ levels are found to be 155 mEq/L, urine osmolarity was 200 mOsm/L. What is the definitive management in this patient?
options: DDAVP for 2 weeks and then discontinue
Upsetting of receptors so no treatment is required
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. DDAVP supplementation for lifelong

Based on the given clinical vignette, the most likely diagnosis is central diabetes insipidus. Lifelong supplementation of desmopressin (DDAVP), a synthetic analog of AVP, is the definitive management in this scenario.

Diabetes insipidus (DI) is a syndrome characterized by the excretion of abnormally large volumes of dilute urine. The 24-hour urine volume exceeds 40 mL/kg body weight, and the 24-hour urine osmolarity is <280 mOsm/L. There will be a slight increase in plasma osmolarity/sodium that stimulates thirst (polydipsia). Hence, clinical symptoms and signs of dehydration are uncommon unless thirst and/or water intake are also impaired.

Causes of central diabetes insipidus include

• Idiopathic
• Familial and congenital diseases -  familial neurohypophyseal DI, Wolfram syndrome, congenital hypopituitarism
• Neurosurgery and trauma - Trauma to the hypothalamus and posterior pituitary or neurosurgery with a transsphenoidal approach.
• Neoplasms
• Hypoxic encephalopathy
• Infiltrative disorders-  Langerhans cell histiocytosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, autoimmune lymphocytic hypophysitis, and sarcoidosis

Treatment of central diabetes insipidus due to resection of pituitary tumor includes lifelong supplementation with vasopressin analogs desmopressin (DDAVP) (1-deamino-8-D-arginine vasopressin).

Note: If partial hypophysectomy, which is the usual procedure, is done, DDAVP supplementation is usually required only for a short duration as there is only a transient AVP deficiency. However, in complete hypophysectomy which results in permanent diabetes insipidus, life-long administration of desmopressin may be required.
questions.learning: DDAVP supplementation for lifelong — Based on the given clinical vignette, the most likely diagnosis is central diabetes insipidus. Lifelong supplementation of desmopressin (DDAVP), a synthetic analog of AVP, is the definitive management in this scenario.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements correctly describes the characteristics of health propaganda?
options: It aids in developing a reflective behavior
questions.explanation: Health propaganda is a method of persuasion that primarily appeals to emotions and impulsive responses rather than relying on logical, evidence-based reasoning. Its goal is often to induce a specific behavior through fear, pressure, or biased information. Option A is incorrect as propaganda is usually "passively received" or imposed, unlike health education which is actively acquired. Option C is a distractor; while propaganda aims to change behavior, it is not "behavior-centered" in the pedagogical sense of building sustainable skills. Option D describes health education, which encourages critical thinking and reflective behavior. Propaganda is often one-way communication intended for rapid mass indoctrination. In the medical field, clinicians strive to avoid propaganda in favor of authentic health education, which empowers patients by providing objective facts and supporting autonomous decision-making. Recognizing the emotive nature of propaganda is essential for patients to distinguish between credible medical advice and manipulative marketing or misinformation
questions.learning: Health propaganda is a method of persuasion that primarily appeals to emotions and impulsive responses rather than relying on logical, evidence-based reasoning.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is a PCSK-9 inhibitor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Evolocumab

PCSK9 (Proprotein Convertase Subtilisin/Kexin Type 9) is a liver enzyme that regulates LDL receptor degradation.

Normally:

1️⃣ LDL receptors bind LDL cholesterol

2️⃣ LDL is taken into hepatocytes

3️⃣ LDL receptors are recycled back to the cell surface

But when PCSK9 binds LDL receptors, it causes: Receptor degradation

This results in higher LDL levels in blood.

Evolocumab is a PCSK-9 inhibitor that increases LDL receptor recycling on hepatocytes. This leads to marked reduction in LDL-cholesterol, especially in high-risk ASCVD patients.

| Drug | Type

| ---- | ----

| Evolocumab | Monoclonal antibody

| Alirocumab | Monoclonal antibody

Indications include:

• Familial hypercholesterolemia
• Very high-risk ASCVD
• Patients not controlled with statins + ezetimibe

Ezetimibe inhibits intestinal cholesterol absorption, evinacumab targets ANGPTL3, and everolimus is an mTOR inhibitor.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Whitaker test is indicated for which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hydronephrosis

Whitaker test is indicated for Hydronephrosis to compare the hydrostatic pressure between the renal pelvis and bladder.

Hydronephrosis is the aseptic dilatation of the kidney caused by obstruction. It is the most common urologic abnormality found on ultrasound evaluation.

WHITAKER TEST

The Whitaker test accurately detects the functional effect of upper urinary tract dilatation by measuring hydrostatic pressures in the renal pelvis and bladder while infusing a saline and contrast solution into the renal pelvis through a catheter.

The patient is positioned in the prone position on the fluoroscopic table with a bladder catheter in place, and a cannula is introduced percutaneously into the renal pelvis and attached to a pressure transducer. At a rate of 10 mL/min, a mixture of saline and contrast material is administered through the renal cannula, and pressures are monitored. The urinary tract is deemed nonobstructed if the renal pelvic pressure is less than 15 cm H2O, equivocal between 15 and 22 cm H2O, and obstructed if the pressure is greater than 22 cm H2O.

With the introduction of noninvasive imaging technology, the test should be used exclusively in the following situations to examine probable upper urinary tract obstruction:

* equivocal results from less invasive testing,

* suspected blockage with poor kidney function,

* loin discomfort with negative diuresis renogram findings,

* suspected intermittent obstruction,

* extensive dilatation with positive diuresis renogram findings are all possibilities.

Pearl PF1685: Causes of Hydronephrosis

Unilateral hydronephrosis

Extramural obstruction

* Tumor from adjacent structures, e.g., cervix, prostate, rectum, colon, or cecum

* Retrocaval ureter

* Aberrant renal vessels

* Idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis (Ormond’s disease)

Intramural obstruction

* Congenital PUJ obstruction - most common congenital cause

* Congenital stenosis

* Ureterocele

* Ureteric stricture - iatrogenic/ inflammatory

* Neoplasm of the ureter or bladder involving the ureteric orifice

Intraluminal obstruction

* Renal stones - most common acquired unilateral cause

* Sloughed papilla in papillary necrosis (especially, in patients with diabetes, analgesic abuse, or sickle cell disease)

Bilateral hydronephrosis

Congenital

* Posterior urethral valves (associated with pulmonary hypoplasia)

* Urethral atresia

* PUJ obstruction

Acquired

* Benign prostatic hypertrophy or carcinoma of the prostate

* Idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis (Ormond's disease)

* Postoperative bladder neck scarring

* Urethral stricture

* Phimosis

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: You are starting services for hypertension in your PHC. 50 patients who required antihypertensive treatment were transferred from another center. 40 of them were on amlodipine (5mg PO) and 10 were on lisinopril (10 mg PO) as they had contraindications to the use of amlodipine. The drugs are supplied at the PHC on a monthly basis and you have to place an order for their medications. What is the number of tablets that you will order and the reorder factor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1600, rf= 2

The Quantity to Order (QO) or the reorder quantity of medicines to be placed at each order interval is calculated using the reorder formula as given below:

QO = CA x (LT + PP) = CA x Rf

where QO is the quantity to order, CA is average consumption in a month, LT is lead time, PP is procurement period and Rf is the reorder factor. Reorder factor (Rf) is the sum of lead time (LT) and procurement period (PP). Lead time (LT) is the time between the initiation of a purchase order and receipt at the warehouse from the supplier. The procurement period (PP) covers the time until the next regular order will be placed.

In the given question, lead time (LT) and procurement period (PP) are 1 month each.

Average consumption (CA) in a month = (40 tablets of amlodipine + 10 tablets of lisinopril) x 30 days = 1500 tablets

Reorder factor (Rf) = LT + PP = 1 + 1 = 2

Since these patients got transferred from another center there is no safety stock for them at present at the facility. So in order to prevent stockouts for them, an extra number of tablets must be ordered, which makes 1600 tablets with a reorder factor (Rf) of 2 the correct option.

Factors determining the reorder formula are:

1. Average consumption or demand of the drug (CA) in a month
2. Supplier Lead time (LT): is the time between initiation of a purchase order and receipt at the warehouse from the supplier.
3. Safety stock (SS): is the stock that should always be on hand to prevent stockouts. The safety stock level and reorder level will be the same if consumption and lead times are predictable and stable.
4. Procurement period (PP): it covers the time until the next regular order will be placed. In a scheduled system this is in multiples of one month and in a perpetual system, it is counted in days or weeks. Note: Quantity ordered (QO) + Safety Stock (SS) must cover the time until the next order is received, which is given by the Reorder factor (Rf) = Procurement Period (PP) + Lead Time (LT).
5. Reorder level: is the quantity of remaining stock that should trigger a reorder of the item. In a basic purchasing formula, reorder level is calculated by multiplying the average lead time by the average consumption of the drug during the lead time.
6. Maximum stock level: is the same as the target stock level, which is required to satisfy demand until the next order is received.
7. Stock position: is the sum of stock on hand (working and safety stock) and stock on order, minus any stock back-ordered to clients.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which drug has been shown to be most effective in improving survival in patients with chronic stable angina who also exhibit features of heart failure?
questions.explanation: For patients with chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), ACE inhibitors like Lisinopril are a cornerstone of therapy. They work by blocking the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, reducing ventricular remodeling, and lowering afterload. Lisinopril has a proven mortality benefit, meaning it effectively improves the lifespan of these patients. Nifedipine (Option A) is a calcium channel blocker used for angina but can actually worsen outcomes in systolic heart failure. Digoxin (Option B) can improve symptoms and reduce hospitalizations but has never been shown to decrease overall mortality. Torsemide (Option D) is a loop diuretic essential for managing fluid overload; while it improves quality of life, it does not provide a mortality benefit like ACE inhibitors or beta-blockers. Therefore, because Lisinopril directly targets the disease process to extend life, it is the most effective choice among the options provided

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presented with abdominal pain and sterile pyuria, and the x-ray showed the following features. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Putty kidney

A patient with abdominal pain and sterile pyuria, with the given x-ray showing diffuse alveolar calcification in the right renal region point towards a diagnosis of a putty kidney.

The putty kidney is a characteristic finding of genitourinary tuberculosis (TB), specifically renal TB. The given image shows a homogenous and ground-glass-like calcification of the kidney appearing like putty. It is caused by the dissemination of the organism through the bloodstream and is thus always a secondary TB. There is either reinfection or reactivation of old TB.

Genitourinary TB is a cause of sterile pyuria. Diagnosis is confirmed with a tuberculin test, or at least 3 consecutive early-morning specimens of urine are examined for acid-fast bacilli. They are stained with a Ziehl-Neelsen stain and subsequently cultured.

CT is the most sensitive modality and is the preferred means of visualizing renal calcifications. CT urography is done to assess the various stages of renal TB and its manifestations, which are as follows:

• Early:

• Papillary necrosis

• Progressive:

• Multifocal strictures
• Generalized or focal hydronephrosis
• Mural thickening and enhancement
• Poorly enhancing renal parenchyma

• End-stage:

• Progressive hydronephrosis
• Amorphous dystrophic calcification that involves the entire kidney - putty kidney

Treatment involves short-course therapy with antitubercular drugs like pyrazinamide, isoniazid, and rifampicin. Partial nephrectomy, nephrectomy, or reconstructive surgery is often done.

Option B: Nephrocalcinosis - This condition is characterized by the deposition of calcium in the kidney parenchyma or tubules, often seen in hypercalcemic conditions like hyperparathyroidism. However, it would not explain the clinical presentation of sterile pyuria.

Option C: Staghorn calculi are large kidney stones that fill the renal pelvis and extend into the renal calyces, often caused by urinary tract infections with organisms such as Proteus, Pseudomonas, and Staphylococcus. While these calculi can cause abdominal pain, they usually do not result in sterile pyuria, as they are associated with infection.

The image below shows a staghorn calculus of the left kidney.

Option D: Psoas calcification - This refers to calcification within the psoas muscle and is often seen after acute renal failure and rhabdomyolysis. It is not associated with sterile pyuria and is not the cause of the patient's symptoms.
questions.learning: Putty kidney — A patient with abdominal pain and sterile pyuria, with the given x-ray showing diffuse alveolar calcification in the right renal region point towards a diagnosis of a putty kidney.

questions.text: A 50-year-old man comes to the OPD following transsphenoidal resection of a growth hormone secreting pituitary adenoma. Three months ago, the patient was diagnosed with acromegaly. MRI of the pituitary showed a 14 mm sellar mass pressing on the optic chiasm and extending into the right cavernous sinus. The surgeon was able to only partially resect the pituitary mass because of the extension into the right cavernous sinus. Medical therapy for acromegaly with octreotide is planned. Which of the following changes are likely to occur following octreotide treatment in this patient?
options: GH low, IGF-1 low, adenoma size low
GH low, IGF-1 low, adenoma size unchanged
GH low, IGF-1 unchanged, adenoma size low
GH unchanged, IGF-1 low, adenoma size unchanged
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. GH low, IGF-1 low, adenoma size low

Octreotide, a somatostatin analogue, is used for medical treatment of acromegaly, especially when pituitary adenoma cannot be completely resected.

Mechanism and effects:

• Inhibits growth hormone (GH) secretion from pituitary somatotroph cells
• Leads to decreased hepatic production of IGF-1
• Has an antiproliferative effect on the pituitary adenoma, often causing tumor shrinkage

Result after treatment:

• ↓ GH
• ↓ IGF-1
• ↓ Adenoma size

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A study utilizes office records from the past 20 years to compare the incidence of a disease between factory workers exposed to aniline dye and unexposed clerical staff. What type of epidemiological study does this represent?
questions.explanation: This study is a retrospective study (specifically a retrospective cohort) because it utilizes existing past records to assess exposure and outcomes that have already occurred. Subjects were grouped by their historical exposure status (aniline dye vs. clerical) and followed through the records to determine disease incidence. A prospective study (Option A) would follow individuals forward in time from the present into the future. A case-control study (Option C) would start by identifying individuals who already have the disease and looking back for exposure; here, the study started with exposure groups. An ecological study (Option D) compares whole populations or geographic areas rather than using individual-level data from office records. Retrospective studies are generally less expensive and time-consuming but are dependent on the accuracy of historical documentation
questions.learning: This study is a retrospective study (specifically a retrospective cohort) because it utilizes existing past records to assess exposure and outcomes that have already occurred.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with a nodule of the neck presents to the surgery OPD. A junior resident performs the following method to palpate it. Identify the procedure shown in the video below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lahey's method

The video depicts Lahey’s method of palpation of the left lobe of the thyroid gland.

In Lahey's method, for palpating the left lobe, the examiner initially pushes the right lobe medially with the left hand, and then using the right hand, the border and consistency of the left lobe is palpated.

Other options:

Option B: In Crile's method the patient is asked to swallow, while the examiner palpates the gland with the thumb. This gives a clear indication regarding the slight enlargement of the thyroid gland or small nodules.

Option C: Kocher's method is done to demonstrate the pressure effect of the thyroid gland on the trachea or larynx. Lateral compression will result in stridor.

Option D: Pemberton's sign (not method), is engorgement of neck veins when the patient is asked to raise their hands above the head and the arms should touch the ears. It is seen in patients with retrosternal goiter.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient presents with vault prolapse associated with both cystocele and rectocele. Considering this combination of pelvic organ prolapse, what would be the most appropriate and effective management strategy?
questions.explanation: Pelvic organ prolapse often involves multiple compartments simultaneously. A cystocele (bladder prolapse) represents a defect in the anterior vaginal wall, while a rectocele (rectum prolapse) represents a defect in the posterior wall. To comprehensively repair the pelvic floor in a patient with both these conditions along with vault prolapse, the most optimal surgical approach is to perform both anterior colporrhaphy and posterior colpoperineorrhaphy (Option C). Anterior colporrhaphy (Option A) specifically reinforces the anterior wall to correct the cystocele. Posterior colpoperineorrhaphy (Option B) reinforces the posterior wall and the perineal body to correct the rectocele. A hysterectomy (Option D) addresses uterine prolapse but will not fix the underlying fascial defects of the bladder or rectum on its own. Therefore, a combined multi-compartment repair is necessary to achieve a successful functional and anatomical outcome for the patient
questions.learning: Pelvic organ prolapse often involves multiple compartments simultaneously. A cystocele (bladder prolapse) represents a defect in the anterior vaginal wall, while a rectocele (rectum prolapse) represents a defect in the posterior wall.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with diffuse, heavily contaminated peritonitis undergoes laparotomy, after which the abdomen is intentionally left open. Which of the following measures would be most beneficial in this situation?
questions.explanation: Vacuum-Assisted Closure (VAC) therapy is highly effective for managing an "open abdomen" in patients with severe, contaminated peritonitis. It uses negative pressure to continuously remove infected exudates and edema, reducing local inflammation and promoting granulation tissue. Normal saline-soaked gauze (Option B) only keeps the tissue moist but does not actively drain infectious material. Immediate primary closure (Option C) is strictly avoided in such cases because it carries a high risk of sepsis and abdominal compartment syndrome in a swollen, infected cavity. Antibiotic-soaked gauze (Option D) has limited benefits as it lacks the active drainage and wound contraction provided by negative pressure. VAC therapy allows for gradual wound contraction, facilitates re-entry laparotomies if needed, and eventually enables a safe definitive closure once the infection has cleared

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements about Multiple Sclerosis are incorrect? A) 70% of patients with MS develop Optic Neuritis during the course of illness B) Oral steroids are first line for acute relapses C) Loss of colour and depth perception is proportional to loss of visual acuity D) Fundus examination can be normal
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. A, B, C

In multiple sclerosis, optic neuritis occurs in \~50%, not 70%, making statement A incorrect.

Autoimmune attack on optic nerve myelin

↓

Demyelination of optic nerve fibers

↓

↓ Conduction velocity

↓

Visual symptoms:

- Blurring of vision

- Pain on eye movement

- Color vision loss (early)

↓

Fundus initially normal (retrobulbar neuritis)

| Feature | Description

| ------- | -----------

| Vision loss | Subacute, unilateral

| Pain | On eye movement

| Color vision | Earliest affected

| Pupillary reflex | RAPD (Marcus Gunn pupil)

| Fundus | Normal initially

Acute relapses are treated with IV methylprednisolone, not oral steroids, so B is incorrect.

In optic neuritis, loss of color vision (red desaturation) is disproportionately greater than visual acuity loss, making C incorrect.

Fundus can be normal (retrobulbar neuritis), so D is correct; hence A, B, C are incorrect.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which type of PCR is suitable for identifying multiple causative agents?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Multiplex PCR

Multiplex PCR is used for simultaneous detection of multiple pathogens in a single reaction by using multiple sets of primers targeting different DNA sequences.

• Principle:

o    Multiple primer pairs → amplify different targets in one tube

o    Allows identification of multiple causative agents at once

• Advantages:

o    Saves time and cost

o    Requires smaller sample volume

o    Useful in syndromic diagnosis (e.g., respiratory, GI infections)

• Why not others:

o    Conventional PCR: detects single target per reaction

o    Real-time PCR: quantitative, but usually single target (unless multiplexed)

o    Nested PCR: increases sensitivity/specificity, not for multiple agents

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 50-year-old male presents with nasal obstruction. On examination, an irregular mass was visualized in the nasal cavity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Antrochoanal polyp

Most likely diagnosis is antrochoanal polyp.

Antrochoanal polyp is a type of non-neoplastic nasal polypoidal masses of edematous nasal or sinus mucosa. It arises from the mucosa of the maxillary antrum near its accessory ostium, comes out of it, and grows in the choana and nasal cavity. It is usually single and unilateral which are more commonly seen in children and young adults.

It has 3 parts namely

* Thin antral stalk,

* Round and globular choanal part, and

* Flat nasal part.

The clinical features include unilateral nasal obstruction, mucoid nasal discharge, and a hyponasal voice.

A large polyp may protrude from the nasal cavity and may appear pink and congested. It is soft and can be moved with a probe.Anterior rhinoscopy may miss it when it starts to grow posteriorly. Posterior rhinoscopy may reveal a globular mass filling the choana and hanging down behind the soft palate.

Diagnosis is made by radiograph of the paranasal sinuses reveals opacity of the involved antrum. Non-contrast CT scan reveals the extent of the polyp. Endoscopic examination reveals the antrochoanal polyp hidden posteriorly in the nasal cavity.

Endoscopic sinus surgery is the treatment of choice. Recurrence is uncommon after the complete removal of the polyp.

Option A thornwaldt cyst is the persistence of pouch of lushka and is located at the midline on the posterior nasopharyngeal wall. It rarely presents as a mass protruding in the nasal cavity

Option B hypertrophic rhinitis is the inflammation and thickening of nasal mucose, submucosa, glands and periosteum. It doesn't present as a mass lesion

Option C deviated nasal septum presents with nasal obstruction, but no mass lesion

Pearl PF1084: Antrochoanal Polyp

* Main etiological factors: Infection and allergy

* Usually affects children

* Site of origin: Mucosa of the maxillary antrum

* Clinical features:

* Usually single and unilateral

* Unilateral nasal obstruction which becomes bilateral when it grows posteriorly and obstructs opposite choana

* Mucoid nasal discharge

* Hyponasal voice

* Findings:

* Grows posteriorly and usually missed on anterior rhinoscopy

* Posterior rhinoscopy: Globular mass filling the choana or nasopharynx

* Investigation of choice: Nasal endoscopy. Shows nasal polyps that are pale, gelatinous and pedunculated

* Treatment of choice: FESS
questions.learning: Antrochoanal polyp Most likely diagnosis is antrochoanal polyp. Antrochoanal polyp is a type of non-neoplastic nasal polypoidal masses of edematous nasal or sinus mucosa.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A child presents with progressive pallor and bone pain, and HPLC analysis shows elevated HbS levels. What is the best treatment to reduce hemolysis in this patient?
questions.explanation: High-Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC) showing elevated HbS confirms a diagnosis of Sickle Cell Disease (SCD). SCD results from a mutation in the beta-globin gene, causing hemoglobin to polymerize in low-oxygen states, leading to RBC sickling and chronic hemolysis. Voxelotor is a novel HbS polymerization inhibitor that increases the affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen. By stabilizing the oxygenated state, it directly reduces sickling and, consequently, the rate of hemolysis. Hydroxyurea (Option A) is widely used in SCD to increase fetal hemoglobin (HbF), which reduces the frequency of painful vaso-occlusive crises, but it has a less direct effect on preventing active hemolysis compared to Voxelotor. Azacytidine (Option B) is used for myelodysplastic syndromes. Bortezomib (Option D) is a proteasome inhibitor used in multiple myeloma. Therefore, Voxelotor is the most effective pharmacotherapy specifically targeted at mitigating the hemolytic process in SCD patients

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: There is a group of 200 hypertensive patients. First group of 100 patients is given medical advice whereas a second group of 100 patients is advised lifestyle changes. Which of the following tests of significance is used to compare the blood pressure after 3 months ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Un- paired t test

The unpaired t-test is used to test the difference between two groups or means when the samples are independent of each other. Here, the blood pressure of the two groups who are given different interventions is being compared, which are independent of each other.

Pearl PF0591: Tests of Significance

How to choose which test to use?

* See the variable. Are the variables quantitative or qualitative?

* If the variables are qualitative (nominal), then Chi square test is used.

* If the variables are quantitative, then see whether 2 groups are being tested, or more than 2 groups.

* If 2 groups are being tested, then T tests are used. In that, if the same group is tested before and after, paired T test is used. Otherwise, unpaired T test is used.

* If more than 2 groups are being tested, then use ANOVA.

The tests:

1. T Tests

* Unpaired t tests

* Also known as the student’s t test, independent t test, two-samples t test.

* It's the most commonly used t test and it tests the difference between two groups (the means of 2 groups) independent of each other and indicates how significant the differences are.

* Paired t tests

* "Pairs before marriage are not the same after!"

* So remember paired test is mainly used in comparison of a before and after scenario

* Also known as correlated t test, dependent samples t test.

* It is mainly used on dependent samples For example, the cholesterol level of a person before and after using a specific drug.

* It can also be used when you put the same condition under test using different items or things. For example, same crash safety tests for different cars.

* T scores

* The t score is referred to as the ratio of the difference between two groups and the difference within the groups.

* The smaller the t score, the more similarity there is between two groups and vice versa.

2. Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)

* The analysis of variance test (ANOVA) is used to test the difference between two or usually more than two groups (means) and here the inferences are made by analyzing the variances.

3. Chi-Square Test

* The Chi-Square test (χ2) is a non-parametric(non-numeric) test and it is used to test hypotheses in relation to nominal scale data or categorical data.

* It is a test of proportions and associations.

* A Chi-square distribution is usually positively skewed but it approaches a normal distribution as its degrees of freedom increases.

* If the frequency of any of the cells of the categorical table is <5, then Fisher’s exact test is used.
