questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: While performing a fasciotomy for compartment syndrome, the following layers are incised:
options: Skin, Subcutaneous tissue, Superficial fascia and Deep fascia
Skin, Subcutaneous tissue, Superficial fascia, Deep fascia and a few muscular fibres
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Skin, Subcutaneous tissue, Superficial fascia and Deep fascia

The incision for a fasciotomy involves the skin, subcutaneous tissue, superficial fascia, and deep fascia.

Fasciotomy involves incising the deep muscle fascia and is best carried out via longitudinal incisions of skin, subcutaneous fat, and superficial and deep fascia. The muscle will be seen bulging out through the fasciotomy opening.

The lower limb can be decompressed via two incisions, each being lateral to the subcutaneous border of the tibia. This gives access to the two posterior compartments and the leg's peroneal and anterior compartments.
questions.learning: Skin, Subcutaneous tissue, Superficial fascia and Deep fascia The incision for a fasciotomy involves the skin, subcutaneous tissue, superficial fascia, and deep fascia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following conditions is characterized by the absence of P waves?
questions.explanation: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a common supraventricular tachyarrhythmia characterized by the complete absence of distinct P waves on an electrocardiogram . Instead of an organized P wave representing atrial depolarization, the baseline shows fine or coarse fibrillatory waves. The QRS complexes occur at irregular intervals, leading to the classic "irregularly irregular" pulse. Ventricular tachycardia (Option A) is a wide-complex rhythm where P waves may be buried or dissociated but not fundamentally absent in the same physiological sense as AF. Focal atrial tachycardia (Option B) involves a specific ectopic focus and typically produces a recognizable, albeit abnormal, P wave. Ventricular fibrillation (Option C) is a pulseless cardiac arrest rhythm where all complexes (P, QRS, and T) are absent and replaced by chaotic, disorganized electrical activity. Therefore, AF is the definitive choice for a recognizable rhythm characterized specifically by the loss of the P wave due to disorganized atrial activity
questions.learning: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a common supraventricular tachyarrhythmia characterized by the complete absence of distinct P waves on an electrocardiogram .

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 35-year-old man is undergoing induction of general anesthesia. The anesthesiologist wishes to select an intravenous induction agent that is least likely to cause pain during injection. Which of the following agents is least commonly associated with injection pain?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ketamine

Unlike propofol, etomidate, and concentrated thiopentone solutions, ketamine does not typically cause pain on intravenous injection. In fact, because of its intrinsic analgesic properties, it is generally well tolerated during administration.

Educational Objective:

Ketamine is the IV induction agent least likely to produce injection pain, whereas propofol is the most commonly implicated.
questions.learning: Ketamine Unlike propofol, etomidate, and concentrated thiopentone solutions, ketamine does not typically cause pain on intravenous injection. In fact, because of its intrinsic analgesic properties, it is generally well tolerated during administration.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25 year old male presented with difficulty in swallowing food and weight loss for past few months. He also complains of regurgitation of undigested food and halitosis. Barium swallow was performed. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Achalasia cardia

The given complaints of difficulty in swallowing, weight loss, regurgitation of undigested food and halitosis along with the barium swallow showing bird beak appearance is suggestive of achalasia cardia.

Achalasia is a primary esophageal motility disorder caused due to the degeneration of neurons in the myenteric plexus of the esophagus. It is characterized by the absence of esophageal peristalsis and impaired relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES), thereby causing a functional obstruction at the gastroesophageal junction.

The patients present with a triad of dysphagia, regurgitation, and weight loss. The dysphagia initially begins with liquid and then progresses to solid foods, halitosis is present due to the accumulation of food. Patients may develop pneumonia, lung abscess, etc. at a later stage.

The initial diagnosis is made by barium swallow or endoscopy, which shows the presence of dilated esophagus due to the constriction of the lower esophageal sphincter (bird beak appearance). The gold standard test to confirm achalasia cardia is esophageal manometry. The findings are impaired lower esophageal sphincter (LES) relaxation and absent peristalsis with elevated LES pressure.

Management includes:

• Surgical esophagomyotomy.
• Non-surgical measures like sublingual nitroglycerin, nitrates, or calcium channel blockers.
• Injection of botulinum toxin
• Peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM)
questions.learning: Achalasia cardia — The given complaints of difficulty in swallowing, weight loss, regurgitation of undigested food and halitosis along with the barium swallow showing bird beak appearance is suggestive of achalasia cardia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the major contributor to frailty?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sarcopenia

Frailty is a geriatric syndrome characterized by reduced physiological reserve and increased vulnerability to stressors. Sarcopenia (age-related loss of skeletal muscle mass, strength, and function) is the major biological contributor to frailty and is central to its pathogenesis.

Why is A correct?

• Sarcopenia leads to:

• Decreased muscle strength
• Reduced physical performance
• Increased risk of falls
• Functional dependence

• It is the primary contributor to the development and progression of frailty.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old man suddenly develops a severe headache described as the worst of his life, followed by vomiting and photophobia. On examination, neck stiffness and a dilated right pupil are noted. CT imaging shows hemorrhage in the subarachnoid space. What is the most common underlying cause of this condition?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a sudden "thunderclap" headache (the worst headache of one's life), vomiting, and neck stiffness is classic for subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). The most common cause of spontaneous SAH is the rupture of an intracranial aneurysm, accounting for approximately 50% of cases. Hypertension (Option A) is a major risk factor but is less often the direct cause of the bleeding compared to an aneurysm. Arteriovenous malformations (Option C) are a significant cause but are less frequent than aneurysms. Brain tumors (Option D) can cause bleeding via vessel erosion but are a rare cause of SAH. The dilated pupil on the right side suggests a posterior communicating artery aneurysm compressing the third cranial nerve. Diagnosis is primarily by non-contrast CT, and management involves early surgical clipping or endovascular coiling to prevent rebleeding
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a sudden "thunderclap" headache (the worst headache of one's life), vomiting, and neck stiffness is classic for subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text:
A 9-month-old boy presents with progressive pallor and abdominal distension. The Mentzer index was found to be less than 13. What are the investigations to be done in this patient?

1. High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC)
2. PT and APTT
3. Bone marrow
4. Peripheral blood smear
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1 and 4

The investigations to be done in this patient are HPLC (high-performance liquid chromatography) and peripheral smear

The clinical history of a child with pallor, Mentzer's index <13, and abdominal distention (suggestive of hepatosplenomegaly) is suggestive of thalassemia.

Peripheral smear shows hypochromic microcytic anemia, target cells, basophilic stippling, fragmented red cells, and nucleated RBCs. HPLC showing decreased levels of HbA and an increase in HbA2 and HbF levels is sufficient to make a diagnosis.

The Mentzer index is the ratio of MCV (mean corpuscular volume) to RBC count. It is used to differentiate between iron-deficiency anemia and β-thalassemia trait. MCV and MCH (mean corpuscular hemoglobin) are low in both IDA and thalassemia. RBC count may be normal in thalassemia, whereas it is reduced in IDA. The Mentzer index is <13 in thalassemia minor syndrome.

Bone marrow examination (option 3) and coagulation studies (option 2) have no role in the diagnosis of thalassemia.

Thalassemia is a hemoglobinopathy that arises due to deficient synthesis of the globin chains. Depending on the chain affected, it is classified into α-thalassemia and β-thalassemia.

There is a deficit in the synthesis of HbA with an elevation of HbA2 and HbF levels in β-thalassemia. Children with severe thalassemia present with facial features (shown below) such as maxilla hyperplasia, a flat nasal bridge, and frontal bossing. Other manifestations include pathologic bone fractures, significant hepatosplenomegaly, and cachexia.

Hb Electrophoresis and HPLC are used as screening tests for thalassemia. DNA diagnosis to detect β-thalassemia mutations is used for definitive diagnosis. A radiographic image of the skull shows the classic 'crew cut' appearance.

Blood transfusions are administered every 3-4 weeks to maintain a pretransfusion hemoglobin level of 9.5-10.5 g/dL. Oral iron chelation to prevent iron toxicity is also recommended. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the only definitive therapy.

Antenatal counseling and heterozygote screening can be used in the prevention of the condition.

α-thalassemia is caused by deficient synthesis of α-chains. Deletion or malfunction of three α-globin chains can result in HbH disease. Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis is due to the absence of any normally functioning α-globin genes.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old male presented with complaints of bleeding gums. Blood investigations showed iron deficiency anemia. Which of the following vitamin deficiencies do you expect in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vitamin C

Dietary deficiency of vitamin C can lead to scurvy which can manifest as microcytic anemia, defective collagen synthesis, and bleeding manifestations.

Vitamin C is a water-soluble vitamin. It is mainly required for the hydroxylation of prolyl and lysyl residues of collagen reactions. It also maintains vitamin E and many metal cofactors (eg. copper) in a reduced state. It also facilitates the absorption of iron by reducing it from a ferric to a ferrous state.

Hence, vitamin C deficiency leads to defective collagen synthesis, fragile blood vessels, and iron deficiency anemia. Other clinical features of scurvy include spongy gums, loose teeth, swollen joints, subcutaneous hemorrhage, and bone fractures.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A young patient, in the first decade of life, presents with a grade II splenic injury without evidence of active bleeding. What is the appropriate management for this patient?
questions.explanation: In pediatric trauma management, conservative (non-operative) management is the gold standard for hemodynamically stable patients with splenic injuries, regardless of the injury grade (provided there is no active bleeding). Children have a more robust splenic capsule and more efficient vasospasm, which facilitates self-healing. Furthermore, maintaining the spleen is vital in children to prevent the life-threatening risk of Overwhelming Post-Splenectomy Infection (OPSI). Splenectomy (Option A) is reserved for patients with uncontrollable hemorrhage or hemodynamic instability. Splenorrhaphy (Option B) or embolization (Option C) are interventions used if conservative measures fail or in specific adult scenarios, but they are not the initial treatment of choice for a stable pediatric Grade II injury. Management involves admission to the intensive care unit for strict bed rest, serial physical examinations, and regular monitoring of hemoglobin levels. Most such injuries heal completely without surgery within a few weeks. This "spleen-sparing" approach has significantly improved long-term outcomes in pediatric trauma care
questions.learning: In pediatric trauma management, conservative (non-operative) management is the gold standard for hemodynamically stable patients with splenic injuries, regardless of the injury grade (provided there is no active bleeding).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 70-year-old male patient presents with decreased hearing in higher frequencies. It was noted that the basilar membrane was affected. Which of the following structures lie near the affected structure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Oval window

The affected structure in high-frequency hearing loss is the basal turn of the cochlea. Among the given options, the structure that lies near it is the oval window.

The traveling wave theory of von Bekesy states that a sound wave, depending on its frequency, reaches maximum amplitude at a segment on the basilar membrane and stimulates that segment. The high frequencies are represented in the basal turn of the cochlea and the progressively lower ones towards the apex.

The cochlea has a bony core called the modiolus, and a spiral canal that runs around it. At the base of the canal, the two main openings are the oval window and the round window. The footplate of stapes rests against the oval window. The base of the modiolus transmits nerves and vessels to the cochlea. (option A)

The inner ear consists of a bony labyrinth and a membranous labyrinth. The bony labyrinth consists of the vestibule, semicircular canals, and the cochlea. The membranous labyrinth consists of the cochlear duct, the utricle and saccule, semicircular ducts, and the endolymphatic duct and sac.

The cochlear duct has three walls- the basilar membrane, Reissner's membrane, and the stria vascularis. The basilar membrane supports the organ of Corti, which is the sensory hearing epithelium. The length of the basilar membrane increases from the base to the apex. As a result of this, higher frequency sound is heard at the basal coil while lower frequencies are heard at the apex.

The stria vascularis is involved in the secretion of endolymph and contains vascular epithelium. (Option B)

The helicotrema (option D) is an opening at the apex of the cochlea, at which the scala vestibuli and scala tympani communicate. The scala vestibuli, tympani, and media are three compartments of the bony cochlea.
questions.learning: Oval window — The affected structure in high-frequency hearing loss is the basal turn of the cochlea. Among the given options, the structure that lies near it is the oval window.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient presents with a firm, painless lump on the upper eyelid that has been gradually increasing in size over several months. The swelling is situated away from the eyelid margin. Based on these clinical features, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A chalazion is a chronic, non-infectious granulomatous inflammation of a Meibomian gland. Its classic clinical features match this scenario perfectly: it is a firm, painless nodule that develops slowly over weeks or months. Crucially, it is typically located within the tarsal plate, away from the lid margin (Option C). In contrast, a Stye or hordeolum (Option A) is an acute bacterial infection of the hair follicle or gland, which is intensely painful and located directly on the eyelid edge. Entropion (Option B) is the inward turning of the eyelid margin, not a discrete lump. Blepharitis (Option D) is a diffuse, chronic inflammation of the entire lid margin characterized by crusting and redness rather than a localized firm nodule. Therefore, based on the chronic, painless, and localized nature of the eyelid mass, chalazion is the correct diagnosis
questions.learning: A chalazion is a chronic, non-infectious granulomatous inflammation of a Meibomian gland. Its classic clinical features match this scenario perfectly: it is a firm, painless nodule that develops slowly over weeks or months.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which entity is responsible for overseeing the school health programs?
questions.explanation: The school health program is a vital part of the community health services in India. The primary responsibility for planning, executing, and overseeing these programs at the local level lies with the "Primary Health Centre (PHC)". The Medical Officer of the PHC is tasked with coordinating regular health check-ups for students, ensuring vaccinations are up to date, and providing health education. While the sub-centre (Option C) provides ground-level assistance through ANMs, the organizational leadership comes from the PHC. District hospitals (Option B) and sub-divisional hospitals (Option D) serve as referral centers for specialized care but do not manage the routine school outreach. The goal of the school health program is the "early detection" of defects and diseases, correction of nutritional deficiencies, and promotion of a healthy environment for children, which is best managed by the community-based PHC infrastructure
questions.learning: The school health program is a vital part of the community health services in India. The primary responsibility for planning, executing, and overseeing these programs at the local level lies with the "Primary Health Centre (PHC)".

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: As filtrate flows through PCT, the concentration of all of the following decreases except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chloride

As the filtrate flows through the proximal convoluted tubule, the concentration of the chloride increases.

* The concentration of chloride in the early part of the pCT is ≈105 mEq/L.

* As the sodium is reabsorbed, it preferentially carries glucose, amino acids, and bicarbonate.

* This leaves behind the solute, that has a higher concentration of the chloride, which as it reaches the second half of the PCT is ≈140 mEq/L.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presents with SOB and fatigue. CXR was done. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Asbestosis is an occupational interstitial lung disease caused by the inhalation of asbestos fibers. The hallmark radiologic finding is the presence of calcified pleural plaques, particularly along the parietal pleura and the diaphragm, often referred to as "peripheral pleural calcification". This is usually accompanied by interstitial fibrosis that predominantly affects the lower lobes. Symptoms include progressive shortness of breath (SOB) and restrictive patterns on pulmonary function tests. Tuberculosis (Option A) typically involves the lung apices and presents with cavitary lesions rather than pleural plaques. Silicosis (Option C) is characterized by upper lobe nodules and "eggshell" calcification of hilar lymph nodes. Byssinosis (Option D) is related to cotton dust exposure and generally does not show pleural calcifications on imaging. Given the specific visual findings of pleural plaques, asbestosis is the most likely diagnosis

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 1-day old neonate presented with scaphoid abdomen, respiratory distress and mediastinal shift. All of the following can be done except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Bag and mask ventilation

Congenital diaphragmatic hernia presents with respiratory distress, scaphoid abdomen, and mediastinal shift due to herniation of abdominal contents into the thoracic cavity causing lung compression.

• Immediate management focuses on preventing further gastric distension and lung compression
• Bag and mask ventilation is contraindicated because it forces air into the stomach, worsening respiratory compromise
• Endotracheal intubation with controlled ventilation is preferred
• Nasogastric tube should be inserted for gastric decompression

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A neonate presents with forceful, non-bilious vomiting and visible gastric peristalsis. A barium meal study is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The presentation of forceful (projectile) non-bilious vomiting in a neonate (typically at 3–6 weeks of age), along with visible gastric peristalsis (stomach movements), is classic for Congenital Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis (CHPS). The "non-bilious" nature of the vomit is critical as it indicates the obstruction is proximal to the second part of the duodenum. The barium meal image provides the definitive diagnosis, showing the "string sign"—the elongated, narrow pyloric canal. Duodenal atresia (Option D) would show bilious vomiting and a "double bubble" on X-ray. Jejunal atresia (Option C) also causes bilious vomiting and distal obstruction. Hirschsprung's disease (Option A) causes low intestinal obstruction and delayed meconium passage . CHPS is also associated with a palpable "olive-shaped" mass in the epigastrium and hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. Surgical management involves a Ramstedt’s pyloromyotomy
questions.learning: The presentation of forceful (projectile) non-bilious vomiting in a neonate (typically at 3–6 weeks of age), along with visible gastric peristalsis (stomach movements), is classic for Congenital Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis (CHPS).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The full form of the Urban HEART programme is:
options: Urban health equity assessment and response tool
Urban health evaluation assessment and response tool
Urban health equity assessment and response technique
Urban health evaluation assessment and response technique
questions.explanation: Urban HEART stands for the Urban Health Equity Assessment and Response Tool. Developed by the World Health Organization, it is a structured framework designed to help local policymakers and communities identify and address health inequities in urban environments. Options B, C, and D are incorrect as they substitute "evaluation" for "equity" or "technique" for "tool" . The tool uses various health and social indicators to map disparities between different urban neighborhoods, allowing for targeted interventions to improve the well-being of vulnerable populations. By focusing on "equity," the program ensures that health resources are distributed according to need, aiming to close the gap in health outcomes caused by socioeconomic factors. Implementing Urban HEART allows city officials to visualize complex data and make evidence-based decisions to create healthier, more inclusive urban spaces. Therefore, the name reflects its specific focus on identifying and responding to urban health gaps

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The Sabin-Feldman dye test is an indirect fluorescent antibody test which is used to detect antibodies against which of the following organisms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Toxoplasma gondii

Toxoplasmosis is caused by the intracellular protozoan Toxoplasma gondii. The Sabin–Feldman dye test is the classical reference serological test for detecting IgG antibodies against T. gondii. Although it has largely been replaced by modern ELISA-based assays, it remains an important exam topic.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. Leishmania donovani: Diagnosed by rK39 antigen test, demonstration of LD bodies, or PCR.
• C. Coxiella burnetii: Diagnosed by indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA), the reference test for Q fever.
• D. Trypanosoma cruzi: Diagnosed by serology, PCR, or parasite demonstration in Chagas disease.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 35-year-old male presents with a deformed eye. He was treated for a corneal ulcer 2 weeks back which took a long time to heal despite antibiotics treatment. His physical examination is remarkable for the findings shown in the image. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Anterior staphyloma

The clinical vignette is suggestive of a diagnosis of anterior staphyloma.

Staphyloma (a bunch of grapes) is a clinical condition characterized by ectasia of the outer coats (cornea, or sclera or both) of the eye, with the involvement of the uveal tissue. The basic underlying pathology is the weakening of the eyewall, which can be caused by many inflammatory or degenerative diseases involving these structures.

Types of staphyloma

* Anterior staphyloma: an ectasia of the pseudocornea, which results from the total sloughing of the cornea. It is lined internally by the iris and externally, by the newly formed epithelium.

* Intercalary staphyloma: This is located at the limbus and is lined by the root of the iris.

* Ciliary staphyloma: Ectasia of weak sclera lined by the ciliary body. This affects the ciliary zone that includes the region up to 8 mm behind the limbus.

* Equatorial staphyloma: This occurs at the equatorial region up to 14 mm behind the limbus of the eye.

* Posterior staphyloma: This affects the posterior pole of the eye.

Note:

*  The most common cause for anterior staphyloma is sloughing corneal ulcer.

*  The most common cause for posterior staphyloma is degenerative high axial myopia.

Image showing the types of staphyloma.

Treatment: Local excision and repair with a corneal and scleral patch graft. Enucleation and replacement with an implant can be done for disfigured and blind eyes. Degenerative diseases responsible should be treated early to prevent secondary glaucoma and staphyloma formation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 14-year-old girl presented with cyclical abdominal pain and a midline hypogastric lump. She has not achieved menarche yet. The per vaginal examination is shown below and a bluish swelling is seen along with it. What is the likely cause of her condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Imperforate hymen

The given case scenario is suggestive of an imperforate hymen, which has led to cryptomenorrhoea. This is a condition where menstruation occurs but is not visible due to an obstruction of the outflow tract.

The menstrual fluid gets collected in the reproductive tract. When this collection occurs in the vagina, it is known as hematocolpos. If the collection extends to the uterus, it is known as hematometra. The collection of blood in the fallopian tubes is called hematosalpinx.

The most common causes of cryptomenorrhea are:

* Intact/imperforate hymen - a bluish convex bulge is seen.

* Transverse vaginal septum - a pinkish concave covering is seen

Ultrasound pelvis confirms the diagnosis.

Management:

Imperforate hymen - A simple cruciate incision of the hymen allows the free drainage of the collected menstrual blood, and leads to normal reproductive function.

Transverse vaginal septum - Extensive dissection and vaginoplasty is required.

Option A: Bartholin's cyst appears as a swelling on the inner side of the labia majora. Larger cysts can bulge across the introitus. Small cysts can remain asymptomatic.

Option D: Endometriomas are endometriotic lesions seen on the ovary. They present as adnexal masses. Endometriosis is a complication in cryptomenorrhea, due to retrograde menstruation.
questions.learning: Imperforate hymen — The given case scenario is suggestive of an imperforate hymen, which has led to cryptomenorrhoea. This is a condition where menstruation occurs but is not visible due to an obstruction of the outflow tract.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which is not a part of the Anemia Mukt Bharat Programme?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 6 health functionaries

Among the listed options, 6 health functionaries are not a part of the 6x6x6 strategy employed by the Anemia Mukt Bharat Program.

The Anemia Mukt Bharat scheme is an initiative that aims to strengthen the existing mechanisms and foster newer strategies for tackling anaemia. The 6 x 6 x 6 strategy represents:

• 6 beneficiaries (option A)
• 6 interventions (option B)
• 6 institutional mechanisms (option C)

The 6 beneficiaries include:

• Preschool children (6-59 months of age)
• Children (5-9 years of age)
• Adolescents (10-19 years of age)
• Pregnant women
• Lactating mothers
• Young women in the reproductive age group (20-24 years of age)

The 6 interventions include:

• Prophylactic iron and folic acid supplementation
• Deworming
• Intensified year-round “behaviour change communication campaign”
• Testing of anaemia using digital methods and point-of-care treatment
• Mandatory provision of iron and folic acid-fortified foods in government-funded health programs
• Addressing non-nutritional causes of anaemia in endemic pockets, with a special focus on malaria, hemoglobinopathies, and fluorosis

The 6 institutional mechanisms include:

• Intra-ministerial coordination
• National Anemia Mukt Bharat unit
• National Center of Excellence and Advanced Research on Anemia Control
• Convergence with other ministries
• Strengthening supply chain and logistics
• Digital Anemia Mukt Bharat dashboard and online portal
questions.learning: 6 health functionaries Among the listed options, 6 health functionaries are not a part of the 6x6x6 strategy employed by the Anemia Mukt Bharat Program.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old male presents with chest pain and breathlessness which increases on lying down and is relieved on sitting upright. On examination, heart sounds are muffled. His chest X-ray is shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pericardial effusion

The given clinical features and X-ray appearance of the money bag heart is suggestive of pericardial effusion.

Plain PA chest X-ray shows an enlarged cardiac silhouette. There is effacement of the normal cardiac borders, development of a ‘flask’ or ‘water bottle’ cardiac configuration, and bilateral hilar overlay which are features of pericardial effusion. It is also known as money bag or leather bottle-shaped heart.

Pericardial effusions occur when excess fluid collects in the pericardial space (a normal pericardial sac contains approximately 30-50 mL of fluid).

Investigation of choice: Echocardiography.

Signs on plain radiograph include:

* Globular enlargement of the cardiac shadow giving a water bottle configuration.

* Lateral CXR may show a vertical opaque line (pericardial fluid) separating a vertical lucent line directly behind the sternum (paracardial fat) anteriorly from a similar lucent vertical lucent line (epicardial fat) posteriorly; this is known as the Oreo cookie sign.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which is the type of cartilage present in the histology section given below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hyaline cartilage

The type of cartilage shown in the above image is hyaline cartilage.

On microscopy, hyaline cartilage can be identified by:

* Presence of chondrocytes within lacunae.

* Group of two or more chondrocytes which are known as isogenous cell aggregates or cell nests.

* Basophilic territorial matrix and pale interterritorial matrix

* Presence of perichondrium with outer fibrous and the inner cellular layer

Hyaline cartilage is made up of chondrocytes and matrix. The chondrocytes in the deeper matrix are rounded in shape and may appear in a group of eight that originate from the mitotic divisions of a single chondroblast. These groups of cells are called isogenous cell aggregates or cell nests. The important components of the matrix are type II collagen, aggrecan (proteoglycan) and chondronectin (glycoprotein). The matrix which immediately surrounds the chondrocytes is basophilic and is known as the territorial matrix and the matrix which are more distant from the cells appears pale and is known as the interterritorial matrix.

It is found in:

* Larger respiratory passages (nose, larynx, trachea and bronchi)

* Thyroid cartilage

* Cricoid cartilage

* Base of the arytenoid cartilage

* Ventral end of ribs where they articulate with the sternum

* The epiphyseal plate of long bones

* Articular cartilage of synovial joint

* Temporary skeleton in embryo

Other Options:

Option A: Articular cartilage despite being a type of hyaline cartilage lacks perichondrium.

Option B: The elastic cartilage, like the hyaline cartilage, contains individual or small groups of chondrocytes that are surrounded by type II collagen fibrils. However, it differs from hyaline cartilage in that, much of the interterritorial matrix consists of fine yellow elastic fibres containing elastin protein and the surface of elastic cartilage is covered by perichondrium.

Option D: The fibrocartilage is an intermediate between dense fibrous connective tissue (tendon and ligaments) and hyaline cartilage. It consists of bundles of collagen fibres (both type I and II) with rows of chondrocytes present between the bundles. They are not covered by perichondrium.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: The serotonergic cell bodies of the analgesia pathway projecting to the dorsal horn of the spinal cord are located in which part of the brain?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Nucleus raphe

The descending pain inhibitory (analgesia) pathway modulates pain transmission at the dorsal horn of the spinal cord.

Key components of this pathway:

1.      Periaqueductal gray (PAG) in the midbrain receives pain signals.

2.      PAG activates neurons in the nucleus raphe magnus (raphe nuclei) in the medulla.

3.      Serotonergic neurons from the nucleus raphe descend to the dorsal horn of the spinal cord.

4.      These neurons stimulate enkephalin-releasing interneurons, which inhibit pain transmission from primary afferent neurons.

Important neurotransmitters:

• Serotonin (5-HT) from raphe nuclei
• Enkephalins in the spinal cord

Other structures:

• Locus ceruleus: provides noradrenergic modulation of pain.
• PAG: initiates the descending analgesic pathway but is not the source of serotonergic projections.
questions.learning: Nucleus raphe — The descending pain inhibitory (analgesia) pathway modulates pain transmission at the dorsal horn of the spinal cord. Periaqueductal gray (PAG) in the midbrain receives pain signals.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true regarding the fifth stage of the demographic cycle?
options: Birth rate falls below death rate
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Birth rate falls below death rate

In stage 5 of the demographic cycle, the birth rate falls below the death rate.

In this stage, the death rate attains a low stable rate while the birth rate keeps declining. Thus, the curve of the birth rate will cross the curve of the death rate in a graph of the demographic cycle and falls further below.

The demographic gap is negative and the population is declining. So, this stage is known as the declining stage.

Pearl PF0983: Demographic Process and Cycle

* Demographic process

* Fertility

* Mortality

* Marriage

* Migration

* Social Mobility

* Demographic cycle

* Stage 1 : High stationary

* High birth rate and high death rate render the population stationary.

* Narrow demographic gap.

* Stage 2 : Early expanding

* Death rate declines and birth rate remains unchanged

* Demographic gap starts increasing and then becomes maximum

* Stage 3 : Late expanding

* Death rate decline further and birth rate falls

* India is in this stage, currently

* Demographic gap starts declining

* Stage 4 : Low stationary

* Low birth rate and low death rate renders the population stationary

* Narrow demographic gap

* Stage 5 : Declining

* Population begins to decline as birth rate is lower than death rate

* Demographic gap is negative
questions.learning: Birth rate falls below death rate — In stage 5 of the demographic cycle, the birth rate falls below the death rate. In this stage, the death rate attains a low stable rate while the birth rate keeps declining.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Acrodermatitis enteropathica is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder which affects the absorption of which one of the following micronutrients?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Zinc

Acrodermatitis enteropathica is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the SLC39A4 gene, resulting in defective intestinal absorption of zinc. Zinc deficiency leads to characteristic skin lesions, alopecia, diarrhea, and impaired immunity.

Symptoms usually begin after weaning from breast milk, as breast milk contains highly bioavailable zinc. Lifelong oral zinc supplementation results in dramatic clinical improvement.

Why not the other options?

• A. Iodine: Deficiency causes goiter and hypothyroidism, not acrodermatitis enteropathica.
• C. Iron: Deficiency causes microcytic hypochromic anemia.
• D. Selenium: Deficiency is associated with cardiomyopathy (Keshan disease) and myopathy, not the characteristic dermatitis of acrodermatitis enteropathica.
questions.learning: Zinc Acrodermatitis enteropathica is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the SLC39A4 gene, resulting in defective intestinal absorption of zinc.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In the anteroposterior diameters of the pelvic inlet, the true conjugate is:
options: The distance from the midpoint of the sacral promontory to the uppermost margin of the symphysis pubis
The shortest distance between the sacral promontory and the symphysis pubis
The distance from the lowest margin of the symphysis to the sacral promontory
The distance from the posterior margin of the sacral promontory to the symphysis pubis
questions.explanation: The True Conjugate (Anatomical Conjugate) is defined as the distance between the midpoint of the sacral promontory and the uppermost margin (superior border) of the symphysis pubis. It normally measures about 11 cm. Obstetric conjugate (Option B) is the shortest distance between the sacral promontory and the posterior surface of the symphysis (approximately 10 cm); this is the most clinically important diameter for labor. Diagonal conjugate (Option C) is the distance from the lowest margin (inferior border) of the symphysis to the sacral promontory (approximately 12.5 cm); it is the only AP diameter that can be measured during a digital vaginal examination. Option D provides a description that does not match standard anatomical nomenclature for pelvic conjugates. Precise knowledge of these diameters is essential for identifying cephalopelvic disproportion. Therefore, the measurement to the superior border defines the true conjugate
questions.learning: The True Conjugate (Anatomical Conjugate) is defined as the distance between the midpoint of the sacral promontory and the uppermost margin (superior border) of the symphysis pubis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 4-year-old child is brought to the emergency department with high-grade fever, poor oral intake, and increasing lethargy for the past 2 days. On examination, the child appears ill and has cold extremities with delayed capillary refill. Continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring is initiated, as demonstrated in the accompanying video. Based on the vital parameters displayed in the video, which of the following best describes the child’s current hemodynamic status?
options: Compensated shock with maintained blood pressure
Isolated respiratory distress without circulatory compromise
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Decompensated shock with hypotension

• The monitor in the video shows marked tachycardia (\~160/min) with a low blood pressure (\~66/33 mmHg). In a child with fever, poor intake, altered sensorium, cold extremities, and delayed capillary refill, these findings strongly suggest shock with cardiovascular decompensation.
• Children can initially maintain their blood pressure despite significant circulatory compromise through tachycardia and peripheral vasoconstriction. Therefore, hypotension is generally a late and concerning sign of pediatric shock.
• The combination of tachycardia + hypotension + clinical evidence of poor perfusion indicates decompensated shock and requires urgent resuscitation.
• Normal systolic BP for this age is roughly 90–100 mmHg; a systolic of 66 is well below the 5th percentile threshold for hypotension, which by the common formula is 70 + [2 × age in years] = 78 mmHg).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman with a family history of breast and ovarian cancer seeks counseling about her risk and inquires about BRCA1/ BRCA2 genetic testing. In which of the following situations is BRCA1/BRCA2 testing not indicated?
options: Breast cancer diagnosed in a postmenopausal female >50 years of age
questions.explanation: Genetic testing for BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations is prioritized for individuals with clinical features suggesting a high probability of a hereditary cancer syndrome. Testing is strongly recommended for male breast cancer (Option B), as a significant percentage of these cases are linked to BRCA2 mutations. Bilateral breast cancer (Option C) and the occurrence of both breast and ovarian cancer in the same individual (Option D) are classic hallmarks of the Hereditary Breast and Ovarian Cancer (HBOC) syndrome and warrant testing. Breast cancer diagnosed in a postmenopausal woman over the age of 50 without a significant family history (Option A) is much more likely to be sporadic rather than hereditary. Guidelines typically recommend testing if breast cancer is diagnosed at age , or if older, only when specific family history criteria are met. Therefore, routine testing for an isolated case of postmenopausal breast cancer over 50 is not standard practice
questions.learning: Genetic testing for BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations is prioritized for individuals with clinical features suggesting a high probability of a hereditary cancer syndrome.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient with renal disease undergoes a kidney biopsy. Congo red staining of the tissue reveals deposits exhibiting apple-green birefringence under polarized light. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The demonstration of extracellular proteinaceous deposits that exhibit apple-green birefringence when stained with Congo red and viewed under polarized light is the pathognomonic finding for amyloidosis. In the context of renal disease, this often signifies AA (secondary) amyloidosis resulting from chronic inflammation. Under standard light microscopy, these deposits appear as amorphous, eosinophilic substances. Option B (Minimal change disease) shows normal glomeruli on light microscopy and foot process effacement on electron microscopy, but no amyloid deposits. Option C (Diabetic nephropathy) is characterized by nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions). Option D (Membranous nephropathy) features a thickened basement membrane with subepithelial "spikes". Neither diabetes nor membranous disease shows the specific staining properties of amyloid. Thus, the Congo red staining property definitively confirms the presence of amyloid fibrils in the tissue
questions.learning: The demonstration of extracellular proteinaceous deposits that exhibit apple-green birefringence when stained with Congo red and viewed under polarized light is the pathognomonic finding for amyloidosis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Corticosteroid indicated for the stimulation of fetal lung maturation in preterm labor is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Betamethasone

Betamethasone is indicated for the stimulation of fetal lung maturation in preterm labor.

As compared to cortisol, betamethasone binds to maternal proteins less and has less placental metabolism. This allows increased transfer to the fetus. Additionally, infants exposed to betamethasone are less likely to require postnatal resuscitation. 2 doses of 12 mg each are administered 18-24 hours apart when the delivery is anticipated before 34 weeks of gestation.

Dexamethasone, another long-acting glucocorticoid is also indicated. It has benefits such as less risk of intraventricular hemorrhage and a shorter length of stay in the NICU.
questions.learning: Betamethasone Betamethasone is indicated for the stimulation of fetal lung maturation in preterm labor. As compared to cortisol, betamethasone binds to maternal proteins less and has less placental metabolism.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 70-year-old woman had her routine follow up and her USG of the liver is shown below. She is asymptomatic at present but has a history of mild right hypochondriac pain which is relieved by taking analgesics. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gallstones

The USG shows a gallbladder wall that is thickened with no edema in the pericholecystic fat. The gallbladder contains biliary sludge and gallstones, shown as the acoustic shadowing. There are no signs of current cholecystitis and thus the diagnosis is gallstones.

Ultrasonography is the most accurate initial imaging modality of choice for the diagnosis of gallbladder stones. They appear as echogenic foci producing acoustic shadows. Size of the gallbladder, presence of stones or polyps, and the thickness of the wall are measured. Inflammation around the gallbladder, the size of the common bile duct, and stones in the extrahepatic biliary tree can also be determined. The sensitivity of UG is > 95%. Small stones can be differentiated from small polyps by the presence of mobility or of an acoustic shadow.

The image below shows ultrasonography of the gall bladder:

Amoebic liver abscess ( Option b)  shows necrotic material and debris on usg without any acoustic shadows. Diagnosis is often found using aspiration.

Hydatid cysts (option c) can present similarly. There is tenderness and enlargement of the liver with blood investigations show eosinophilia, elevated liver enzymes. USG can show various stages, classical being multiple septations and rosette or honeycomb appearance, Water Lilly sign when the cyst wall detaches

The image below shows the multiple septations in ultrasonography of hydatid cyst.

An ultrasound scan in acute cholecystitis (Option d ) demonstrates a distended gallbladder with a thickened wall of >3 mm, pericholecystic fluid, the presence of gallstone( when it is due to associated cholelithiasis), and the sonographic Murphy's sign. Gallbladder distension (diameter >5 cm), pericholecystic fluid, gallbladder wall striations, and, occasionally, wall hyperemia on Doppler examination may also be seen in USG.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Molluscum contagiosum is caused by:
questions.explanation: Molluscum contagiosum is a common, benign skin infection caused by the Molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV), which is a member of the Poxviridae family (a large, enveloped DNA virus). It is characterized by small, firm, skin-colored, dome-shaped papules with a central dimple or umbilication. The infection is spread through direct skin-to-skin contact, including sexual contact, or via contaminated fomites. It is neither a bacteria (Option A), fungus (Option B), nor protozoa (Option C). Histologically, it is noted for the presence of "Henderson-Paterson bodies" (large cytoplasmic inclusion bodies) within the keratinocytes. While the condition is usually self-limiting in immunocompetent individuals, it can be extensive and persistent in patients with HIV or other forms of immunosuppression. Recognition of its viral etiology is important for counseling patients on transmission prevention. Therefore, Molluscum contagiosum is definitively classified as a viral skin disorder
questions.learning: Molluscum contagiosum is a common, benign skin infection caused by the Molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV), which is a member of the Poxviridae family (a large, enveloped DNA virus).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Through which of the following foramen does the nerve supplying the muscle of mastication passes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2

The muscles of mastication are supplied by the mandibular nerve (V3), it is the only motor division of the trigeminal nerve.

V3 exits the cranial cavity through the foramen ovale to enter the infratemporal fossa.

Optic canal transmits CN II, jugular foramen transmits CN IX–XI, and hypoglossal canal transmits CN XII, none of which supply muscles of mastication.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient is brought with symptoms of diarrhea, hair loss, and poor wound healing. Which mineral deficiency is responsible for these symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Zinc

The symptoms and clinical findings suggest a probable diagnosis of acrodermatitis enteropathica which is due to the deficiency of zinc.

It is an autosomal recessive disease due to a defect in zinc-absorbing transmembrane protein.

The symptoms are:

* Growth retardation

* Diarrhea

* Alopecia

* Rash involving the extremities, face, and perineum - rash is characterized by vesicular and pustular crusting with scaling and erythema

* Gonadal atrophy

* Muscle wasting

* Impaired wound healing

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 7-year-old intellectually disabled boy was brought with large warty crusts on the trunk, hands, and feet as shown below. Severe fissuring and scaling of the skin are present over the soles. What is the possible diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Norwegian scabies

The clinical scenario is suggestive of Norwegian scabies or human-crusted scabies.

Individuals who are intellectually challenged, suffering from dementia, or with Down's syndrome are frequently associated with Norwegian scabies.  Lack of appreciation of pruritus could be a reason for this.

Crusted scabies (Norwegian or hyperkeratotic scabies) is seen in individuals who are immunocompromised due to any underlying disease or therapy, patients with HIV infection, and in people who use topical steroids and pimecrolimus.

Crusted scabies occurs in people with an inadequate immune response to the mite, allowing them to multiply. It is called 'Norwegian' because it was first described in lepers of Norway.

Large warty crusts form on the hands and feet. Palms and soles may be irregularly fissured and thickened. Horny debris get accumulates beneath the thickened and discolored nails. Erythema and scaling occur in the scalp face and seborrheic area. The itching will be absent often.

Scrappings teeming with mites and eggs confirms the diagnosis.

All patients should be hospitalized and isolated due to the risk of transmission due to physical contact. Treatment includes oral ivermectin, topical scabicide, and keratolytic agents for the crusting.

The images given below show hands in Norwegian scabies.

Other options:

Option A- If topical steroids are used on scabies lesions, the clinical picture modifies to mimic other conditions. This is termed as scabies incognito.

Option B-  Animal scabies transmission to humans is rare. Lesions are similar to human scabies with itchy papules except for the burrows. It is rare.

Option C-  Nodular scabies presents as violaceous, pruritic localized nodules over the groin, axilla, and genitalia. They represent a hypersensitivity reaction to the mite antigens and can persist after treatment.
questions.learning: Norwegian scabies — The clinical scenario is suggestive of Norwegian scabies or human-crusted scabies. Individuals who are intellectually challenged, suffering from dementia, or with Down's syndrome are frequently associated with Norwegian scabies.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following congenital heart diseases are associated with a split second heart sound? 1. ASD 2. VSD 3. PDA 4. TOF
questions.explanation: Split second heart sound (S2) occurs when aortic (A2) and pulmonary (P2) valve closure becomes asynchronous. Conditions causing increased right heart volume/flow delay pulmonary valve closure, producing wide splitting of S2. 1 ASD Causes fixed wide splitting of S2 — the hallmark finding. Increased right heart volume delays pulmonary valve closure consistently throughout respiration. 2 VSD Increased pulmonary blood flow delays P2 closure, producing wide splitting of S2. 3 PDA Increased pulmonary circulation delays P2, causing wide splitting of S2. Why TOF is excluded: 4 TOF is incorrect because in Tetralogy of Fallot, severe pulmonary stenosis causes markedly diminished pulmonary blood flow. P2 becomes so soft it is virtually inaudible, resulting in a single S2 rather than split S2. The aortic component dominates completely, making splitting absent. Why other options are wrong: (B,C) are incorrect because they include TOF which characteristically produces single S2, not split S2. (D) is incorrect because TOF does not produce split S2, making "all correct" invalid
questions.learning: Split second heart sound (S2) occurs when aortic (A2) and pulmonary (P2) valve closure becomes asynchronous. Conditions causing increased right heart volume/flow delay pulmonary valve closure, producing wide splitting of S2.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 24-year-old woman presents to an infertility clinic with a history of recurrent pregnancy losses and is diagnosed with a septate uterus. Which corrective procedure is associated with the best obstetric outcomes in this condition?
questions.explanation: A septate uterus is a congenital uterine anomaly associated with the highest risk of recurrent pregnancy loss. The modern "gold standard" procedure that yields the most favorable obstetric outcomes with the least morbidity is Hysteroscopic Transcervical Resection of the Septum (TCRS) (Option D). This minimally invasive technique involves using a hysteroscopic resectoscope or scissors to divide the septum without making an incision in the abdominal or uterine wall. This allows for a shorter recovery time and, most importantly, allows the patient to attempt a vaginal delivery in the future. In contrast, Jones (Option A) and Tompkins (Option C) metroplasties are older, invasive abdominal surgeries that require a Cesarean section for all subsequent deliveries. Strassman metroplasty (Option B) is specifically utilized for the correction of a bicornuate uterus rather than a septate uterus. Therefore, hysteroscopic resection is the definitive contemporary choice

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 25-year-old male presented with symptoms of inability to flex the distal interphalangeal joint of the 4th and 5th digits. He was also not able to hold a piece of paper between his fingers. What is the likely site of injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. C

The given clinical situation with a positive card test and an inability to flex the distal interphalangeal joint of the 4th and 5th digits, suggests an ulnar nerve injury. The most likely site of injury would thus be medial epicondyle: site C

Injury at the medial epicondyle damages the ulnar nerve, leading to paralysis of flexor carpi ulnaris (loss of ulnar deviation) and medial half of flexor digitorum profundus (loss of distal interphalangeal joint flexion). It leads to hypothenar paralysis (lead to atrophy) and sensory loss. Also, flexor digitorum superficialis (supplied by median nerve) and extensor digitorum (supplied by the radial nerve) are still functional. Hence complete paralysis of the 3rd and 4th digits is not seen.  The positive card test is due to the weakness of palmar interossei leading to loss of adduction.

Ulnar nerve branches and supply:

Superficial branch supplies palmaris brevis, skin on the palmar surface of medial 1½ fingers. The deep branch runs within the concavity of deep palmar arch and supplies all intrinsic muscles of the hand (except first 2 lumbricals and thenar muscles).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A farmer working in a paddy field presented with fever, muscle pain, nausea and vomiting. The microscopic agglutination test was positive. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Leptospirosis

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of leptospirosis (Weil's disease). A microscopic agglutination test is used for the diagnosis of leptospirosis.

Leptospirosis is a zoonosis caused by spirochetes of the genus Leptospira. Patients with mild disease may present with flu-like symptoms of sudden onset, fever with chills, headache, abdominal pain, conjunctival suffusion, and myalgia. The muscle pain usually affects the calves, abdomen, and back. The life cycle of Leptospira is depicted below:

Severe cases of leptospirosis, which can progress rapidly and have a high fatality rate, are associated with Weil's syndrome, characterized by a triad of:

* Hemorrhage

* Jaundice

* Acute kidney injury

Jaundice, when present, can be profound, and physical examination may reveal an enlarged, tender liver. Temperature-pulse dissociation or relative bradycardia may also be observed.
The image below shows icterus and conjunctival suffusion in a patient with leptospirosis:

The progression of leptospirosis and the utility of diagnostic investigations is given in the graph below.

Diagnosis includes:

* Microscopy -

* Examination of blood - Leptospires may be demonstrated under the dark field microscope or by immunofluorescence. The organism disappears from blood after 1 week.

* Examination of urine: Leptospires appear in the urine in the second week of the disease. Centrifuged deposit of the urine may be examined under dark ground illumination.

* Serotype-specific tests:

* Microscopic agglutination test (more specific)

* Macroscopic agglutination test

* A rapid diagnostic test to detect leptospira-specific IgM antibody in human sera.

* Culture - With semisynthetic media like EMJH (Ellinghausen, McCullough, Johnson, Harris) or Korthof's, Stuart's, and Fletcher's media.

The image below shows EMJH (Ellinghausen-McCullough-Johnson-Harris) medium, with Dinger's ring/zone. The growth of the leptospires is at a maximum density at this zone. It is identified as an area of increased turbidity, beneath the surface of the semi-solid medium. It is the zone of optimum oxygen tension for the growth of the bacteria.

The treatment of choice is IV penicillin or IV ceftriaxone. Doxycycline 200 mg orally given once a week is effective in prophylaxis.

Other Options:

Option A:  Syphilis caused by Treponema pallidum, demonstrated by dark-field microscopy. It is the the most specific and sensitive technique to visualize the organism when an active chancre or condyloma lata is present.

Option C: Anthrax during microscopy of the smears shows bacilli arranged end to end in the form of long chains. This is called bamboo stick appearance. Under the low-power microscope, the edge of the colony is composed of long, interlacing chains of bacilli, resembling locks of matted hair, called Medusa head appearance.

Option D: Mycobacterium tuberculosis colonies on LJ medium are dry, rough, raised, irregular colonies with a wrinkled surface, tenacious, difficult to emulsify, creamy white and buff-colored. (Rough, tough, buff).
questions.learning: Leptospirosis — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of leptospirosis (Weil's disease). A microscopic agglutination test is used for the diagnosis of leptospirosis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In treatment, the V-Y procedure is employed for which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: The V-Y plasty is a fundamental reconstructive technique used in plastic and oculoplastic surgery, particularly for correcting cicatricial (scar-related) ectropion. Ectropion is a condition where the eyelid margins turn outward, exposing the bulbar conjunctiva. Cicatricial ectropion occurs when skin shortening or scarring pulls the eyelid away from the globe. The V-Y procedure involves making a V-shaped incision and closing it in a Y-shape; this effectively increases the length of the skin in the direction of the vertical stem of the Y, relieving the tension pulling the eyelid down. Option A (Entropion) is the inward turning of the lid, usually requiring different surgical procedures. Option C (Blepharophimosis) and Option D (Ptosis) are congenital or myogenic conditions involving lid drooping, requiring surgeries like levator resection or frontalis slings. The V-Y plasty is highly effective for localized skin deficiency and is a classic solution for lid malpositions caused by facial burns or trauma
questions.learning: The V-Y plasty is a fundamental reconstructive technique used in plastic and oculoplastic surgery, particularly for correcting cicatricial (scar-related) ectropion.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: At what CD4 count is Kaposi sarcoma likely to occur?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. <500/ μL

The likelihood of developing Kaposi sarcoma increases when absolute CD4 lymphocyte count is <500/ μL.

Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a vascular neoplasm caused by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV8) and is very common in patients suffering from acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). KS is considered to be an AIDS-defining disease.

AIDS-associated KS is an AIDS-defining illness and is the most common malignancy associated with HIV infection. Involvement of the oral cavity is most common in AIDS-related KS, but it can be seen in other variants also. Oral KS (OKS) most often involves the hard and soft palate, gingiva, and dorsal tongue with plaques or tumors. The color of the lesions may range from non-pigmented to brownish-red or violaceous.

Other forms of KS include

* Classic Kaposi sarcoma: It has the following three clinical stages patches, plaques, and nodules.

* Endemic African KS

* Transplant-associated KS is more common after solid organ transplant patients receive immunosuppression as compared to marrow or stem-cell transplant patients.

The given images show coalescent red-purple macules and plaques of the skin.

There is no definitive cure but KS is highly radiosensitive and achieves complete response in most cases. In AIDS‐associated KS, instituting highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) often (but not always) results in regression of KS. In localized cutaneous KS, excision and cryotherapy can be used. Intra-lesional administration of vinblastine, interferon‐α2b, and imiquimod is also effective.

One-liners about HIV

* Sexual contact is the least efficacious yet most common mode of spread of HIV infection

* ELISA is used for the detection of antibodies against viral proteins. This is the most sensitive and the best screening test for the diagnosis of AIDS.

* Western blot is the most specific or the confirmatory test for HIV.

* Candidiasis is the most common fungal infection in patients with AIDS.

* Cytomegalovirus (CMV) chorioretinitis exclusively in patients with CD4+ T cell counts less than 50 per microliter.

* Toxoplasma gondii causes encephalitis and is responsible for 50% of all mass lesions in the central nervous system.

* John Cunningham virus (JC virus) is a human papovavirus that causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy.

* Persistent diarrhea in AIDS is caused by Cryptosporidium, Isospora belli, or microsporidia.

* AIDS-dementia complex is the most common neurological manifestation of HIV infection.

* Inflammatory myopathy is the commonest skeletal muscle disorder in HIV.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents with features of adenoid facies and symptoms of a mild upper respiratory infection and is diagnosed with chronic adenoid hypertrophy. In view of this diagnosis and the need for definitive management, which surgical procedure is considered the most appropriate treatment for chronic adenoid hypertrophy in this patient?
questions.explanation: Chronic adenoid hypertrophy is a common condition in children and may present with adenoid facies, nasal obstruction, mouth breathing, and recurrent upper respiratory infections. When symptoms are persistent and significant, definitive management is surgical removal of adenoids (adenoidectomy). The standard and most commonly accepted technique for adenoidectomy, especially in exam settings, is curettage. In this method, a curette is used to remove hypertrophied adenoid tissue from the nasopharynx. It is simple, effective, widely practiced, and considered the conventional gold standard in many clinical and exam contexts. Why other options are wrong: (A) Coblator : A newer technique using radiofrequency ablation; effective but not the standard answer in most MCQs (B) Microdebrider : Endoscopic-assisted technique; more precise but not traditionally considered first-line in exams (D) Breathing exercise and symptomatic treatment : Not definitive for chronic hypertrophy with structural obstruction
questions.learning: Chronic adenoid hypertrophy is a common condition in children and may present with adenoid facies, nasal obstruction, mouth breathing, and recurrent upper respiratory infections.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the term used to describe the demise of a twin in the second trimester, accompanied by maceration? (NEET PG 2017)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Fetus Papyraceus

Fetus papyraceus refers to the compressed, mummified remains of a dead fetus retained in a multiple pregnancy after demise in the second trimester.

Pathogenesis:

• One twin dies in utero
• Dead fetus undergoes dehydration and compression between the uterine wall and surviving twin
• Produces a flattened, parchment-like fetus

Important distinction:

• Vanishing twin → early first-trimester fetal loss with resorption
• Fetus papyraceus → later fetal demise with retained macerated fetus

Complications:

• Preterm labor
• Coagulopathy (rare)
• Neurologic injury in surviving monochorionic twin due to shared circulation
questions.learning: Fetus Papyraceus Fetus papyraceus refers to the compressed, mummified remains of a dead fetus retained in a multiple pregnancy after demise in the second trimester.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
A female patient was diagnosed with gastric cancer. On immunohistopathology, the biopsy sample was found to be positive for CD117 and negative for LCA, cytokeratin, and S100. What is the diagnosis?

LCA - Leukocyte common antigen

GIST - Gastrointestinal stromal tumors

SCC - Squamous cell carcinoma
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. GIST

The given clinical scenario, along with the immunohistopathology findings showing positivity for CD117 and negativity for LCA, cytokeratin, and S100, is suggestive of gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST).

Other IHC markers mentioned are seen in:

• S-100: In melanoma (S-100,HMB-45,Melan-A).
• Cytokeratin: In squamous cell carcinoma (SCC).
• Leukocyte common antigen: In lymphomas.
questions.learning: GIST — The given clinical scenario, along with the immunohistopathology findings showing positivity for CD117 and negativity for LCA, cytokeratin, and S100, is suggestive of gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is not used for the identification of the facial nerve trunk?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Inferior belly of omohyoid muscle

The inferior belly of the omohyoid muscle is not used as an anatomical landmark for the identification of the facial nerve trunk.

There are two methods for localization of the facial nerve trunk:

1. Anterograde method: The facial nerve trunk is identified based on the anatomical landmarks after it exits from the stylomastoid foramen. This includes:

• Tragal pointer/Conley's pointer - It is the inferior portion of the cartilaginous canal. The facial nerve trunk lies 1 cm deep and inferior to its tip.
• Posterior belly of digastric - The facial nerve lies superior to the upper border of the muscle.
• Squamotympanic fissure - It is a fissure in the temporal bone, which runs from TMJ to the tympanic cavity. The facial nerve runs through this fissure.
• Styloid process - The facial nerve lies superficial to it.
• Mastoid process - Upon drilling it, the nerve is identified proximally.

2. Retrograde method: The main branches of the facial nerve trunk are identified and are then traced proximally until the main tunk is identified. Some branches used for tracing the facial nerve trunk include:

• Buccal branch - It lies in relation to the parotid gland.
• Marginal mandibular branch - It lies in relation to the facial vessels.
questions.learning: Inferior belly of omohyoid muscle — The inferior belly of the omohyoid muscle is not used as an anatomical landmark for the identification of the facial nerve trunk.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the composition of lactulose?
questions.explanation: Lactulose is a synthetic, non-absorbable disaccharide widely used as an osmotic laxative and in the management of hepatic encephalopathy. It is composed of the monosaccharides galactose and fructose. 1. Glucose + Galactose (Option A) forms lactose, the natural milk sugar. 2. Glucose + Fructose (Option B) forms sucrose (table sugar). 3. Fructose + Ribulose (Option D) is not a physiologically relevant disaccharide. Humans lack the intestinal enzyme (lactulase) required to digest lactulose, so it reaches the colon unchanged. Colonic bacteria ferment lactulose into short-chain organic acids (e.g., lactic and acetic acids), which acidify the colonic lumen. This acidic environment converts ammonia (NH₃) into ammonium (NH₄⁺), a non-absorbable form, thereby reducing systemic ammonia levels—the key mechanism in treating hepatic encephalopathy. Additionally, its osmotic effect draws water into the colon, producing a laxative action
questions.learning: Lactulose is a synthetic, non-absorbable disaccharide widely used as an osmotic laxative and in the management of hepatic encephalopathy. It is composed of the monosaccharides galactose and fructose.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding the procedure carried out using the instrument shown below?
options: A condensing lens is not required
It is used very close to the patient's eye as possible
A real, inverted image is seen
questions.explanation: The instrument shown is a "Direct Ophthalmoscope". One of its defining characteristics is that it produces a virtual, erect (upright) image of the retina. Therefore, statement C is false. In contrast, an indirect ophthalmoscope produces a real, inverted image. Direct ophthalmoscopy provides high magnification (approximately 15 times) but offers a limited field of view of about 10 degrees. Because it is a handheld device, it does not require a separate condensing lens (statement A), unlike indirect ophthalmoscopy which requires a 20D lens. To obtain the best view, the examiner must be as close to the patient's eye as possible (statement B). While easy to use and portable, the direct ophthalmoscope lacks stereopsis (3D depth perception), which is why indirect methods are preferred for detailed evaluations of the peripheral retina or when examining patients with cataracts
questions.learning: The instrument shown is a "Direct Ophthalmoscope". One of its defining characteristics is that it produces a virtual, erect (upright) image of the retina.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which type of refractive error is illustrated in the given image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Astigmatism

Astigmatism is a refractive error where light rays focus at different planes instead of a single point due to unequal curvature of the cornea or lens.

• Formation of two focal lines (not a point focus)
• Leads to blurred or distorted vision
• Can affect both near and distance vision

Optical concept: Produces conoid of Sturm with two principal meridians

Correction of astigmatism :

• Cylindrical lenses (aligned along specific meridian)
• Toric contact lenses or refractive surgery
