questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In a patient with pulmonary embolism causing complete obstruction of blood flow. Which of the following point on V/Q curve corresponds with given condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Point D

In pulmonary embolism with complete obstruction of blood flow, the affected lung region receives normal ventilation but zero perfusion, creating alveolar dead space. The V/Q ratio approaches infinity (V/Q → ∞).

The formula: V/Q = Ventilation/Perfusion = Normal/0 = ∞

At Point D:

• PO₂ ≈ 150 mmHg (approaches inspired air PO₂)
• PCO₂ ≈ 0 mmHg (no CO₂ delivered from blood)
• Alveolar gas resembles humidified inspired air
• No gas exchange occurs despite normal ventilation

Pulmonary embolism

↓

Blood flow blocked (Perfusion = 0)

↓

Alveoli still ventilated

↓

No gas exchange possible

↓

Alveolar gas ≈ Inspired air

↓

V/Q → ∞ (Dead space)

This represents pure dead space ventilation where air enters and exits the alveoli without participating in gas exchange, essentially wasting ventilation.
questions.learning: Point D — In pulmonary embolism with complete obstruction of blood flow, the affected lung region receives normal ventilation but zero perfusion, creating alveolar dead space.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient was brought to the emergency department after a road traffic accident. His CT scan is shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Subdural hemorrhage

The given CT image shows a crescent-shaped lesion that crosses suture lines and is indicative of acute subdural hematoma/hemorrhage.

Subdural hemorrhage (SDH) is a collection of blood between the dura and the arachnoid layers of the meninges. Most commonly, it results from the rupture of cortical bridging veins. Non-contrast CT is the investigation of choice.

Radiographic features of subdural hemorrhages:

* Crescent-like distribution around the periphery of the brain.

* They are not limited by sutures.

* Crescent-shaped hypodense lesion on axial CT: Chronic subdural hemorrhage

* Crescent-shaped hyperdense collections on CT: Acute subdural hemorrhage.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A person of eonism derives pleasure from __________.
options: Kissing and licking of anus by a sexual partner
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Wearing clothes of opposite sex

A person of eonism (transvestism) derives pleasure from wearing clothes of the opposite sex. It is usually found in males. His dress, manner, occupational interests, and associations are all designed to increase his feeling of being a woman.

Other options:

Sexual pleasure from

• Kissing and licking of anus by a sexual partner - Anilingus
• Sexual interest in nonliving objects that are used to generate sexual excitement.  -Fetichism
• Seeing a female undressing - Voyeurism or scoptophilia

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A vaccinated dog bites a person and causes bleeding. What is the category of rabies exposure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Category III

Rabies exposure is classified according to the WHO categories based on the type of contact with a suspected rabid animal. Any transdermal bite or scratch causing bleeding is Category III exposure, regardless of whether the dog is vaccinated or unvaccinated.

This is Category III exposure, which requires:

• Immediate wound washing
• Rabies vaccine (PEP)
• Rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) infiltration into the wound (if not previously vaccinated)

The vaccination status of the dog does not change the exposure category. It only influences subsequent management if the dog remains healthy during observation.

Why not the other options?

• A. Category I: Touching/feeding animals or licks on intact skin; no PEP required.
• B. Category II: Minor scratches or abrasions without bleeding; vaccine required but RIG not indicated.
• D. Category IV: No WHO Category IV exists.

| Category | Type of Exposure | Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP)

| -------- | ---------------- | -------------------------------

| Category I | Touching/feeding animals, licks on intact skin | No PEP

| Category II | Minor scratches/abrasions without bleeding, nibbling of uncovered skin | Rabies vaccine

| Category III | Single or multiple transdermal bites/scratches, bleeding, saliva on broken skin or mucosa, bat exposure | Wound washing + Rabies vaccine + RIG

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 15-year-old patient presents with a history of severe itching and recurrent eye. On examination, a shield ulcer is present, which has developed as a sequela of the underlying disease. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vernal keratoconjunctivitis

A 15-year-old with a history of severe itching and recurrent eye redness with shield ulcer points is highly suggestive of a diagnosis of Vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC).

VKC, also known as spring catarrh or warm weather conjunctivitis, is a recurrent inflammation of the conjunctiva with seasonal incidence, commonly occurring in individuals with an atopic background and seasonal allergies due to Th2 lymphocyte alteration followed by IgE response. It is a Type I hypersensitivity reaction.

Classical features of conjunctiva in VKC:

Palpebral VKC

* Cobblestone papillae: upper tarsal conjunctiva

* Associated with ropy discharge

* Maxwell–Lyon sign: pseudomembrane formation of the upper lid when everted and exposed to heat

* Limbal VKC: Horner–Trantas spots are white dots consisting of eosinophils and epithelial debris in the limbal area.

Corneal signs in VKC:

* Shield ulcers

* Vernal plaques

* Subepithelial scarring

* Pseudo-Gerontoxon resembles arcus senilis; it has a cupid's bow outline

The condition presents in three types, which are :

* Palpebral, affecting the upper tarsal conjunctiva, characterised by hypertrophied 'cobblestone' papillae

* Bulbar-limbal, characterised by dusky red triangular congestion of the conjunctiva, gelatinous limbal papillae and Horner-Tranta's spots that are formed due to eosinophils and epithelial debris at the limbus

* Mixed

Treatment of VKC includes allergen avoidance, antihistaminics, steroids, and immunomodulators both topical and systemic depending on the severity of the disease.

The image below represents Horner-Trantas spots.

The above image shows cobblestone appearance.

Other options:

Option B: Phlyctenular conjunctivitis presents with small whitish nodules at the limbus due to hypersensitivity (usually to TB or staphylococcus) and does not lead to shield ulcer formation.

Option C: A bacterial ulcer typically presents with acute pain, redness, watering, purulent discharge, and a corneal infiltrate, often with hypopyon in severe cases and not shield ulcer. The ulcer, in this case, is oval with an associated hypopyon (shown below)

Option D: Herpes simplex keratitis, a form of viral keratitis, is characterized by pain, watering, and photophobia. A distinctive feature is a dendritic ulcer on the cornea, which, upon fluorescein staining, reveals terminal bulbs.The below image shows the characteristic dendritic ulcers of herpes simplex keratitis.
questions.learning: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis — A 15-year-old with a history of severe itching and recurrent eye redness with shield ulcer points is highly suggestive of a diagnosis of Vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text:
Which of the following statements are true regarding mitochondrial DNA?

1. Higher rate of mutations as compared to the nuclear genome
2. Double-stranded circular DNA with about 16,000 base pairs
3. A slight change in nucleotide sequence as compared to cellular DNA
4. Encodes all electron transport chain proteins

(DNA - Deoxyribose nucleic acid)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 and 2

Statements 1 and 2 are true regarding mitochondrial DNA; it has a higher rate of mutations as compared to the nuclear genome and is a circular double-stranded DNA with about 16,000 base pairs.

Mitochondrial DNA is circular, double-stranded DNA composed of heavy and light chains and comprises about 1% of total cellular DNA. It contains about 16,569 base pairs and encodes about 13 protein subunits of the electron transport chain, of a total of about 67 protein subunits.

Its genetic code/ nucleotide sequence largely differs from that of the standard cellular code. For example, the standard stop codon UGA is read as tryptophan (Trp); in addition, few untranslated sequences exist and a very high mutation rate, about 5-10 times compared to that of nuclear DNA of the cell is observed.

As all mitochondria are contributed by the ovum during zygote formation, human mitochondrial DNA is transmitted by maternal non-mendelian inheritance. This is clinically significant because in diseases resulting from mutations of mitochondrial DNA, except in a few cases, an affected mother would pass the disease to all of her children but only her daughters would transmit the trait.

The below image shows the mitochondrial inheritance
questions.learning: 1 and 2 Statements 1 and 2 are true regarding mitochondrial DNA; it has a higher rate of mutations as compared to the nuclear genome and is a circular double-stranded DNA with about 16,000 base pairs.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient who engaged in strenuous exercise, skipped a meal, and later consumed alcohol at a party— which metabolic process is inhibited by alcohol intake in this scenario?
questions.explanation: Alcohol metabolism in the liver significantly increases the ratio of to . This high ratio shifts metabolic reactions away from producing glucose. Specifically, it diverts pyruvate to lactate and oxaloacetate to malate, effectively inhibiting gluconeogenesis. In the scenario provided, the patient has already depleted their glycogen stores through strenuous exercise and fasting (starvation). Since they cannot perform gluconeogenesis due to alcohol, they are at a very high risk of developing severe, life-threatening fasting hypoglycemia. Alcohol does not primarily inhibit glycogenolysis (Option B); in fact, the body would have already used this process up during exercise. The HMP shunt (Option C) and ketone body formation (Option D) are not the primary targets of alcohol-induced metabolic inhibition. Clinical awareness of this "starvation + alcohol" interaction is vital for emergency room physicians, as these patients may present as unconscious or "drunk" when they are actually suffering from profound hypoglycemia that requires immediate intravenous glucose

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient has cheilosis with koilonychia and anemia. Diagnosis is?
questions.explanation: Plummer-Vinson syndrome is characterized by a classic clinical triad: iron deficiency anemia, esophageal webs, and glossitis or cheilosis. Koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails) and cheilosis (cracking at the mouth corners) are physical signs resulting from severe, chronic iron deficiency. This condition is most common in middle-aged women and carries an increased risk of developing esophageal squamous cell carcinoma if left untreated. Esophageal cancer (Option B) may be a long-term complication but is not the primary diagnosis for this triad. Achalasia cardia (Option C) is a motility disorder that causes dysphagia but is not associated with anemia or iron-deficiency skin signs. Tylosis palmaris (Option D) is a genetic condition involving thickened skin on the palms and soles, which is also linked to esophageal cancer risk but unrelated to anemia. Therefore, the described findings are diagnostic of Plummer-Vinson syndrome

questions.text: The maternal mortality ratio is defined as?
options: Maternal Deaths per 10,000 women in reproductive age group
Maternal Deaths per 100,000 women in reproductive age group

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents to the outpatient department with a 3 cm breast lump located in the upper medial quadrant. The mass has an irregular, bosselated surface with mild ulceration of the overlying skin. Histopathological examination shows the provided features. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The histological finding of hypercellular stroma arranged in "leaf-like" projections into epithelial-lined clefts is diagnostic of a Phyllodes tumor. These tumors typically present as large, rapidly growing masses with an uneven, bosselated (lobulated) surface. Ulceration of the overlying skin can occur in aggressive or malignant variants. A galactocele (Option B) is a cystic, milk-filled mass seen in lactating women, which is smooth and non-ulcerated. Fibroadenoma (Option C) is benign and well-defined but lacks the stromal hypercellularity and leaf-like growth pattern. Paget's disease (Option D) involves the nipple-areolar complex with eczematous changes and is associated with underlying ductal carcinoma. Management for Phyllodes tumors requires wide local excision with a margin of healthy tissue or mastectomy, as they have a high tendency for local recurrence

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 33-year-old patient with a long history of tobacco chewing presents with a persistent whitish lesion in the gingivobuccal sulcus for the past seven months, raising suspicion of malignancy. What is the appropriate line of management for this patient?
questions.explanation: The presence of a persistent whitish lesion (leukoplakia) in the gingivobuccal sulcus, especially in a chronic tobacco user, is a classic precancerous presentation that necessitates definitive diagnosis. The correct management is an incisional or excisional biopsy to rule out squamous cell carcinoma or varying grades of dysplasia. "Wait and watch" (Option B) is dangerous and inappropriate, as a biopsy is the only way to confirm if malignancy is already present. Steroidal injections (Option C) are used for inflammatory conditions like lichen planus but would be ineffective and potentially mask the progression of a cancer. Sclerotherapy (Option D) is used for vascular malformations or varicose veins and has no role in the management of oral mucosal lesions. Therefore, given the high correlation between tobacco chewing and oral cancer, immediate biopsy via local excision is the only safe and professional course of action to ensure early detection and treatment
questions.learning: The presence of a persistent whitish lesion (leukoplakia) in the gingivobuccal sulcus, especially in a chronic tobacco user, is a classic precancerous presentation that necessitates definitive diagnosis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which part of renal tubules reabsorbs maximum water in the presence of ADH?
questions.explanation: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin) acts mainly on the late distal tubule and collecting duct, increasing their permeability to water by inserting aquaporin-2 channels into the tubular membrane. This allows maximum water reabsorption under the influence of ADH. Although a large amount of water (~65%) is reabsorbed in the PCT, this process is ADH-independent (obligatory reabsorption). The question specifically asks for water reabsorption in the presence of ADH, making the collecting duct the correct answer. Why other options are incorrect: (A) PCT: Reabsorbs maximum water overall, but not regulated by ADH (B) DCT: ADH has some effect, but less significant than in collecting duct (C) Loop of Henle: Descending limb is water-permeable but not under ADH control Thus, ADH-dependent maximal water reabsorption occurs in the collecting duct
questions.learning: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin) acts mainly on the late distal tubule and collecting duct, increasing their permeability to water by inserting aquaporin-2 channels into the tubular membrane.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 10-year-old girl who is not attending school presents for a health checkup, and her hemoglobin level is low. Which government program is most likely to provide significant health benefits for her condition?
questions.explanation: The Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK) is a comprehensive child health initiative of the Government of India aimed at the early identification and management of the “4 Ds”: Defects at birth, Diseases, Deficiencies, and Developmental delays (including disabilities). The program covers all children from birth to 18 years of age, including out-of-school children, making it especially relevant for vulnerable populations. In this case, the 10-year-old girl with anemia falls under the category of “Deficiencies”, one of the core components of RBSK. Therefore, she would be screened and managed by RBSK mobile health teams, with referral to District Early Intervention Centres (DEICs) when required, ensuring free treatment and follow-up care. Janani Suraksha Yojana (Option B) focuses on maternal health and institutional deliveries. The Mid-Day Meal Scheme (Option C) benefits only school-going children and does not cover out-of-school children. Navjat Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (Option D) is limited to newborn care and resuscitation. Thus, RBSK is the most appropriate program, as it ensures universal child health screening and management, particularly for nutritional deficiencies like anemia, regardless of school enrollment status

Correct answer: A. Symposium

A symposium is method of health communication and it comprises of a series of speeches on the topic with the chairman summarizing at the end.

A symposium is a series of speeches on a selected subject by experts. Each expert presents an aspect of the subject briefly, after which the audience is allowed to ask questions. There is no discussion among symposium members. The chairman makes a comprehensive summary at the end of the session.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: An infant presented in the surgical OPD with complaints of a unilateral swelling in the neck. The swelling was soft, cystic, partially compressible and brilliantly transilluminant. The most probable diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cystic hygroma

Cystic hygroma (also called cystic lymphangioma) is a congenital lymphatic malformation that typically presents in infancy or early childhood as a soft, cystic, painless neck swelling. It is partially compressible and brilliantly transilluminant, making it the classic diagnosis in this scenario.

Why not other options?

• A. Branchial fistula:

• Presents as a persistent sinus or external opening along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle with intermittent discharge, not as a transilluminant cystic swelling.

• B. Branchial cyst

• Usually presents in older children or young adults as a painless lateral neck swelling.
• It is not brilliantly transilluminant.

• D. Thyroglossal cyst

• Presents as a midline neck swelling that moves with deglutition and protrusion of the tongue.
• Usually not transilluminant.
questions.learning: Cystic hygroma Cystic hygroma (also called cystic lymphangioma) is a congenital lymphatic malformation that typically presents in infancy or early childhood as a soft, cystic, painless neck swelling.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Effacement of podocyte foot processes is seen in which of the following diseases?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Minimal change disease

Effacement of the podocyte foot processes is characteristically seen in minimal change disease (MCD), which is also called lipoid nephrosis.

It is also seen in other conditions such as membranous nephropathy and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. Since the podocytes are affected in these diseases, they are also known as podocytopathies.

The effacement of foot process can only be observed on electron microscopy.
questions.learning: Minimal change disease Effacement of the podocyte foot processes is characteristically seen in minimal change disease (MCD), which is also called lipoid nephrosis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A hypertensive patient is taking three antihypertensive medications, including diuretics, but his blood pressure is uncontrolled. In addition, he has hypokalaemia. Which of the following drugs should be prescribed to treat this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Eplerenone

The given clinical case with resistant hypertension and labs showing hypokalaemia suggests a diagnosis of primary hyperaldosteronism, which is treated with aldosterone receptor antagonists like spironolactone and eplerenone.

For the diagnosis of resistant hypertension, the patient should have uncontrolled hypertension despite taking three antihypertensive drugs, including at least one diuretic. Most patients with CKD/diabetes develop resistant hypertension.

While a calcium channel blocker, beta blocker, or alpha blocker can be part of the antihypertensive regimen, the inclusion of a diuretic is necessary for the diagnosis of resistant hypertension. The diuretic helps in addressing fluid retention, which is often a significant contributor to hypertension. Resistant hypertension is more common in patients aged >60 years than in younger patients. It may be related to nonadherence to therapy, obesity, and excessive alcohol intake. In the absence of a specific identifiable cause, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists like spironolactone have been found to be the most effective add-on drugs for the treatment of resistant hypertension.

Management of resistant hypertension according to NICE guidelines:

* Aldosterone antagonist (spironolactone) is to be used only when serum potassium is <4.5 mmol/L.

* A higher dose of thiazide is to be used only when serum potassium is >4.5 mmol/L.

* β-blocker or α1-blocker is to be considered only if an aldosterone antagonist or higher-dose thiazide is ineffective or not tolerated or contraindicated.

Primary hyperaldosteronism, also known as Conn’s syndrome, is characterized by excessive production of aldosterone by the adrenal glands, leading to sodium retention, potassium excretion, and subsequent hypertension. Drug-resistant hypertension is a hallmark of this condition. The initial test for this condition is the concurrent measurement of plasma renin and aldosterone, followed by the calculation of the aldosterone-renin ratio (ARR). The aldosterone-renin ratio is the most appropriate screening test for primary hyperaldosteronism; this can be followed by a saline infusion test, which is used to confirm the diagnosis of Conn’s syndrome.

Spironolactone has some significant adverse effects, especially in men (erectile dysfunction, gynecomastia, and benign prostatic hyperplasia).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A middle-aged man presents with a facial lesion and has a known history of acne rosacea. What is the most likely diagnosis of this condition?
questions.explanation: The image depicts rhinophyma, which is a slow-growing, benign enlargement of the nose characterized by sebaceous gland hyperplasia and fibrosis. This condition is the end-stage manifestation of phymatous acne rosacea, which explains the patient's medical history. The nose typically appears bulbous, pitted, and irregularly thickened. Rhinoscleroma (Option B) is a chronic granulomatous disease caused by Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis, presenting with "woody" hard nodules. Rhinosporidiosis (Option C) is a fungal infection (actually an aquatic protist) that causes leafy, strawberry-like vascular polyps. Scleroderma (Option D) causes the skin to become tight, shiny, and thin, which is the opposite of the thickened, pitted appearance of rhinophyma. Rhinophyma is primarily a cosmetic concern but can also lead to significant psychosocial distress and functional nasal obstruction. Treatment usually involves surgical shaving or CO2 laser resurfacing to restore the nasal contour

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A cattle farmer presents with a skin lesion on the arm. Gram staining of the lesion reveals gram- positive rod-shaped organisms, as shown in the image below. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: The clinical combination of an occupational history (cattle farmer) and a painless skin lesion with a characteristic central black eschar (malignant pustule) is pathognomonic for Cutaneous Anthrax. The microscopic identification of large, non-motile, gram-positive rods in chains (resembling bamboo sticks) further confirms the diagnosis of Bacillus anthracis. Bacillus cereus (Option A) also forms gram-positive rods but is primarily a cause of food poisoning. Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Option C) is a gram-negative rod associated with blue-green pus. Brucella abortus (Option D) is a small gram-negative coccobacillus that causes a systemic undulant fever. Anthrax is a zoonotic infection; its spores are highly resilient and found in soil or animal products. Management involves prompt administration of antibiotics like ciprofloxacin or doxycycline. If untreated, cutaneous anthrax can become systemic with high mortality. This case highlights the vital importance of matching clinical morphology with gram-stain characteristics and patient history
questions.learning: The clinical combination of an occupational history (cattle farmer) and a painless skin lesion with a characteristic central black eschar (malignant pustule) is pathognomonic for Cutaneous Anthrax.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 4-month-old infant who appeared healthy at birth is brought for evaluation of recurrent episodes of fasting hypoglycemia and progressive muscle weakness. The parents report that symptoms are most prominent after prolonged fasting, such as overnight. Physical examination reveals hepatomegaly. Laboratory investigations demonstrate elevated AST and ALT levels along with ketoacidosis (arterial pH 7.25). Liver biopsy shows excessive glycogen accumulation, accounting for approximately 8% of liver weight. A glucagon stimulation test is performed: • After a carbohydrate-rich meal: Blood glucose rises appropriately. • After an overnight fast: No significant increase in blood glucose is observed. Which enzyme deficiency best explains these findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Debranching enzyme

This infant most likely has glycogen storage disease type III (Cori/Forbes disease), caused by deficiency of the glycogen debranching enzyme.

The key findings are:

• Fasting hypoglycemia
• Hepatomegaly
• Elevated AST and ALT
• Ketosis/ketoacidosis
• Progressive muscle weakness
• Excess accumulation of structurally abnormal glycogen in the liver

Glucagon stimulation test

• After a carbohydrate-rich meal: Blood glucose rises because recently synthesized glycogen has relatively long outer chains. Glycogen phosphorylase can initially break these α-1,4 bonds and release glucose-1-phosphate.
• After an overnight fast: The outer glycogen chains have already been shortened to within four glucose residues of the branch points. Without the debranching enzyme, further glycogen breakdown cannot occur, so glucagon produces little or no rise in blood glucose.

This characteristic response supports debranching enzyme deficiency.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• B. Muscle glycogen phosphorylase: Causes McArdle disease, presenting with exercise intolerance, muscle cramps, and myoglobinuria. It does not cause hepatomegaly or fasting hypoglycemia.
• C. Glucose-6-phosphatase: Causes von Gierke disease. It produces severe fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, and hyperlipidemia, but muscle weakness is not a prominent feature. Glucagon fails to raise blood glucose in both fed and fasting states.
• D. Liver glycogen phosphorylase: Causes Hers disease. It leads to mild fasting hypoglycemia, ketosis, and hepatomegaly but generally does not cause progressive muscle weakness.
questions.learning: Debranching enzyme — This infant most likely has glycogen storage disease type III (Cori/Forbes disease), caused by deficiency of the glycogen debranching enzyme.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 20-year-old woman presents with breathlessness and chest pain. She is a known case of mitral stenosis. Her pulse is irregularly irregular. No thrombus is seen on echocardiography. What is the best agent to prevent future thrombotic events?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Oral warfarin

The clinical presentation of breathlessness, chest pain, and irregularly irregular pulse is suggestive of atrial fibrillation. Since the patient is having mitral stenosis oral warfarin is the best agent to reduce the risk of thrombotic events.

Anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation:

Anticoagulation is indicated for patients with mitral stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, previous history of stroke. In nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, the risk of stroke and the need for anticoagulation is assessed with the CHA2DS2-VASc score.

Anticoagulants that can be used include:

• Vitamin K antagonist - Warfarin
• Antithrombin inhibitor - Dabigatran
• Factor Xa inhibitors - Rivaroxaban, Apixaban, and Edoxaban

In AF patients with rheumatic mitral stenosis or mechanical heart valves, the anticoagulant of choice is warfarin. The newer anticoagulants are not yet tested for rheumatic heart disease.

Warfarin is a less compliant drug because it requires routine PT/INR monitoring for dose adjustments and has many drug interactions. The newer oral anticoagulants are easy to use and do not require PT/INR monitoring for dose adjustments.

Bleeding is an important risk of anticoagulation. The newer oral agents have a lower risk of intracranial bleeding when compared to warfarin. The risk factors for bleeding include age >65–75 years, renal insufficiency, heart failure, prior bleeding, and excessive alcohol or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug use.

Reversal agents for anticoagulants are as follows:

• Warfarin - Vitamin K and fresh frozen plasma
• Dabigatran - Idarucizumab
• Factor Xa inhibitors - Andexanet alpha and Ciraparantag
questions.learning: Oral warfarin — The clinical presentation of breathlessness, chest pain, and irregularly irregular pulse is suggestive of atrial fibrillation. Since the patient is having mitral stenosis oral warfarin is the best agent to reduce the risk of thrombotic events.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A man regularly derives sexual gratification by inflicting pain upon his partner. He would often produce cuts and cigarette burns on his partner's arms. This is best described as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sadism

The given scenario is suggestive of sexual sadism. It is seen more commonly in men. It develops due to early experiences of brutality in sex.

The sadist may bite, beat, whip, produce cuts or cigarette burns etc on their sexual partner. In extreme cases, the victim's nipples may be bitten off, items such as a bottle or sticks are inserted into the vagina. Blunt trauma causing fractures and rupture of internal organs may also be seen.

Other options:

Option A - Voyeurism: it is the act of obtaining sexual gratification by observing an unsuspecting person who is naked, disrobing or engaging in sexual activity.

Option B - Fetishism: it is a form of sexual behaviour in which gratification is associated with an abnormal stimulus which may be an object, activity or part of the body.

Option D - Masochism: this is opposite to sadism. Sexual gratification is obtained by suffering the pain.
questions.learning: Sadism — The given scenario is suggestive of sexual sadism. It develops due to early experiences of brutality in sex.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 65-year-old patient presents with shortness of breath and chest pain. Examination reveals reduced breath sounds on the right side, and chest X-ray shows a right-sided pleural effusion. Which factor is most likely responsible for the development of an exudative pleural effusion in this patient?
questions.explanation: Pleural effusions are classified into transudates and exudates based on Light's criteria. Transudates result from systemic factors that alter hydrostatic or oncotic pressure, whereas exudates result from local inflammatory processes that increase capillary permeability. Heart failure (Option A), liver failure (Option B), and nephrotic syndrome (Option D) all cause transudative effusions due to increased venous pressure or decreased serum albumin. Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an inflammatory systemic disease that can cause localized inflammation of the pleura, resulting in an exudative effusion. Characteristically, RA-related effusions have very low glucose levels, high LDH, and a low pH. Other causes of exudates include infections (pneumonia, TB), malignancies, and pulmonary embolism. Given the 65-year-old patient's acute presentation, identifying the nature of the fluid through thoracentesis is crucial. Since RA causes pleural inflammation, it is a recognized cause of exudative effusion, unlike the other three options which typically produce clear, protein-poor transudative fluid
questions.learning: Pleural effusions are classified into transudates and exudates based on Light's criteria. Transudates result from systemic factors that alter hydrostatic or oncotic pressure, whereas exudates result from local inflammatory processes that increase capillary…

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A boy presented with a fever and chills. Rapid test was positive for specific antigen HRP-2. Which of the following species of Plasmodium is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Plasmodium falciparum

The given clinical scenario and the HRP-2 positivity are suggestive of P. falciparum malaria.

Malaria is a parasitic infection caused by the Plasmodium species transmitted by the Anopheles mosquito. It is characterized by many nonspecific symptoms, including but not limited to tachycardia, tachypnea, chills, malaise, fatigue, diaphoresis (sweating), and headache. The fever of malaria is characterized by periodicity depending on the infective Plasmodium species. The fever returns every other day for P. vivax, P. ovale, and P. falciparum, and every three days for P. malariae.

The newer tests include rapid antigen detection tests that employ immunochromatographic methods. The parasite-F test is one of them. This test is based on the detection of histidine-rich protein-2 (HRP-2) which is produced only by the asexual forms of Plasmodium falciparum that are present on the surface of RBCs. The test strip has monoclonal antibodies against the HRP-2 antigen. This test has very high sensitivity and specificity. The disadvantages of the test include that it can detect only Plasmodium falciparum HRP-2 antigen but not the other three species of Plasmodium. Also, the test remains positive until 2 weeks after the cure.

Another diagnostic test of significance is the dual antigen test. This test detects both the parasite lactate dehydrogenase of trophozoites and gametocytes of all the Plasmodium species and HRP-2 produced by P. falciparum simultaneously.
questions.learning: Plasmodium falciparum — The given clinical scenario and the HRP-2 positivity are suggestive of P. falciparum malaria. Malaria is a parasitic infection caused by the Plasmodium species transmitted by the Anopheles mosquito.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following ultrasound findings is diagnostic of polycystic ovarian morphology?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. ≥20 follicles in one ovary

The international diagnostic guidelines for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)—specifically the updated consensus recommendations—define Polycystic Ovarian Morphology (PCOM) by the presence of 20 or more follicles (measuring 2–9 mm) in at least one ovary when using high-resolution transvaginal ultrasound transducers (>8 MHz). Alternatively, an ovarian volume of >10 mL in at least one ovary satisfies the definition. It does not require both ovaries to meet the threshold simultaneously

High-Yield Points

• Current cutoff: ≥20 follicles in one ovary (using high-frequency transvaginal ultrasound ≥8 MHz).
• Older Rotterdam criterion (2003): ≥12 follicles and/or ovarian volume >10 mL.
• Only one ovary needs to meet the criterion.
• PCOM alone does not diagnose PCOS; diagnosis requires fulfillment of accepted PCOS diagnostic criteria after excluding other causes.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: While calculating the ‘total dependency ratio’, which one of the following is used in the denominator?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Population 15 to 64 years

The Total Dependency Ratio (TDR) measures the burden of the dependent population on the working-age population.

Formula:

• Total Dependency Ratio = [(Population 0–14 years + Population ≥65 years) ÷ Population 15–64 years] × 100

Why is C. correct?

• Population 15–64 years forms the denominator because it represents the economically productive (working-age) population.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In the civil negligence case against a doctor who bears the onus of proof?
options: Police not under rank of sub inspector
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Patient

In the case of civil negligence, the burden of proof is on the patient.

The question of civil negligence arises when a suit is filed in a civil court:

• By a patient or his/her relatives against the doctor for getting compensation from the doctor if he/she has suffered an injury due to the doctor's negligence.
• By a doctor against the patient or his/her relatives to collect the fees, the payment of which has been refused due to alleged professional negligence by the doctor.

In either case, the patient has to prove that the doctor has committed professional negligence.

To prove negligence, all the following four elements must be present:

• Duty - A duty of care by the doctor must exist.
• Dereliction - The physician must maintain the standard of a 'prudent physician' under similar circumstances. If the physician fails to maintain the standard of care, it is called dereliction.
• Direct causation - The negligent act or omission must directly cause the injury without any intervening cause.
• Damage - The negligent act must cause damage of a type that would have been foreseen by a reasonable physician.
questions.learning: Patient — In the case of civil negligence, the burden of proof is on the patient. The question of civil negligence arises when a suit is filed in a civil court: • By a patient or his/her relatives against the doctor for getting compensation from the doctor…

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient presented with chronic knee pain but has no history of trauma. Identify the condition shown in the radiograph below and the appropriate management.
options: Bipartite fracture patella, X-ray of other knee
Fracture of upper pole of patella, Cylindrical cast
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bipartite fracture patella, X-ray of other knee

The given X-Ray shows a patella with a smooth discontinuity suggestive of an unfused accessory ossification center. Since this should arouse the suspicion of a bipartite patella, appropriate management would be to take an X-Ray of the other knee.

A bipartite patella (two-part patella) is a patella with an unfused accessory ossification centre, typically at the superolateral aspect. It usually is asymptomatic and is noted incidentally, however pain, when present, can be caused by overuse (such as in a cyclist or climber).

There are three types of bipartite patella

1. Type I (5%) occurs at the inferior pole
2. Type II (20%) occurs along the entire lateral border of the patella
3. Type III (75%) the most common type, occurs as an elliptical area in the superolateral portion of the patella

Depending on the number of fragments they may be classified as bipartite, tripartite or multipartite. For diagnosis, a conventional skyline view is followed by a skyline view with the patient in a squatting weight-bearing position to assess if the pain is caused by a nonunion at the bipartite site. If the gap is higher in the squatting weight-bearing posture than in the standard skyline view, the test result is considered positive. MRI is not required to diagnose the condition.

If pain occur with a bipartite patella, limiting and restricting activity, correcting the activity that is causing an overuse syndrome, and prescribing nonsteroidal antiinflammatory agents can result in improvement in 3 weeks. Operative treatment with the Ogata technique is rarely necessary.
questions.learning: Bipartite fracture patella, X-ray of other knee — The given X-Ray shows a patella with a smooth discontinuity suggestive of an unfused accessory ossification center.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Following complete ileal and partial jejunal resection, the patient is most likely to have
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin B12 deficiency

After complete ileal and partial jejunal resection, the patient is likely to have vitamin B12 deficiency.

Vitamin B12 is absorbed in the ileum. B12 binds to intrinsic factor, a protein secreted by the parietal cells of the stomach, and the complex is absorbed across the ileal mucosa. Hence after ileal resection, there is impaired absorption of vitamin B12.

Clinical features of megaloblastic anemia (cyanocobalamin and folate deficiency):

System
Clinical features

Oral

Glossitis

Angular cheilosis

Gastrointestinal

Anorexia

Weight loss

Diarrhea

Constipation

Skin
Hyperpigmentation (reversible)

Hematological

Thrombocytopenia

Leucopenia

Ineffective erythropoiesis and unconjugated jaundice

Cardiovascular

Atherosclerosis leading to PVD, CAD (due to elevated homocysteine)

Neurological (only B12)

Peripheral neuropathy

Subacute combined degeneration (degeneration of the posterior and pyramidal tracts of the spinal cord)

Pregnancy (only folate)

Recurrent fetal loss

Neural tube defects

Others

Mild fever in severe cases

Psychiatric disturbances

Peripheral smear findings:

* Macro-ovalocytes are seen.

* Most macrocytes lack the central pallor of normal red cells and even appear hyperchromic, but the MCHC is not elevated.

* Reticulocyte count is low.

* Nucleated red cell progenitors occasionally appear in the circulating blood when anemia is severe.

* Neutrophils are also larger than normal (macro polymorphonuclear) and show nuclear hypersegmentation, with five or more nuclear lobules.

Bone marrow findings:

* Markedly hypercellular as a result of increased hematopoietic precursors

* Sieve-like pattern of chromatin of immature precursors (Megaloblasts)

* Granulocytic precursors display dysmaturation in the form of giant metamyelocytes and band forms

* Megakaryocytes abnormally large and have bizarre, multilobate nuclei

* Derangement in DNA synthesis causes most precursors to undergo apoptosis in the marrow (ineffective hematopoiesis) and leads to pancytopenia

Pearl PF1304: Major Sites of Absorption of Hematopoietic Factors

* Duodenum + upper jejunum: Iron

* Jejunum: Folate

* Terminal Ileum: Vitamin B12

Mnemonic - Dude Is Just Feeling Ill Bro
questions.learning: Vitamin B12 deficiency After complete ileal and partial jejunal resection, the patient is likely to have vitamin B12 deficiency. Vitamin B12 is absorbed in the ileum.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: As a senior resident in the OBG department, You would consider uterine artery embolization as a treatment option in all of the following cases except ________
options: Prior to the removal of Placenta accreta in Multiparous woman
Patient diagnosed with calcified and pedunculated submucous fibroids
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Patient diagnosed with calcified and pedunculated submucous fibroids

Uterine artery embolization is indicated in all the above-given cases except in a patient with calcified and pedunculated submucous fibroids.

A calcified fibroid does not shrink with the procedure. The pedunculated fibroids can fall off after the procedure resulting in intrauterine or peritoneal infections.

Hence, the calcified, submucous, and subserous types of fibroids are contraindications for this procedure.

Other indications for Uterine artery embolization(UAE) include,

* Postpartum hemorrhage.

* Placenta accreta to reduce bleeding prior to placental removal, or caesarean delivery.

* This technique is most suited for menorrhagia in a multiparous woman

Technique:

* Under local sedation, bilateral UAE is approached through percutaneous femoral catheterization.

* It is done using polyvinyl alcohol (PVA), gel foam particles or metal coils.

Embolization reduces vascularity and the size of the fibroid in 3–4 months

Advantages of UAE:

* No major surgery.

* No intraoperative bleeding.

* Short hospital stay.

* Less abdominal adhesions.

Pearl PF1535: Contraindications to Uterine artery embolization

Absolute contraindications:

* GnRH agonist use

* Asymptomatic fibroids

* Pregnancy

* Pelvic inflammatory disease

* Uterine malignancy

* Calcified fibroid

Relative contraindications:

* A desire for future pregnancy: Poor uterine perfusion and pelvic adhesions following UAE would negatively impact fertility, and result in obstetric complications or adverse fetal effects.

* Postmenopausal status: The procedure is indicated primarily for premenopausal women since fibroids tend to decrease in size and symptoms improve or resolve after menopause. An enlarging uterus after menopause should raise the suspicion of malignancy and careful follow-up is warranted.

* Subserosal or submucosal fibroids: They are pedunculated and may detach either intraperitoneally or within the uterine cavity. Detachment may be associated with sterile peritonitis or intrauterine infection.

* Size or number of fibroids: The volume of necrosis after UAE in a large fibroid uterus can be substantial with a proportionate level of postprocedural pain and risk of infection.

* Contraindications to radiologic contrast agents.
questions.learning: Patient diagnosed with calcified and pedunculated submucous fibroids Uterine artery embolization is indicated in all the above-given cases except in a patient with calcified and pedunculated submucous fibroids.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-year-old child presents with diarrhea and weight loss. On examination, the height and weight are lesser than expected. Laboratory investigations were positive for class II HLA-DQ2. Which of the following will you advise the child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Gluten-free diet

The clinical scenario of diarrhea, steatorrhea, weight loss, and growth retardation, along with positive class II HLA-DQ2, is consistent with a diagnosis of celiac disease. Patients with celiac disease are advised to avoid gluten.

The dietary recommendation for celiac disease is as follows:

Diet avoided (gluten)

“BROW”

Diet Allowed

“So MRP ”

Barley
Soya bean

Rye
Maize

Oats
Rice

Wheat
Potato

Celiac disease/celiac sprue/gluten-sensitive enteropathy is an immune-mediated disorder triggered by gluten-containing foods. The presence of one of the two locus antigens HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8 is necessary, but not sufficient for the development of this condition. Detection of these is not useful for the diagnosis, however, their absence helps to exclude celiac disease.

The pathogenesis involves an inflammatory response to gluten and gliadin (gluten-derived peptide). In the small intestine, gliadin is deamidated by the tissue transglutaminase (tTG), an intestinal enzyme. The deamidated gliadin is more immunogenic and is presented to helper T cells, which mediate mucosal inflammation and cause tissue damage.

Children usually present with diarrhea, weight loss, and growth failure. Other features include malabsorption, bloating, irregular bowel habits, iron deficiency anemia, osteoporosis, ataxia, and abnormal liver enzymes.

Screening for celiac disease is done by testing for serum antibodies, including tissue transglutaminase IgA, anti-endomysial, and deaminated anti-gliadin antibodies. The diagnosis in patients with positive antibodies is confirmed by biopsy of the second part of the duodenum or proximal jejunum. Microscopic findings of biopsy show intraepithelial CD8+ lymphocytes, villous atrophy, and crypt hyperplasia.

The image given below shows microscopic findings seen in celiac disease.

Other options:

Option A: Fat-free diet is advised for various disorders causing steatorrhea. These include pancreatic insufficiency, cystic fibrosis, and familial hypercholesterolemia.

Option B: Lactose-free diet is advised for lactose intolerance. It occurs due to lactase deficiency. Patients usually present with diarrhea, abdominal pain, gassiness, and bloating. A lactose tolerance test or breath hydrogen test may be used for the diagnosis.

Option C: Low-carbohydrate diet is advised for diabetes mellitus.
questions.learning: Gluten-free diet — The clinical scenario of diarrhea, steatorrhea, weight loss, and growth retardation, along with positive class II HLA-DQ2, is consistent with a diagnosis of celiac disease.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a class of 75 students, 80% received the measles vaccine. After one student contracted measles, 12 more students were infected due to exposure. What is the secondary attack rate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 86%

The secondary attack rate is 86%.

To calculate the secondary attack rate, we first determine the number of susceptible students, which is the total class size (75) minus the immunized students (80% of 75 = 60 students), leaving 15 susceptible students. We also have to subtract the student who was primary case from the susceptible individuals (15-1=14).

Secondary attack rate = (Number of exposed persons developing the disease within the range of incubation period)/ (Total number of exposed or susceptible contacts) x 100.

= 12/14 x 100 = 86%

This gives a secondary attack rate of 86%, meaning that 86% of the susceptible students who were exposed to the primary measles case contracted the disease. This rate reflects the transmission efficiency of the disease among susceptible individuals in the class.

Pearl PF0956: Morbidity Measurements in Epidemiology

Morbidity Measurements in Epidemiology

Incidence rate = ( Number of new cases of a disease in a specified period of time/Population at risk during that time ) x 1000

Incidence rate of spells of sickness = ( Number of spells of sickness starting in a specified period /Mean number of people exposed to that risk in the specified time ) x 1000

Attack rate = ( Number of new cases of a disease in a specified period of time /Total population at risk during the given time ) x 100

Secondary attack rate = ( Number of exposed persons developing the disease within the range of the incubation period/Total number of exposed or susceptible contacts ) x 100

Prevalence = ( Number of all cases (new+old) of a specified disease at a given point in time/ Estimated population at the same point in time ) x 100
questions.learning: 86% The secondary attack rate is 86%. To calculate the secondary attack rate, we first determine the number of susceptible students, which is the total class size (75) minus the immunized students (80% of 75 = 60 students), leaving 15 susceptible students.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 28-year-old lactating female presents 2 weeks after delivery, with a 3 cm subareolar mass in her right breast. The mass is associated with redness, tenderness, and mild warmth. She reports no fever but mentions difficulty in breastfeeding from the affected breast. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lactation Mastitis

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of lactational mastitis.

Lactational mastitis is caused by a local bacterial infection when the breast is most vulnerable due to cracks and fissures in the nipples.

Mastitis occurs due to a combination of factors such as inadequate milk drainage and the introduction of bacteria present on the skin. The cracks in the nipple serve as an entry point, thus resulting in infection. The most common organism causing acute mastitis is Staphylococcus aureus.

Acute bacterial mastitis typically occurs during the 1st month of breastfeeding (lactational breast abscess).

Staphylococcal acute mastitis typically results in localized abscesses. Signs and symptoms of this condition involve:

* Fever and malaise

* Localized pain and tenderness

* Redness and swelling of the affected breast

* Fluctuation test positive due to pus in the abscess. It is a late sign.

Management includes analgesia, continued expression from the breast, antibiotics such as amoxiclav, and repeated aspiration of pus. In case of aspiration and antibiotics failure, incision and drainage can be done.

Other Options:

Option A: Mondor’s disease is characterized by thrombophlebitis of the superficial veins of the breast and anterior chest wall.

Option B: Breast abscess is a sequela of untreated bacterial mastitis, which occurs due to the growth of staphylococcus or streptococcus due to breast milk stasis. Patients usually present with fever and malaise, localised pain and tenderness, redness and swelling of the affected breast and fluctuation test positive due to pus in the abscess, which is a late sign of breast abscess.

Option C: A galactocele is a milk-filled cavity in the breast of a woman who is usually lactating. It can be caused due to lactation problems, prolactin stimulation by drugs, or duct obstruction. It presents as a palpable, round, well-circumscribed, and freely mobile mass with no fever, pain, or inflammation. It is usually subareolar and unilateral.
questions.learning: Lactation Mastitis — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of lactational mastitis. Lactational mastitis is caused by a local bacterial infection when the breast is most vulnerable due to cracks and fissures in the nipples.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 38-year-old male presents to the outpatient clinic with complaints of excessive stress and difficulty maintaining a work-life balance. On examination, his blood pressure is 150/100 mm Hg. His fasting blood glucose is 150 mg/dL and he is slightly overweight. He has no significant past medical history and is not on any medications. Physical examination is otherwise unremarkable. What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
options: Advise rest and no pharmacological treatment is required
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Start telmisartan

This patient has Stage 2 hypertension (150/100 mm Hg) with metabolic risk factors (diabetes, overweight).

Guidelines recommend immediate pharmacologic therapy plus lifestyle modification for BP ≥140/90 mm Hg.

Telmisartan (ARB) is appropriate as it provides BP control and metabolic/renal protection, especially in diabetics.

Lifestyle measures alone are insufficient, and tirzepatide or steroids are not indicated for BP control.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 32-year-old pregnant woman attends a routine antenatal visit at 28 weeks of gestation. She has a history of obesity but no prior diagnosis of diabetes. Her fasting plasma glucose is 104 mg/ dL, and her 2-hour plasma glucose level following a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) is 167 mg/dL. Based on these results, what is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Start lifestyle modifications and repeat OGTT at 32 weeks gestation.
Diagnose her with pre-existing diabetes and initiate insulin therapy.
Diagnose her with GDM and initiate dietary modifications with close monitoring of blood glucose levels.
Monitor her closely without intervention since her glucose levels are borderline.
questions.explanation: According to standard diagnostic criteria, Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) is diagnosed if the fasting plasma glucose is mg/dL or the 2-hour post-OGTT level is mg/dL. This patient meets both criteria ( mg/dL and mg/dL), confirming a diagnosis of GDM. The immediate next step is dietary and lifestyle modifications combined with frequent blood glucose monitoring to ensure levels stay within the target range. Regarding the distractors, repeating the test (Option A) is unnecessary as the diagnosis is already established. Pre-existing diabetes (Option B) requires much higher thresholds (fasting mg/dL) and history before conception. Simply monitoring without intervention (Option D) is inappropriate, as uncontrolled GDM increases the risk of macrosomia and other fetal complications. Thus, the establishment of a management plan for GDM is required

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the investigation of choice in a 55-year-old woman who presents with post-menopausal bleed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Endometrial biopsy

Endometrial biopsy is the investigation of choice in a case of post-menopausal bleed, as the chances of endometrial cancer are quite high.

For those who undergo TVUS (transvaginal USG) and have an EEC (endometrial echo complex) >4 mm, localized thickening, or an indistinct or nonvisible EEC, endometrial sampling is a reasonable next step.

Investigations for endometrial carcinoma include:

* Endometrial aspiration biopsy is the first investigation for abnormal uterine bleeding, especially in females >35 years.

* Dilatation and fractional curettage was the best method to diagnose but now it is not used.

* Hysteroscopy and biopsy: The investigation of choice for endometrial cancer.

* Transvaginal USG is used as an adjunct to endometrial biopsy.

* A Pap smear is not reliable to diagnose endometrial carcinoma. It is more useful as a screening tool rather than a diagnostic tool.

If symptoms of postmenopausal bleeding persist, imaging of the endometrial cavity should be performed with one or a combination of the following: TVUS, contrast sonography, or hysteroscopy.

Note: Surgical staging is the gold standard investigation for staging endometrial carcinoma.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The best method of teaching an urban slum about ORS is ________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Demonstration

The best method of teaching an urban slum about ORS is by demonstration.

* Demonstration is a carefully prepared presentation on how to perform a certain task or skill or procedure.

* It shows the step by step process of a task.

* Demonstration arouses interest and incites ‘learning by doing,’ and ‘seeing is believing’ philosophies.
